I finished this game many times, on various difficulties and finally decided to do my own review of this game. Rise of the Tomb Raider continues where previous game ended, and as a part of trilogy it have to be review as such. Lara is older, more confident at herself, more skillful hunter and warrior. Story continues from the previous game, its all about stopping Trinity but this time she is hunting them. Rise of Tomb Raider is focused more about killing enemies and less about surviving, some part of the game has so many enemies it feels like a third person shooter. Maps are lot bigger with lot more things to do, hunting animals, birds, deer, wolves and collect crafting materials to upgrade your weapons and skills. At her camp Lara now has dozens different outfits she can wear, each giving her different bonuses, skills have also advanced with more options to choose from. During the game there are lot of side quests to complete, they are not mandatory but each giving you nice reward. Maps have lot more crypts and tombs to complete, they are lot bigger now, with more things to do, challenge tombs are more difficult ones but rewarding :) Rise Of Tomb Raider is a big game, took me 28 hours on my first playthrough, alot bigger then previous Tomb Raider game. Of course you can rush it and do it faster, but if you are looking for better gear grinding will consume so much more time. DLCs are mostly good and worth picking up. Mostly, because some are very short only one side quest, but some of them are really big and worth your money. My favorite DLCs are Blood Ties and Baba Yaga which is the biggest DLC for this game. I really enjoyed playing Rise Of the Tomb Raider, I still do, big game with lots of improvements, good storyline lot of collectables and hidden places to discover. This is my favorite Tomb Raider from the rebooted trilogy. Only thing I don`t like is that sometimes it feels there is too much shooting and less exploring to do. After all, this is Tomb Raider game and it should feel like Tomb Raider, exploring and solving puzzles....

A unique experience, oddly apropos of 2020 with its mysteriously pandemic-ravaged landscape and plot centered on the uncertainty of American presidential leadership. This game has certainly found its own jam. Through its obviously very high production values (realistic celebrity appearances and all) it will lend its hand eagerly as it guides you through its bizarre setup, plot, and core mechanics as it eventually makes a poignant statement about the importance of human connection, both intimate and at scale. And it succeeds, I think, and not cheaply - it won't convince everybody to come along for the ride, but those who keep with it will have an experience not to be soon forgotten. (+) Visually stunning (+) Very, very good voice acting (+) Manages to make a compelling central gameplay mechanic out of what would, with different treatment, be just a list of chores. As a result, you will build a lot of empathy by overcoming the challenges you face in completing these "chores," while listening to running commentary by the main character, Sam (++) Exceptionally clever multiplayer component (mind you, this is a single-player game). Not only is it simple and satisfying to engage with, but it also fits brilliantly into the overall narrative. (+) Ultimately the plot builds to an engaging final act, with a number of satisfying (and tear-jerker) moments (+/-) Many fantastical, film-like cutscenes that are as impressive as they are indulgent. (+/-) Complex story with loads of supernatural sci-fi elements for which explanations arrive slowly, or not at all. (Possibly as compensation: much of the dialog is overly expository - thank god?) (-) A slow first act means the game takes awhile to find its groove. (-) An overwrought score and rewards system that hardly seemed worth paying attention to.

DBD is a game with an at times grossly strict meta, a toxic array of people to encounter, pricey cosmetics and window techs. Despite this I have sunk 470 hours into it and plan to sink many more. It's fun enough, better with friends, there's plenty to do (see: Bloodwebs going on forever when Survs get shit all BPs) and it improves tenfold as you learn more about what to do, how to do it, and when. The game is deceptively simple with a fun layer of mind-games and counter-play hidden in it if you reach higher ranks and learn about the ins-and-outs. I can't play it for hours and sometimes I want to punch my teammates in the head, but being grabbed by a Scratched Mirror Myers on Lery's and shitting yourself makes it worth it. This is by no means a perfect game, but it is worth the experience of asymmetrical horror at the very least, and has potential for some. Pick it up on sale, get BBQ&Chilli, you're in business. P.S- If you're new and pick this game up to play with experienced friends you're going to suffer for at least 10 hours. The game has a reasonable learning curve (counter this with YT videos or Twitch marathons) and the matchmaking system currently favours the highest ranked person, meaning you'll most often be versing much more experienced people just to play with your mates. Try not to let it dishearten you, your first interaction with DBD won't be your best. P.P.S- Don't attempt to free yourself off the hook as a given, it's situational. I learned that the hard way.

This game saved my life. I am 27. My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old. When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide. After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side. Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay. After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as. Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends. I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together. Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that. Thank you

Where to begin. This is the most fresh and fun entry into the RTS genre I've come across in the last.. 5-10 years. No other RTS has got me binging 12 hours over 3 or so days. It takes the solid/proven base building and resource gathering mechanics that we've seen across numerous titles, then picks and chooses a unique combination of them. They then instill in you a tangible sense of dread and put on its head all of the feelings you get from regular RTS games, creating something really quite different. Yes, the entry is rough as there's no tutorial, so I can imagine that without having friends to explain the basics it would be a very difficult start, and yes the unit pathing can be frustrating occasionally, and yes there's some simple features to be added... ...but this is early access for a reason. I do think the default price is a bit steep given that fact, but it is of a decent enough quality that it deserves an early access title, unlike so many cash grabbers releasing buggy nonsense. Looking forward to seeing the extra polish come along, but shall enjoy it in the mean time! EDIT: Over a year later - loved everything they've added in between. Campaign is pretty good - some rather mundane hero missions that are grindy at the best of times, but loved the progression, the map types, the research tree - all very well thought out and is a great experience to progress through. This game isn't for everyone. I personally cannot continue, not because it is hard, but because it is boring. I'm doing a melee build, and there are three parts to combat: move, roll, strike. Power attacks are inefficient and slow. Blocking is worse than rolling %90 of the time. Parrying is unecessary. Weapon arts are a good idea, but poorly implemented. Compare this to a game that most people say is an inferior knock-off: The Surge. While being a soulslike, The Surge had limb targeting, stamina, energy meters, and brutal executions customized to each body part and weapon type. Combat was fast and skill was rewarding, with dodging being only half of it. Every kill was satisfying, as you ripped a peice of loot off of every common mook. DS3 has you wade through mooks as a chore, and it incentivizes simply running past its game content to get to the next bonfire or boss. People applaud the world-building of this game, with good reason. Its lore and history is deep, and some locations are attractive. The characters are likeable, when they appear. However, most enviroments are extremely drab, and the game does a poor job of telling its story. Furthermore, the levels design is questionable. As an example, one bonfire in an early level is only accessable by jumping off a cliff, and has an exit but no other entrance. Overall, I could only enjoy this game for so long before its dated and stale gameplay outweighed its likable aesthetic and atmosphere. if you enjoy a challenge for the sake of it, and are prepared to repeat the same motions for 60+ hours, go for it. For myself, I'll pass.

Okay, so I would like to first point out that this is the first Monster Hunter game I've played. I did know about the series and had interest but never got around to playing it until now. So if you haven't guessed Monster Hunter revolves around hunting Monsters (well, yeah). The gameplay loop is; track monster > find monster > fight monster > defeat monster (slay or capture) > use parts dropped by monster to create better gear > repeat. That's the core of the game pretty much. May seem repetative on paper but the game has enough depth and variety to feel fresh throughout. Combat is very 'weighty' and at first may feel a bit clunky, but it's not really once you get used too it. So it kinda like Dark Souls in that regard. There are 14 weapon classes to choose from, depending on what type of playstyle you want, all are viable. So the game is decently balanced as far as gear goes, can use what you want. The game's power/progression is tied to your gear, not your characters stats or whatever, so you can easily switch to a different weapon type/armor if you want (though you will need the resources to make/upgrade them). The Monsters are pretty well designed and every one of them feels like a boss fight. Some monsters may look like others but they all have unique traits so they do feel different enough. They all have their own personalities and quirks. Monsters do have varying tiers of difficulty which is usually represented by the mission rank. The game does have multiplayer and co-op is very fun. Having a team usually helps in dealing with difficult monsters and playing with others just feels overall better than playing alone. Everyone also gets their own rewards (except from mission reward money, which is split between players). The game is also balanced enough that a lvl 100 Veteran joining a lvl 1's game to help doesn't feel too overpowered, it's less about gear and more about experience and game knowledge. More experienced players generally being more helpful but even a lvl 1 dude still plays their part in a fight. So co-op's good. As for the ports performance, it's pretty good. 60 fps everywhere (there is a mild fps dip when manually saving and loading screens but that's to be expected I guess). Only real negatives I can think of is their are a few very noticable low res textures here and there, though the game does look pretty good overall. There is a free HD texture pack dlc thing but the spec requirements seem awfully high for such a minor improvement, so I don't think the HD dlc is worth it (I could be wrong). Though it's free so whatever. The other negative would be NPC voices, lip syncing is very noticable not synced to the English voices (And I'm guessing most other langauges), and not all lines are actually voiced (speaking to NPC's in the hub world area usually has them just mutter a short generic voiced line while most of the info is just in written text that you scroll through). I can personally overlook these flaws as gameplay is solid, but some people may be bothered by these. Overall, the game is pretty solid, good gameplay, good progression, fun and balanced co-op, Monsters are cool. Game has a few flaws, but nothing is perfect. Very good game, would recommend.

[b] Dawn of War III is not a sequel to Dawn of War I or II. It is, better stated, the third entry in the Dawn of War franchise within the RTS genre. [/b] For starters, I was a 40k player for 10+ years and played both DoW I & II extensively, and I am very much enjoying my time in Dawn of War III; I also had next to no expectations going in. If all you want is DoW I or II, you're going to be disappointed. This is a brand new realization of the DoW IP. The game is a mesh of Warcraft III's hero system and classic RTS gameplay. This is not a MOBA; those that say it is obviously have no idea what a MOBA is. Yes, the elite units have a lot of emphasis put on them - and yes, they are very hard to kill with your run-of-the-mill troops, but by no stretch of the imagination is this MOBA functionality. There is, however, quite a lot of micromanagement and units with abilities and upgrades. That is not a turn off for me, so I have a good time playing with the dozens of troop and elite activatables. The doctrine system allows players to customize their army of choice with their playstyle of choice, but can be a bit overwhelming at first. My chief complaint here is having to unlock each doctrine with Skulls. The single player campaign, thus far, has been better than average, but not spectacular. The story is interesting and I appreciate getting to play as all three factions. I've completed the first 7 missions at the time of this review, and while each was fun, I havent experienced much in terms of brand-new features that I havent seen in another existing RTS's campaign. That said, the FTUE is really good and gets you used to the basics of each race. For me, Dawn of War III shines within its multiplayer. The negative here is due to only having 8 maps to choose from and only having 1 game mode at launch. I feel like I have to state again that just because there's a generator and a turret doesn't make this a MOBA. It does prevent early rushing and places less emphasis on destroying all of your opponent's structures. The bright side to the lighter content is that its very well balanced and polished. I do hope they plan on adding more down the line. As someone who works in the game industry, I see one of the biggest gribes to actually be a huge strength: this game is made for DLC and content updates. Some people seem to think that the game is incomplete without more races or modes. This is a perfect opportunity for Relic to continue investing in the game, expanding upon its content, and ensuring that the game doesn't lose its developer support. I dont mind paying $10 every few months for a new race. A ton of work goes into making balanced content, and if you truly feel your $10 isnt woth the thousands of man hours that go into making this type of product, then you have a messed up value proposition. You get 2 hours of entertainment out of a movie: $20. How is $10 for 10/20/50+ hours of enjoyment a rip off? I understand some complaints. I understand missed expectations and disappointment. I don't understand how this game has a ~50% rating. [b] 4/5 Stars [/b]

I really enjoy this game, but I'm one of the people that always checks negative reviews to better understand what I'm getting into so here goes. Stellaris is a great starting point to an amazing 4x space game. It is made to be mod friendly, and it shows in base gameplay. You can mod in your own races, change starting conditions of the galaxy, and just about anything you can imagine. However, it also seems that it will be up to the mods to really take this game to the next level in the vanilla version. So what holds this game back? I would say the scale of what this game WILL be actually hurts the fun of the vanilla game at launch. The diplomacy is simple. "I like you, no war" or "Ooh, planet. Declare war out of nowhere." The planet screens remind me a lot of MoO or, more accurately, Sid Meier's Colonization town screens. You move your pops, create buildings to increase resource output, and generally try to min/max your tiles. However, 22 years is a long time to leave a concept nearly the same. Combat, oh combat. If you are coming from EU4/CK2 then combat will probably be a step up. You can customize your ships (a la every 4x space game now), and group them in fleets to attack. However, actual combat is just moving stacks onto eachother, as in EU4. The feedback is fairly minimal, but DOES provide the info to know what major adjustments to your ships you need to make. Minor details about which modules are effective would be helpful. So overall opinion: I'm enjoying it. I will spend this week making the galaxy Trump again. However, if you are expecting anything near the polish of EU4, remember what EU4 was like on launch. The DLC and patches for this game will be what really determines how great this game is. Edit: For clarity, the reason it is not recommended is because this is NOT at the same level of polish and complexity as other Paradox games RIGHT NOW. If you are looking for that, wait a little while. However, for the price, I would still recommend it by itself and I fully believe it will end up surpassing my hours on EU4 (556 and counting) as the free patches and DLC expand the gameplay. Edit 2 for more clarity: If you are someone who loves the depth and complexity of EU4/CK2, I recommend you wait for some more content to be added. So it's more of a conditional "don't recommend." Changed my review for the THIRD time. I liked the game when I first played it on EA launch. Then after one year I felt the game still wasn't living up to it's potential. Two years later I feel the game has definitely achieved what it's set out to do. You can see and hear so much of Age of Conan living in this game. You can tell this was their original vision with that game. They just finally have the technology to support their vision. Pros: -The building is amazing. I haven't played any survival game with a building system as good as CE and I've played them all. -The world is beautiful and each biome unique. The enemy types and factions are all unique and offer different challenges. -The feeling of playing with mostly the same group of people every time you log in brings back memories of the original MMOs before dynamic sharding was a thing. Gives you a sense of community. If you're an asshole, people remember you. If you're helpful, people remember you. Cons: -The AI still leaves something to be desired. PVE wise the enemies are dumb as bricks. Most bosses can be bugged out and just stand there letting you kill them easily. The combat style reminds me of Dark Souls, but the enemies AI is so buggy it's impossible to read tells and dodge attacks most of the time because their is no pattern and they don't always attack when they should. Sometimes they'll just stand there staring at you for 10 seconds then randomly lash out and hit you with no chance to dodge. -The combat system. While it's a step in the right direction, it's awful for PVP. There is one meta build. Spears. Use them, or die. And the depth of spear fighting is two buttons. Right click and dodge. There's really nothing else to it. If they could figure out a way to add depth to the PVP this would hands down be the best game I've ever played. I think attack cancelling is bad for the game. I think more weapons would be used if once you started your attack you couldn't unequip it effectively breaking the animation. This eliminates any risk/reward mechanic of seeing an attack through to the end. It also causes the meta of poke/cancel/roll which isn't fun at all and extremely easy to just run around and never die if you really don't want to. That being said. Even with those serious cons. I feel this is the best, most polished survival game out right now. I would recommend it to anyone.

While this game has an interesting storyline and I like the building mechanics, the game can be buggy and laggy to the point sometimes of unplayability. The storyline, as stated before, is incredibly interesting and the environment drives you to explore around. I don't have any real complaints about it at all. The base system is pretty awesome, with the ability to build these large, sprawling bases that all serve different functions or act as checkpoints. However, a lot of issues I've encountered are with the base system itself. I can be about 800m out and the game will render the parts of my base that appear through the glass windows as well as their lighting effects despite me being nowhere close enough to render in any of the other parts of the base, and this typically results in a drop in frames. When I get near my base my frames take a severe plunge as well, although I've noticed that this only really occurs if you have windows or glass parts. For the issues not involving the base system, most haven't hurt performance at all but just make the game feel a bit rushed. Things such as Stalkers just wiggling on the floor after being hit with a knife a few times, peepers swimming on land, and how being in maybe like an inch or two inch deep water makes you automatically swim. For performance related issues, it's often been when I would break a limestone or sandstone crop to collect a resource, there'll be a quick drop in frames and then back to normal. This has happened more at random however and not totally consistent. In addition when running on medium settings at least the game will go ahead and de-render or simplify objects to help with performance, and that's perfectly fine. However a lot of the time I'll enter an alien hallway or compound and then game will simplify the walls to a base flat texture despite it being in my sight and only about 10 feet in front of me, which doesn't surprisingly look that good. On the islands like the floating islands as well I'll be at the top and look down and all the fauna and floral will be gone and it'll just be a base, low-res texture that's mapped onto the island. There have been a few gamebreaking bugs I've experienced in the past but I haven't encountered any at all in my latest play through. Overall while the game's story and building mechanics are great, the way the game handles rendering tends to just ruin the experience a lot of the time, and the various random bugs and glitches just make the game feel unfinished. It's not like I'm on a bad card or processor either, with an R9 295x2 and a R7 2700X while running Subnautica off a SSD. It's just hard to recommend when one of the core features of the game results in noticeable performance issues.

I know this isn't the most difficult thing in the world, but it's not MY job to decide how to balance my loadout to make the game fair and balanced, I don't want to have to think about that, and then get annoyed at myself when a level is too easy because I gave myself too generous of a loadout. Or get mad because I spent 30 minutes dying because I didn't give myself enough ammo. This is such an easy change, and in a game with such polished mechanics, it feels like both this, the lack of checkpoints, and the pace-killing keycard hunting were intentional choices to regress the game in order to make it feel more "retro." This is the most frustrating kind of game, because the soundtrack is fantastic, the shooting is pretty good (although nowhere close to Ultrakill or DOOM Eternal) the environments are really creative and awesome, especially in the second half of the game, and the game handles very well, but the keycard hunting and lack of checkpoints **really** killed most of the fun I could've had in this otherwise fantastic game.

Terraria is a great indie game that I'm sure anyone will enjoy. As others have said, this is not Minecraft, nor does it in any way try to be. You start off with little knowledge on what to do, basic tools and a helpful NPC by your side. Eventually you learn a few tricks and provided you survive your first night, you carry on surviving, building bigger houses and a bigger inventory of wonderful items. Speaking of items, this game has thousands. There as so many blocks, weapons, armors, tools and variations of each that is is highly unlikely you will ever discover them all in less than a few hundred hours of playing. There are also lots of helpful NPCs that gradually join you in your journey and they take away that lonely feeling games like Minecraft have in singleplayer. There is multiplayer, which is alright if you have friends but public servers are only really good if you want quick access to the best items, as your singleplayer and multiplayer inventories carry over... which I think is a great idea. This game has a building aspect to it and although it is a 2D game, the amount of decoration items and blocks means that building is actually fun and you can make architectural masterpieces of you wish to do so. When it comes to animals and monsters, Terraria excels. There are tons of different enemies with their own drops, stats and traits, as well as variations of each. The bosses are challenging, even with the best gear and the "waves" and "events" that cause an army of enemies to swarm your beloved home are great fun and a great challenge. There are also lots of cute little crittiers running around your world that you will most likely be chopping to pieces for fun whenever you feel like it. All in all, this is an awesome game for people who are completely new to gaming and its also great for experienced gamers as it is very challenging when set to the highest difficulty. This doesn't win awards for visuals, but thats not what they were aiming for and it does honestly look quite beautiful for what it is. Pair that with an immersive assortment of music and sound effects and you have yourself a very nice atmospere. Terraria is one of those games every collector should have in their library and I see it achieving a sort of "legenadary" status in the future as it becomes a classic. It also runs on my toaster, so it should easily run on yours.

The multiplatform answer to Mario games! A Hat in Time, while obviously of a childish nature, is plenty interesting for any type of gamer purely based on how well it plays, how fluid mobility is and all the movement options available. It just plays well. I won't include a full blown Cons list until I stumble on something I really really dislike. I will, however, have a personal tastes section confirming things that might turn some people off. Pros: - Runs perfectly with all the fun features like no frame cap. - Fluid mobility through wall running (up/down), double jump, air dash/slide with a boost if you time the "exit jump", hats (powers) that add more mobility options. You can play this really fast. - Great platforming. They get you requiring to control the air dash correctly fairly in the game. - Evolving levels. As you progress, "something might have happened" in the level which means that specific act has the level be very different in the way you approach obstacles. - Useful "currency you loot throughout the entire game". I swear, that's a thing that always bugged me about many Mario games. Coins just aren't that important. Here, you buy badges (passives) with them, you need them to unlock some levels. They at least have some use. - The OST is very good. The same songs being remixed for different versions of the same level, or evolving boss themes based on how much faster it's getting. It's an engaging OST. Very "cute" as well. Exactly what you'd expect for a game with these aesthetics. - Honestly, and I'm not kidding here: The loading screens. They're all tailored for the "Act" being loaded, and they all look like movie posters, or comic book covers. They're really nice. Nice enough to be listed in the Pros of the game. Up to personal tastes: - Very, VERY "cute" in nature. You play a little girl, and a lot of adult themes, like "the Mafia", are dumbed down to childish levels (obviously). They do, however, suggest some things in the dialog that could be applied in an adult fashion. Like "how Mafia deals with adult girl". I personally like it, but it might turn off a lot of people. Its got childish aesthetics from the get-go though. Simply impossible to go into this not expecting it from any media you'll see or hear. - Graphics fit the game perfectly and are pleasing to the eye, but again, might not be for everyone. - Easy game. It's not difficult and it's not made to be difficult. I'll assume the main target of this is for a very casual, young audience, and that's fine. Of course you wouldn't go into this expecting Boshy designed levels. I do get hit sometimes, so if the difficulty bores you, hey, this WOULD still be a difficult 100% no-hit! :D A big part of the ease is due to the abundance of healing. Reduce heart drops and spawns by 90% and it would actually be a challenging game. Any modders? I'm having a blast with this so far and I want to see more of the hats, the levels, how they change through the acts, and some of the interactions. Nyakuza, just in name and images, already sounds like it'll be a blast.

You play Wilson, a mad scientist who makes me look sane and who seems to have faffed about with powers better left alone and wound up trapped in some bizzarre paralel universe where he has to rely on his wits to stay alive. Challenge is right up there even at the weaker difficulty settings, but it's one of those games where even when you fail you want to try harder to win. Ok, if you're 12, you might find the ability make every npc naked to be exciting, but when you grow up, digital nudity being one of the major selling points causes you to see this game is rather shallow and made to appeal to young teens, you know, the ones who technically aren't old enough to play it. Combat is arcade style, where you have limited attacks and limited defenses. There's no real skill sets to seperate one character from another. The building creation system is much better than other games in that it includes triangle shapes that actually give you a lot more freedom to create than almost every other game out there. However, the similar nature of the building tiles themselves remove a lot of creativity. You can make a sandstone castle, or a stronger stone castle that looks almost identical, or the strongest stone castle which...looks almost the same as the previous stone. All similar shades of orangish tan. Sure, there's wood you can use to build with too, for a tiny bit more variety. Biomes, ok, clearly that's your goal, get to the next biome. But, what if you want to explore? Go ahead, your weapon type can't hurt creatures in higher biomes, because, well, those hours of resource gathering you didn't do in each preceding biome are integral to the game. No, just no. You MUST go from a to b to c to d, and skipping from a to c simply means you can't hurt the creatures and they kill you easily because...you just can't hurt them, literally, your weapon type is too low to cause them any damage at all. Single player? That's a joke just to get people to buy the game. A single player can't fight the boss monsters, nor can they do much with thier time besides harvest resources because it literally takes hours to gather resources to equip your character or build a base. And you get to do it for each and every biome. And reset your feats when you want to make weapons, or armor, or a base, because you don't get enough points to actually learn all the skills. So, just get to 60 and change up the skills you do know as you need them. But mostly, spend your time gathering. That 40 person limit on servers, that can work depending on what your server is meant to do. If it's pvp, then you need a lot of people who actually work together to make it enjoyable and a second group to fight against. If it's pve, you...need to build an impressive castle or something so everyone spends all their time harvesting. If you join a pvp server, you get the typical higher level players killing the low level ones. If you join a pve server, you find a group looking to add more resource gathering members. Oh, and you get the petty children who like to grief others by killing thier thralls. Game has it's pros, like building nice castle structures. Game has it's cons, like being simplistic in both gameplay and content. It's not a solo game. It's not an mmo. It's in that middle ground where console games go. It's unfortunate, because this wasn't a console port. It was a pc game they decided to port to console and that's where the game design went to hell. Instead of making a good pc game, they made a poor pc game that could work multiplatform. Tried it again on 1/24/19 to see if they made it any better. Sometimes when you knock an opponent out to make them into your thrall, they fall through the world, so hey, clearly some people value freedom more than life and this bug lets you find them. I played over 400 hours during this game's beta period. It's a fantastic blend of action, realism, teamwork, tactics and rewarding objective-based gameplay, enhanced by an incredible sound design, ongoing content drops and performance improvements, and now a thrilling ranked competitive mode. The gunplay is tight and rewards good aim but punishes recklessness and unpreparedness with its low TTK and varying ADS times depending on stamina/weight/movement/stance. Map knowledge is key and so is knowledge of the game mechanics. Just having good aim will not get you wins. There are a number of different game modes to try. If you're more of a casual player, coop is a great way to get into the game by playing against AI opponents. There are also two "sustained operations" Versus game modes brought over from the previous Insurgency, Push and Skirmish. I also consider these more on the casual side but they can be quite intense when you're working hard for the objectives and avoiding enemy air support/call-ins. The other two modes, Versus Firefight and Ranked Competitive are quite similar in that they both ditch the commander/observer/demolitions roles and revolve around three objectives where your team only respawns when capturing an objective. These modes are my favorite because they bring out the competitive focus that I feel this game excels at. Ranked has fewer roles to choose from and more expensive equipment costs, so you have to be more judicious with your equipment selections than Versus Firefight. Having played a bunch of the original Insurgency: Modern Combat mod for Half-Life 2 and a little of the standalone Insurgency Source game, I really appreciate the game design changes for Sandstorm, which make it quite a bit more fluid and dynamic compared to the previous games. The sound design is also vastly improved versus the previous game. New World has stated they plan to bring back some of the classic maps from Insurgency including Ministry and Sinjar, as well as open up the game to custom maps and modding -- only fitting considering their origins as a mod team themselves. Even some of the existing maps have clear influences in their design; Summit has areas closely resembling the classic Market map, while Precinct contains improved versions of Contact and District. As an old veteran of the previous Insurgency games I appreciate the lineage in the level design and can't wait to see what other classics return in Sandstorm. All in all, Insurgency: Sandstorm is an excellent effort from New World and shows genuine promise for the coming year. For the price I can't really think of many other games that provide as much value as Sandstorm. With the additional content promised and planned in the future I see Sandstorm having a long and bright future.

I use a HDD @ 7200 RPM so this makes me a happy camper. Not as positive points of my experience: - Still havent been auto-saved by a body guard or spy in an assault. Maybe I'm not doing it right though? - Dominating (Branding) orcs tends to leave a hand-shaped burn on their face. Kinda ruins some of the cooler looking dudes that I've tried to recruit. - Legendary orcs from loot chests, no matter the type of chest, seem to have some huge weaknesses making them effectively useless in a lot of scenarios. Pretty disappointing to get these guys honestly. A big point that I'd like to make for people saying that you have to grind insanely hard at the end game in order to gain any ground with your fortresses: Take your time playing the game. Play the missions, Get your skill points, Find your gems and mirian, get the occasional lucky legendary orc along the way. This game wasnt meant to be completed in 2 days! I don't even run the "main story" missions all that much at this point, it's a blast to run the "OP Elf" missions and do the mini puzzles and memories. I dont feel as though the game is pay to win ultimately. Ah Civilization, one of classics when it comes to strategy video games Civilization V is a very well done game in my opinion, especially with all the DLC expansion. After taking college level world history, there are so many aspects of the game that really do parallel real life history. For example wars over religion, how annexing cities makes more unhappiness than puppetting cities, as there have been conquerors who when they did conquer a land, they really did set up puppet states where they pretty much didn't change anything there, rather than annexing it and forcing them to assimilate and do as you say, causing more unhappiness and a better chance at rebellion. Although in a game with so many different civs, balancing is always going to be an issue. Some civilizations have bonuses that are just overall much more relable or blatently better than other civs. But overall the bonuses are well done to make playing as each Civilization feel different, as the bonuses guide your playstyle. Ai can be a bit unpredictable on how well they do. I feel as though especially in later game the trades they offer can be a bit pathetic, asking for a luxury resource for 3 gold per turn meanwhile I'm making 100 gold per turn. There have been times when an Ai declares war on me and makes me go "oh fuck" as they move in their 20 trebuchets, and there have been times where they declare war on me and attack me with a single archer. The Ai tends to lean towards the better side in that aspect. Overall though they still are pretty well done and tend to stick to strategies that their civilizations had in real life (i.e. Mongols are warmongerors, Chinese are generally isolationists, straying from trade). Multiplayer really needs to be polished in Civ 6. Muliplayer is one of my favorite things in Civ V, but its very buggy, mainly when you want to continue a game. When you load up a game, half of the time someone can't connect or everyone freezes in the loading screen. And when we do all load in, sometimes someone loads in as an AI's civ, or people have switched civs. Basically you have to finish a multiplayer game in one sitting (which is hard to do with multiple people as games take a while) or not finish at all.

They tried to push south but those Vipers are quick, so they ended up moving behind them as Private GuyDude was laying down smoke to allow the team to flank around the fireteams. The marksman was shot in the chest and was knocked down, so the private rushed towards him and lifted him on his back, shouldering his Type 115 and shakily firing the .50 cal underbarrel whenever he saw the faint glimpse of a Viper's shiny green helmet. Unfortunately, the Viper suits were built to be hidden from thermal vision, so GuyDude wasn't able to use his helmet efficiently. Alpha 2-1 had no choice but to retreat somewhere, anywhere, and they decided the best option was to the northwest at capture point A, where more NATO forces were located capturing and fortifying the point we cleaned out. In the midst of all the destruction, GuyDude laid down his injured ally and was able to get him into fighting condition once again, luckily the marksman had an armored vest that slowed down the bullet and lessened the damage. GuyDude took a graze to the shoulder but bandaged it after running behind a tree in the blind spot of the gunfire. He noticed that the Vipers weren't pushing up, so he told the squad leader that there's an opening for retreat. In a last ditch effort, they ran towards the blind spot and were unfortunately caught in an open field with a few rocks, surrounded by Vipers hiding in the jungle. Alpha 2-1 hunched up near the rocks, focusing on one direction: northwest. After surviving an onslaught of gunfire, they pushed northwest back into the slightly safer jungle but were sent back by the Vipers closing the gaps. They were ping ponged like this two more times over the course of fifteen minutes, the rifleman had succumbed to his wounds as GuyDude would have been unable to get him to safety without dying himself. By then they had requested backup at least ten times but to no avail. Angered, Alpha 2-1 hunkered down and decided that the only way out was to kill every last one of the Vipers. Having already used half of their ammo, they made every bullet count. Pushing through the pain of taking a bullet or two in the torso, despite their high tier armor, was difficult. Five minutes later, they receive word that the supply depot and radio tower had been sabotaged, meaning that there'd be no more Vipers available or any major threat for that matter. Still, it felt like more were just seeping out of the forests and they were hopeless that they would survive as their ammo ran low. Private GuyDude tanked a shot to the stomach with the help of his Carrier Special Rig, the standard for medics, but had nowhere to retreat as they were still surrounded. The squad leader was shot in the hip and then the shoulders and was knocked unconscious, still alive. The Vipers on the other hand seemed as if they could have ran a marathon as they were starting to push Alpha 2-1 once more despite their massive losses. Among the destruction, GuyDude wondered why the Vipers haven't retreated yet and realized that the Vipers are most likely trained to never surrender after they enter a battle and wanted to wipe out Alpha 2-1 as they could have changed the tides of the battle had they been free. For those who do not want to read a wall of text, I can firmly state that ArmA 3 is a glorious game if you like realistic military shooters. Now for the "Love-to-read-wall-of-text" people: (if you want my opinion of the singleplayer-campaign: it was pretty dang awesome if- and only if- you, "get into it") ArmA is produced by the company Bohemia Interactive. This company makes military simulators for real-world militaries. The company decided to remake one of their simulators into a video-game. Some tweaking of the game, some texture updates, add a story... and boom: You have ArmA. Simply put; ArmA is built on the backbone of software used my actual militaries. If you see today's Call of Dutys, Counter-Strikes, and even sometimes Battlefields- and think to yourself, " I want a bit more" -- This is the game for you... you get more: Options Custimization Realism Freedom History Education Patience - and above all, the community... Before I go further, yes; you will meet the usual kiddos (who sound between 3-8) in the game, but time and time again the mentality of each server (usually) reflects the upmost maturity. This community and these servers are what allow ArmA to work. You will most likely never find a game where 5-to-100 random people from the internet can come together to achieve a common goal- and have a great time while doing so. Steering the topic back to the realism for a moment: Holy Moly, its good at it... forget the games where one gun is far superior than another one... with the right skill and training, any weapon is the best weapon. ignoring pistols and other small arms, a headshot is almost always an instant kill. Like it should be. Bullet drop, Wind direction, Bullet Velocity; are all calculated. Silencers only silence the muzzle sound; which means that (like in real life) the bullet will make its famous 'crack' sound as it flies past people, regardless of silencing. Gunfights usually take place at distance, but many times fall to close-quarters, street-to-street action. Sounds are calculated correctly, you will see an explosive go off before you hear it. (same with other sounds) Nightvision works best on clear nights, cloudy or stormy nights make the image more blurry. Your gun can deflect bullets... Enough said. Dead bodies remain 'hot' in thermal imaging for a long time because bodies take time to cool off. (im looking at you CoD) Just cause you have the bigger gun doesn't make you unstoppable. Using guns that you're comfortable with is 100x better than the one that is bigger, or stronger, or cooler. Legitimate military tactics and formations are more useful than a fully kit-ed-out team. Brains win wars. I could go on and on about the different things ArmA includes like its accurate star map (oh yea) but I think you should just buy it and see for yourself.

Just as a warning, I own every DLC (Costs a lot of $$$ but this studio deserves the support) and have played this game pretty extensively. Europa Universalis IV is a game focused around war, trade, and exploration. What it really excels in is war, the other two 'focuses' of the game have been improved over time, but the game still revolves around war. This wouldn't be a problem if with every patch they wouldn't make conquest more tedious. From the 1.7 to the 1.8 patch (Art of War, released in November 2014), conquest was made much, much easier, and completing World Conquests (A particular feat, being the only independent nation left in the world) was made much easier. From there, Paradox has been adding roadblock after roadblock to conquest. This is okay, though. If conquest was as easy as point and click, and no thought has to be put into it, then this game wouldn't be such an engaging, addicting, and fun experience. This game's learning curve is interesting. I can't remember much of my early experience but you're given a complex yet simple interface, tooltips that don't mean much (which has been helped with some semi-recent patches), tutorials that also don't help much, and, of course, the shock of "What am I supposed to do? Is there a goal?" The answer to those questions is both simple and intimidating, and it slaps you in the face rather abruptly. It depends. You do whatever it is you like, there is a score system but it doesn't really mean much. That means that short of being in 1st place at the end of the game (which is rather easy for most nations), there is no goal. You take control of your nation, you embody it. That nation is you. It took me about 4-6 hours to understand how to play the game, and another ~100 to 'git good'. I stopped improving as a player (much) at about 1500 hours. In short, this game is about entering the renaissance, takes a huge time investment, is super fun, and hard to learn. 10/10 -IGN.

Doki Doki Literature Club is a game that is impossible to review properly without spoiling the very things that make it one of the best Visual Novels made. While it holds the facade of an average visual novel; this game is so much more. The themes, atmosphere, dialogue, and gameplay all serve to tell a story that is only possible in a video game. This is truly a story that can't exist in any other type of media. For this reason, I have nothing but praise for what this game has to offer. While many new visual novels fail to grab attention or capture the creativity the genre originally had—this one manages to be unique. If you aren't a fan of the genre please at least try this, because you will find a very different game lurking underneath it's bright anime art style. DDLC proves that storytelling can be done through gameplay in a way that is engaging, thought-provoking and impactful without restoring to lengthy cutscenes or a lack of nuanced gameplay. Go into this game knowing as little as possible to give yourself the best possible experience. While in many ways this game avoids the normal expectations of its style, which will be off-putting to some fans. It also pushes to innovate the genre and what can be done with it, choosing to focus on one specific idea and executing it horrifically well.

This game manages to pull off an open-ended RPG feel that most games could only dream of. You can do and be mostly anything you want. Dialogue choices are wide enough that you can play any flavor of good or bad, and even change that notion on a dime. Just character creation and progression in this game is equally as fun to me as it is in Morrowind. The combat in this game is mostly very good. You are able to spec out your character in hundreds of ways, from cutting everyone down with a sword, to turning everyone to stone, you name it. The 2 major downsides of combat, for me, would be: 1) The effects that your abilities will have, especially on terrain, are hard to learn. This can make it very frustrating when you are starting out, and you don't know why you just froze yourself, for example. 2) There are potential ability combinations in this game that are VERY exploitable and cheesy. The best solution is to just not use them. Just make sure to agree with your friends on which one of these ways you want to play. Now for the 1 major downside to this game. As of this review, I have played 318 hours of this game. 317 were something new, experimental, or just plain fun. The very last hour (or so) of this game was incredibly disappointing. Be warned now that the last fight, the last mission, of the entire game, is incredibly bugged. For me, I was not even able to fight the last battle, yet I was able to at least able to see the ending sequence, and some were not even that lucky. [b]Play with hopes of a satisfying end at your own risk[/b]; and I pray that you get it.

PRO: [list] [*]Good graphics, the cutscenes are actually cinematics with the live actors; [*]Stealth missions add some diversity; [*]Certain squadmates can now provide you with ammo/medkits/grenades/etc. It's on a cooldown and you have to call for it but at least they're not completely useless anymore; [/list] NEUTRAL: [list] [*]Keyboard/mouse controls during the tank/plane missions are just too wonky. Given that there's only one mission of each and you don't get any practice before that you'll surely be reloading the checkpoint a couple of times; [*]The drama of the story is too forced. Fist fights, drinking, disobeying orders... While I don't doubt that it could happen I do doubt that a commanding officer would tolerate it happening on a regular basis, especially in a war zone; [*]It takes ~6 hours to complete, and some of that time is spent watching the cinematic cutscenes; [*]Your squaddies won't advance until you do. Well, it's typical for all CoD games; [*]Infinite enemy respawns until you advance to the trigger point. It's amusing to watch how a new machinegunner crawls out of the woodwork as soon as you drop the current one from afar. Also typical for all CoD games; [*]It takes almost 90 GB of the hard drive space. Even a full 6-hour movie would take less. [/list] CONS: [list] [*]Quick-time events. You could drop an A-bomb on a bunker but if there's an enemy inside it who's supposed to be beaten with a frying pan than that's how you'll have to do it and play the "guess which button they ask to push this time" game in the process; [*]When it comes to your squadmates the "I" in the "AI" usually means "idiots". They typically duck in cover and yell hints completely ignoring an enemy that is standing in the open one meter from them shooting at you, and when they do shoot the precision of their aim could make a star wars imperial trooper cry. And don't start me on them getting suicidal and sticking their heads right in front of my gun's muzzle... [/list] So, all in all I'd give it 7.5/10. Two points deducted for the cons and another half-point for it being too short. Not worth the full price of 60 EUR in my opinion.

First: All the "I was minding my own business and got banned" whining is BS. Modding was rampant until RockStar tried to purge it. They got most of them tracing abnomal file shares and extra code. Lots of the current players brag about how much "free money the got" and how some of it still remains. The policy isn't random or automated, you got caught, so suck it. Some modding remains so you see often late night (pacific time) when the oversight is down. Its more griefing type stuff now, as the money cheats are easily traceable. RockStar does act on reports, so they can scan all in a session and see whose code changed. I've seen 3-4 ppl we caught overtly modding, reported, and now are gone. It's not perfect but it is a start. It is also simple to just change sessions and dodge the morons. Makes it easy for 1-2 folks to stay behind and see whom the modder is for reporting purposes. Gameplay: It is GTA open world (freemode) but RockStar didn't do a great job anticipating human nature. Newbies, folks trying to run missions are all right there for anyone to attack. Much of the "griefing" is due to the pvp nature of freemode, so just randomly running around in the city is dangerous, and you can be out matched. However, there are a couple of usable work arounds. 1. You can group up for missions for defense (not always easy unless you have trusted friends). 2. You need to learn how and when to use passive mode to avoid being a victim and to stop spawn camping. 3. It's not hard to move to empty or low pop sessions for solo msns. 4. Learn methods to take cover (being on foot for example much harder to get hit by aircraft). 5. BE AWARE OF WHOM AND WHERE THE KILLERS/FIGHTERS ARE. RockStar put in a couple of ways to track. With good groups, the msns, heists, gunrruning, product runs etc are fun. Races are good too, and the scripted stuff is griefer free (unless the moron is in your party, so learn about kick and block when recruting). Its possible to set up and make 250K about every 3-4 hours solo with the various enterprises (go view/read the guides), so money isnt a big problem but its not instant gratification. High end cars, helos, planes vehicles are fun, and useful to look up all the griefers that used to kill you. Latest content sets up nightclubs and allows centralized control of all your facilities making it much easier to make money and control your supplies. Several new vehicles to help move products around; they also provide some protection (guns, missiles) making them a bit harder to kill by griefers. Fun game once you get the hang of it, and learn to avoid the morons that plague all multiplayer games. Content is gradually improving the overall game experience, and its free to play, not requring pay-to-win if you DONT have attention deficit disorder. Alright, so this is NOT as good as New Vegas, or 3 for that matter. This game doesn't feel like a fallout game. With that being said however, I'll talk about all the good this game is. Fallout 4's story is basically the same basic idea as 3, only this time it's reversed. You try to find your son Shaun. The story is not the best, far from it, but in my opinion, it gets unneeded hate. Now with the gameplay. This is where the game excels at. It introduced (or well expanded from Fallout new vegas) full on weapon modding. You can attach plenty of scopes, grips, receivers, barrels, and more! This is a very nice system, as you don't get these for free (obviously), you have to get a butt load of junk that would be useless in any other game, and use said junk to make a brand new mod for your weapon, whether it be melee, or ranged. Speaking of this system, you can upgrade armor and power armor! The normal armor part is amazing mostly. The reason I say mostly is that it can be overpowered as well, but depending on who you are, you may like that it can be (I know I do). If you join a specific faction (not going to name it), and do enough missions/side missions, you'll be able to make ballistic fiber for clothing. This can be put on normal clothing to make it better in every way to full armor, as it is lighter, better looking (in my opinion), and can add special boosts without needing legendary effects. The coolest part to this however is being able to customize your power armor. It adds older power armor from some of the previous games. This includes the basic T-45, all the way up to X-01! On top of that, you can modify any of 6 pieces like normal armor. Unlike normal armor however, power armor has some unique craftable bonuses, from night vision, to freaking jetpacks! This has a good side, and a downside. The upside is that you can create these bonuses. The bad side is that (at least I think from my 140 hours and counting and never getting one), you can't get legendary power armor pieces (at least legitimately). Now onto the base and settlement system. Again, I love what they did here! Sure you could *kind of* make your own home for people in new vegas, and make your own home in 3, but this version is completely different. You can make an awesome base, with turrets and gunmen guarding every nook and cranny. You see a base that looks like it could net you some profit? Get to planting a load of crops and set up a line from that to your main base, so you can grab it there and sell it for good money! Does the base have water? Grab yourself some huge purifiers and you'll soon have so much food and water, you'll start selling them for a cap a pop if you need to! In conclusion: I feel that Fallout 4 gets too much hate, even though it did SO MUCH right. However, from how they felt to add the "shop" (like in Skyrim, but much worse), I'd say get this on sale, but if possible, get the game of the year edition to have some actually good dlc, like Nuka World, Far Harbor, and extra settlement things, like traps, and being able to make amazing robot companions with Automatron.

review: Here's my 2 cents, as someone who's played around a 1000 hrs give or take: 300+ hours on original Monster Hunter on the PS 2 100+ hours on Freedom 2 on the PSP (before moving to MHFU) 400+ hours on Freedom Unite on PSP 200+ hours on Portable 3rd on PSP 100+ hours on World on PC (Yeah, I'm a filthy casual for having only played 1000 hrs okay?) Simply put world is amazing a huge step up from the older games graphically, monster AI, and interaction with the environment. Though it's not without it's gripes. That's why reviews exist so we can provide criticism on things devs can improve upon. PROS: Maps- Larger than ever. Environmental Traps and the like- really introduced a great way to use the environment to your advantage Monster AI- In previous MH games they'd just gang up on you, a really welcome addition. Hit Boxes- They're certainly not perfect, but they have improved. Anyone remember Plesioth? Fluidity- Back then drinking potions would initiate pointless animation. Picking up herbs would have you stop. So all's well. JUSTIFIABLE Cons: Denuvo- I don't know if CAPCOM will stick with Denuvo, but denuvo is usually there for anti-piracy up till the target sales period is over. So I for one hope they do remove it soon, but it's hardly a mistake if the company wants to protect their sales for the time being. Lack of Content- MHW was built from the ground up. Unlike previous Monster Hunter games wherein they could basically just port the monster over and maybe add a move or two and update their textures, that's simply not the case with world. Though this lack of content disappoints me, if you see it from a developers perspective it really "changes the game". (Yes, shameless pun intended.) RNG- Imagine if you could pick the Jewels you want to have by the end of the quest. After playing a hundred hours or so you'd have no incentive to continue the game. RNG plays an integral part in the end-game. This aspect of the game is most likely targeted to the completionist in us. CONS: Weapon Design- The game for me originally meant, collect everything. Let's face it the end game is fashion hunter and mixed sets. Crappy Menu Design- Especially the Investigations, can they be anymore unorganized? Multiplayer- Servers need to pick up their slack. Multiplayer Quests- The oh so common "failed to join quest" I swear maybe some players just troll without repercussions . Arriving in Astera- I seriously just want to load back into the hub and not go through another loading screen.

I wish there was a neutral option, because this game has a fantastic story and scenes are amazing, very Hideo Kojima you know and love from MGS series, however the gameplay is dog-shit by MGS series standards. Lets start with the positives: The scenery is amazing, the world is amazingly detailed and looks gorgeous, you feel the atmosphere. The music is top notch and fills the atmosphere. The graphics are amazing! even playing at 4k the textures are still high quality and kept in mind for 4k gameplay, the lighting, the effects, particle system, everything graphics wise is amazing in this game. The story is amazing, especially the last like 5 hours are amazing and leaves you satisfied, the story is very Hideo Kojima just like the MGS series, meaning that its very deep and rich and well made. The scenes and cinematography are amazing, meaning the cutscenes are spectacular. Animations are top notch too, no doubt. The online component is great, and makes it easier to progress through the story, people build structures and that gets uploaded online and you can use them to make travelling easier. I liked the characters, they all have their personalities portrayed really well, the character development of Sam is really well done, and it always put a smile on my face to see BB happy. Now the dog-shit: This was a little disappointing, the gameplay sucks, it just really does. No matter how much i tried to justify it, the controls are janky. Controlling sam is janky, if you have a lot of packages equipped you are are even more janky, more prone to falling while running in a straight line. Sometimes i am running and leaning to the left or right, i don't mean leaning due to the wieghts, not that, i mean my path is no longer straight and starts to curve left or right, this is apparent when i have floating carriers attached (its a cart that hovers that you can put cargo on). Climbing also sucks too, you can easily fall, and i am very careful. It's always raining, if you don't carry any spray you risk damaging your cargo, and your spray finishes easily. The bike, OMG, is aboslute dog-shit. I HATE the bike, the worst controls ever. You will be less frustrated driving the truck, and sometimes the truck gets stuck in a small water path, which is stupid. Going down a hill is a risk, there is no climbing mechanism for climbing up or down. The fights against BT have no challenge, you just have to shoot them fast enough to make them flinch, because if they come close to you they will eat you and you die. The game can get pretty boring sometimes. I also don't like that super slow motion thing every time i enter a BT field, super annoying. The gameplay design decisions really really suck, and should've been better made. MGS series was amazing! Even the gameplay of the unfinished MGS V Phantom Pain was fun! But this gameplay sucks, and it's lackluster. The only reason you will play is to get progress through the story, i didn't do any side quests, didn't care, just wanted to see the story end. So, in conclusion. If you want a fantastic story with great story telling, amazing graphics, amazing cut-scenes, amazing scenery and beautifully crafted world and atmosphere, and great music then this is for you. But you will have to muster the bad gameplay, if you can get past the bad gameplay then this will be worth it because the story is just that good. But if you are looking for great gameplay and don't care about the story, then look elsewhere, unless if you want a walking simulator. If you are looking for great gameplay, go play Monster Hunter World, it has phenomenal gameplay but zero story, which is fine actually. I give this a positive review because of the story, its a must see just like Shadow of the Colossus, if the story sucked i would've given this a negative review. Death Stranding is a Monster Hunter World game with a fantastic story rather than gameplay. (for those who love Monster Hunter and MGS series) Hope this helps :)

Mechanics aren't perfect; weapons and abilities need variety not to feel dull sometimes. 3 active abilities per character, including passives, makes it a poor design choice - negates the desire to level up characters. Searching for mechanical parts, weapon parts is a chore; bad habit of searching every corner of the map for parts gets you away from game experience. Loot is dull, many items are in essence the same thing or slightly better, but overall pointless. Stuns are the most absurd feature in the game - 2 turns from absurd distance while ignoring walls (Armor to negate charge is the best solution and your go to). Mutant Year Zero is a stealth game, and if you ignore that fact - you will be punished no matter how much time you spent leveling characters and grinding for parts; getting whole map alerted means death sentence. I adore the fact that there is limited shop items, weapons, but there must be at least some variety and weapons should feel powerful. Side quests exist and at the same time they don't feel like they are - bare bones without solid rewards and feeling of accomplishment. Good idie game - alternative to xcom, but mechanics wise downgrade.

There is something about it that just feels... "real" for the lack of a better word. How settlements are located and how the landscape change between them and the mains cities, the ambience and the fact that almost everywhere there is something interesting to explore, going from the simple note to a fun and interesting side quest. One of the few games that left me with an "empty" felling when I finished it. And to top it off, two excellent expansions. One more story focused (Hearts of Stone) that expand a little the existing map and gives very interesting moments and a very good nemesis, and another (Blood and Wine) that while a little weaker on the story aspect, it gives you a very large and beautiful map to explore and serves a very good bookend to the series.

Pros: - Fast movement, perfect control of the character - Powerful weapons that have an AMAZING sound to them (you can feel the shotgun inside when firing) - Music: the score of this game is awesome. It creates an atmosphere like I haven't felt in a very long time - Levels are not too long nor too short. Well I am a little disappointed. I still have hope for the game, but I was definitely wanting more on the base building front. I loved DoW 1 and was hoping for more base building elements and defensive tactics than this game currently provides. As it stands there is very little defensive nature to this game. If you want the strong base, with a static line throwing out withering amounts of firepower while another force pushes the enemy base, this is not it. You can have elements of that, but not much. Each race has between 5-7 buildings total. Thats it. If you want a feel for the game play, think DoW 2, take your end of campaign OP heros and put them in the DoW 2 multiplayer where you try and destroy each others HQ's. Add in a few more buildings and you have DoW 3. It has a strong MOBA feel to it. While not a pure MOBA, the game relies heavily on elites that are supported by your other units. Unlike the other DoW titles though, you don't get to customize your elites, so no wargear upgrades for them. Units also felt a little bland to me as well. The choices you get per side have very limited load outs and many of their special abilities require manuel control. Manuel control is not new or unique to rts games and in general I think they are just fine if not good, but DoW 3 is going for maximum carnage with heavy elites so don't expect to get much done with your infantry before they get turned into red mist by a heavy walker. It feels like they were just trying to push the "elites" angle and all the other units are just there to get destroyed and show off how powerful the elites really are. Some people will love this game and I couldn't be happier for them. Like I said I still have hope. Hopefully they will see that lots of people WANT more instead of less and will add it in with subsequent dlc (lets face it: there will be dlc, it will cost more money, and it will simply add content that should have been given at initial release). For me this game could be golden if they would change/add a few things. 1) Better cover system (new one is garbage). As it currently stands there are bunker "spots" that infantry can occupy where they are invulnerable to shooting until it is destroyed. Heavy weapons wreck these spots in seconds, you can't repair them or rebuild them, and when they are gone they are gone forever. Also, there are a pathetic amount given on each multiplayer map, so they are gone in about the first 10 minutes of game play. 2) Add turrets for base defense if nothing else. 3) Add a balancing element between heavy elites and the cannon fodder (which happens to be everything else), this could be a new tank for each side that doesn't go down in 3 seconds, cover changes could help, turrets could help, making elites less OP is also an option. I love warhammer in all of its forms: Table top, video games, online battle reports, etc, but DoW 3 was a bit of a let down for me. I am not calling it garbage, but it also doesn't feel complete for me as well. I would hold off buying it till dlc is released and then the game goes on sale. Also, they could make a great change by opening it up to the moding community and steam workshop so that a lot of these changes could be user driven.

The biggest problem with this game, is the price of all the DLC, and the fact that many of these DLC feels very much like something that should just already be in the game. The same goes with CK2 and HoI4. (I have not played with any DLC in Stellaris, so I do not know about that one, but that game feels good, maybe because I am still "innocent to the DLC"). A "good thing", is that if you play with a friend, who got the DLC, then you can also play with the DLC, and after I have done that... I simply can not play this game alone. So many of the features of the DLC I have been using, when playing with friend, feels so much more immersive, and makes the game so much better and more fun, but most of all, most of it just feels like it should already be in the game. With the DLC, you feel more in control of your nation, but without the DLC, I feel like it just feels more random and up to events, and probably also your overall skill and knowledge of the game. EU4 got a pretty steep learning curve, especially if you are new to games of Paradox. They even acknowledge that in some loading screen tips in the game, where it says something like "Even after 1000 hours of gameplay, you will still learn new thing to the game", and that especially goes with all the DLC. It is good that they put out all this DLC, but as said, some of it just really feels so essential for the game to "feel good", especially if you try out the game with DLC, and then go back to no DLC. Overall, the game is great. I love it, and the other Paradox games, but it can be quite pricey in my opinion, especially since some of the DLC feels essential for the game to be "perfect". The game feels even better when playing it with friends, especially if you do not have the DLC, but they got all I would somewhat recommend the game, ESPECIALLY if you wanna spend a lot of money on the DLC, because then, the game is perfect and more fun and you can play it forever. Having sunk quite a few hours into this game (maybe halfway between casual and hardcore) I would happily say this is my favorite Monster Hunter iteraton yet. This review will focus on how this game compares to previous Monster Hunter games. Pros: 1. Quality of Life changes: One of the biggest bastions of the monster hunter series has always been the pre-hunt prep. In the past this has been tedious to downright grindy. There was a certain charm to going out specifically to grab a few extra materials or do some filler quests so your cultivations could finish, but this game just speeds up the process a ton. 2. Inventory split: Being able to have a full inventory of tools, turn-in items, ores and bugs, and still have all the space you need for monster carves really streamlines the experience. You can grab the gathering points you need on the same quest you hunt down a monster in the sprawling biomes. 3. Organic environments: Speaking as someone who had a crappy computer and upgraded just to play this game, the lack of load screens and 3-Dimentional environments are both streamlined and breathtaking. The ability to use the environment itself to get an edge on a monster can change the whole dynamic of fighting them. Ex: Ratholos in the forest vs. Rathalos in the crater are completely different animals. I love how this can make farming the same monster for a while still feel very dynamic. 4. Weapon and Armor customization: So much tedium was removed from swapping sets around and customization added that even sticking to just one or two weapons gives you more options than 60 hours of play can shake a stick at. Yet a brief read of the tutorials that pop up when you try something new keeps it all concise and easy to understand even for Monster Hunter novices. 5. Difficulty Curve: Low rank is easy, it's suppost to be, it's low rank. But to all the people who say High rank is too easy, I challange them thus: Try not bringing the palico. Try the arenas, try not using all the extra traps and bombs. There are plenty of tools added to this game for players who aren't so hard-core to still contribute even in multiplayer, but you also make your own difficulty in some areas. Fighting a monster in a particular zone, or with a particular weapon, can make it a lot harder or a lot easier. With a PC port, I am happy to embrace a certain amount of accessibility. Especially if it means I can play a game with some friends who never had an intrest in Monster Hunter before, and they can still have tons of fun while not feeling like they aren't being "carried." 6. Price for Time: Monster Hunter has always been one of those games you can sink endless hours into. I liken it to Skyrim in that regard. The framework is there to play this game endlessly, because of the enormous variety of monsters and monster-variants, not to mention Capcom has always been great about releasing new *FREE* events every few weeks just to keep things interesting. 7. Controls: They did a good job with this one, be it keyboard and mouse or using an actual controller. It's smooth like buttah. 8. Ecology/Research: Monster Hunter never has really pushed a fantastic story. It's not that kind of game, but this iteration really puts a lot (and I mean a LOT) of effort into bringing life to the monsters, the environment, and the whole dynamic of how these "animals" behave and interact with their world. They even LEARN during a fight, they fight desperately to live, or some aren't even aggressive at all. The quests even make a point to give the player good reasons to kill a few, and leave others very well alone. IT took "The Last Guardian" ten years to make the dog-bird act like a (somewhat) convincing dog-bird. Monster Hunter World makes each and every monster seem that much more alive for taking the time to actually animate and explain their behaviors with a level of detail even zoo sims never seem to get quite right. CONS: 1. Connection instability: I personally have only had issues with this on one night and the problem seemed fixed the very next day. It's been out 2 weeks, I expect it to clear up soon as with any new PC launch of any game. People who think this is new, or just a Capcom problem, are out of touch. It will be fixed or their game will fail. 2. High spec requirements: You gotta have a decent PC to play this game. Of course, if you wanna play in 1080P and 60+ frames per second in environments as enormous, loadscreen free, and dynamic as these, that is also kind of expected as far as I am concerned. You don't buy a 100$ steak if you don't have the proper grill to cook it on. 3. GAME-DESTROYING BUG: There is no doubt in my mind that this will be fixed, and very soon. Neither does it affect more than a fraction of players, but for the love of your 60+ hour playthroughs BACK UP YOUR SAVES before the endgame quest. This is the single thing about the game I take personal issue with. With how much effort and love you spend staring at these character's backsides and working your way through the diverse ecology of this world, having it freeze and corrupt right at the end will absolutely ruin the experience. Patience with this one if you play the game.
