After some awesome feedback in the comments on my review, I repurchased the game to give it another try - I will leave the original up below for context, but aside from the listed retractions, I still feel largely the same way: this is NOT a hard 'NO' on my recommendation - I actually do very much recommend this game, but I strongly advise you make sure it's what you want before your refund period is up. *1) There IS a mode to build up a park from scratch, it is the 'Challenge Mode' - there is a 'Career Mode' that is built around doing challenges, and a 'Challenge Mode' built around creating a singular park from the ground up. This seem backwards to me, hence I completely missed it the first time around. **2) In the 'Challenge Mode' you CAN change the entry way paths, and customize the entryway pretty much any way you wish. 'Sandbox Mode' did not allow me to do this. Huge thanks to those that posted on this and got me to give it another look! -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- TL;DR: It's a very pretty game, and allows for a LOT of minute detail and customization - but if you're looking for a tycoon-management-sim type game, this probably won't scratch that itch for you. This is a very well made theme park builder, and it is absolutely beautiful. However, looks are only skin deep, and unfortunately, so are this games sim-management mechanics. *There are challenges that you can go through to give the feeling of building up a park to see it succeed or fail based on your ability to manage - but it's *very* shallow. You're operating within pre-built parks, with pre existing goals. Essentially, just working a puzzle to get to the arbitrary make 'x' number of dollars, have x number of visitors, etc. to earn the star(s), then you move on to another park/challenge, and do it again. There's a sandbox mode that allows you to operate with unlimited funds and a prebuilt gate that you cannot move or customize apart from changing/adding ticket booths. **You can't even change the path type to match the rest of your park. From there, you can build whatever you want. For me personally, that's just not what I was looking for. I would have preferred to start from complete scratch, build my own gate, basic park, and expand and improve everything as my income begins to build. If you've played this sort of game previously, it's basically the same movement you're used to, however the placement tools are a bit clunky, it can feel as if the game is actively fighting you at times, especially on the paths; you almost have to trick the game into doing what you want, and it can be extremely frustrating - once you get it to work, you don't get a sense of accomplishment, more one of relief... at least until the next time you can't get a path or track to place properly. Between that, the shallow management, and the lack of a 'proper' career (tycoon) mode - I simply didn't find what I wanted here, and requested a refund. That said, if you just want to build an elaborate park (almost) from scratch, and have no interest in actually managing that park, or, enjoy the 'unique fixer-upper opportunity' style challenges with some basic management thrown in - this may be the game for you. However, if you are looking for the spirtual successor to RCT3, you may want to save your money, or wait until they add something like that into the game.

Came in with an open mind, ESO is a popular long standing MMORPG, I was bored and because of the sale it was half price for £7.50, its a game I have thought about before so I gave it a go. So far everything has been pretty disappointing. The AI is absolute dogshit, that was literally the first thing that came to my mind in the first 15 minutes of the game, enemies including humanoids of various classes (fighters, mages, archers, rogues ect) and different monster/animal creatures feel incredibly dull and provide no challenge whatsoever, often you can engage an npc and start fighting meanwhile his buddies are standing just a few metres away doing nothing and being completely oblivious to the fact that we are fighting even if looking directly at us. The hostile NPC "engagement zone" is way to small and ends up just annoying you and wasting your time. What I mean by this is from where the npc stands/roams there is a certain distance that if you go that far the npc goes back to full health, disengages and walks back were he was, this is of course done in many game for good reasons however it happens way to often and without even trying that hard to avoid the monster, I can literally just be walking backwards while fighting for a matter of seconds and the npc disengages. You can avoid the above problem by just standing still and fighting, as most standard encounters are so NOT challenging that you actually don't even need to try at all, you don't have to concentrate or dodge enemy attacks, you can just stand still let them beat on you while you are taking them out one by one because again there is no challenge whatsoever. I have met a few creatures that are meant to pose a challenge but that isn't because of any attempt to make it feel like a good fight but because the HP of that particular one is inflated into the millions (yes literally 1 or 2 or more million health) Looting is pretty boring, in some locations you are just opening containers one by one getting junk, one dungeon had about 20 little jars on each side of the room so you are there just going one by one, many pieces of equipment that you find laying around and can pick up are literally worth 0 gold however you cannot see this until you actually pick it up, considering you start with 60 inventory slots and you are often outside of a city or a place with merchants as you are doing quests, your bag quite easily fills up, you have to buy additional inventory space for in game gold. Also a bug I noticed with looting (first came across it within the first moments of the game) is that when you try to loot something you just killed you get an error saying that you are too far away, even though you standing right on top of the dead body, you then have to start crouching and doing circles until the game decides to give you the loot window, the VERY FIRST animal that I killed that dropped its loot body (not all kills will be lootable) I couldn't even loot it because of said issue, I tried until the body disappeared. Quests are also really boring, there are just so many of them, you are always picking up new quests while performing current ones and just travelling from location to location, they are not engaging at all and end up feeling more like a chore than anything, yes in an mmo you need a grind to keep the game alive with players by consuming their time but this is paid game for starters and I really felt no enjoyment out of most of the quests, in better made games I love reading the dialogs and trying to understand what is going in, here there is no point of doing that as you are getting so many tiny quests you just have to go to where it tells you on the map and that's pretty much job done, you follow some simple instructions for a moment and you carry on elsewhere. On a positive note loading screens are really fast, if there is one it never takes more than a few seconds and I have an older pc too. The only reason I am going to carry on playing this game is so that I can try out the PVP, but if you are someone who knows that PVP is a part of the game they are least interested in then i would say to avoid this game. Yes it could very well be a good time killer but I cannot honestly say that I feel this is a well made game, it just feels way to cheap, extremely bland. I am still low lvl so I havn't experienced much of what the game has to offer, some people might declare that even if what I say is true that the end game content is more interesting, but if just so bad early on then how can one be expected to stick with it to the end? Also the game advertisement says "join over 13 million players", Steam currently has 17k online with a 32k all time peak, so I am guessing that steam accounts for very little of the population however when a company has to use these kind of tactics to make the game sound great/big its never a good sign, there is a huge difference between 13 million individual purchases across 5 years and actually having a good amount of people in game, I know they haven't said anything they shouldn't have much its still a thought out marketing ploy. I will stick it out for a bit more just to try out the pvp and will update the review after that, however based on incredibly boring and unengaging enemy AI I just don't see how the games PVE content can be considered enjoyable. UPDATE : So I couldn't even bare to stick it out to try out the PVP, out of my playtime the only thing I enjoyed was one mini puzzle (about 30 seconds worth of content) and being an MMO the puzzles can't be made that difficult either. If you are obsessed with all things Elder Scrolls and want to have a laugh with friends then maybe this game could work for you, if you want interesting and challenging gameplay then look for it elsewhere.

Dying Light sets itself as what could have made Dead Island more fun and less hated, developed by Techland, as in the same people that made Dead Island and Dead Island: Riptide, you can already imagine the simillar gameplay and the frequent feeling where you're really just playing an improved version of Dead Island. Story has you playing as Kyle Crane, a GRE operative who's mission is to find some file or whatever that is being kept by an infamous and cruel psycopath named Rais. In the quarantined city of Haran, which obviously enough is set in some fictional area in the Middle East, a zombie virus is spreading and you need to find the file for whatever unknown reason only to realise that all of this is some big conspiracy to weaponize the virus (Original..?) Like Dead Island, combat is advanced on a very severe level and the weapon customization is back, altogh not as great as it was in Dead Island. However the game includes First Person parkour around the city of Haran and I must say, I found it rather fun once I got the hang it of it. Way better than Mirror's Edge parkouring in my opinion anyway. Gunplay, of course like in Dead Island also exists in this game, both of which only give the idea of how gunplay is a real asset only when encountering bossess or human enemies. Crafting also makes a return but it can be done just about anywhere unlike Dead Island. So far no cars added in yet, but they are told to make an appearance in a later update, tho the parkouring of course is an amazing form of transportation so I bearly even mind that. Enemy types come in very severe veriety. You got the typical zombie, you know the ones...The infected rusher AKA beserker zombies, The spitters, the giants with concrete hammers, gasmask wearing zombies which are just so joyful to blow up their back gas tank when you get the chance, and of course the charging tankers and more... The amazing feature about Dying Light is how it sets itself apart from your typical Zombie Survival action game by also having horror elements at the night sections. This is due to the zombies being twice as powerful while also adding almost unkillable zombie types that you WILL run away from if you know what's good for you, thankfully the night sections aren't always forced upon you since they are skippable, or if you're feeling like the daredevil you are you can always play in the night instead... The missions are just what you'd expect them to be sadly...Fetch quests...Guh, can't have too many of those huh? Co Op in Dying Light is amazingly fun and is a very good time for you and your friends so I definently think you should play this with a partner. I managed to run Dying Light on high settings without all of the required specs, and that alone shows that the port is good. With all that said, I'd give Dying Light a 9/10. Possibly THE best if not one of the best zombie games I've ever played. And it sets itself apart from your typical L4D or Dead Rising game, it's good, and you should get it if you can buy it.

In my opinion, there's nothing worse than a gamer complaining that a game is badly designed because it is too "hard" for him. 90% of the time, that gamer is someone with a low tolerance for failure and he just needs to try again and get better. I'm in that position with MYZ, but I have decided not to try to get better at this game. And the reason for that is that I don't see any way [i]to[/i] get better at it. This game has a very interesting design. I like tactical battles taking place in areas that can be explored. It's a different approach to the kind of gameplay I have enjoyed with XCOM:EU & XCOM 2. Since I have played and completed the recent XCOM games multiple times, I chose "Hard" difficulty in MYZ, as it recommends. With hundreds of hours of experience with XCOM, I know how to play these kinds of games. The battles at the start of the game are piss easy and require no tactics. Then, when I reached an optional area called The Fallen Angel, I met the biggest, most abrupt difficulty spike I have ever experienced in a video game. All of a sudden I was facing half a dozen enemies at once, and several of them had so many hit points that all three of my squad members attacking a single target could not do enough damage to kill them in one turn. To make matters worse, there was a new enemy type, a medical robot, that could revive "dead" enemies. This robot had a massive pool of HP, armor that reduced the damage of my shots, and it could not be prioritized due to taking so many turns to kill. To make matters even more worse, the medical robot could revive enemies in a single turn, without limit, [i]and the revived enemies had full ability to act on the same turn they are revived![/i] During the course of this long and grindy battle, Selma and Dux were both killed. Of course, there aren't many medkits to find, so I wasn't able to resuscitate anyone before they bled out. Sadly, I don't have an overpowered medical droid with infinite revives on my squad like my opponents do. Bormin was able to take out the last few enemies, and I won the fight. I had exhausted all of my consumables, but I figured that fight was especially difficult because it was optional and future fights wouldn't be so brutal. I hobbled back to the main objective... [b]And the fight for the main objective was even more difficult and frustrating.[/b] There was another awful medical droid, over half a dozen enemies, and a super-soldier with 20+ hit points. Twenty minutes of frustrating, frantic pseudo-tactical gameplay later, my last surviving character, again Bormin, won the fight. I avoided the next big fight in the tunnel, since I had little health and no resources left. I spent the next while exploring the optional areas. When I returned to the main objective, which required boarding a ship, I came upon the straw that broke this camel's back. Brother Bodin is an extremely overpowered enemy, makes his comrades extremely overpowered, and I lost the fight without even coming close to winning. I won't make this review even more long and tedious by explaining all the specific reasons I think Mutant Year Zero's basic tactical gameplay is much inferior to XCOM:EU or XCOM 2's, but those inferiorities would have be more acceptable if the enemies weren't so frustrating to fight or I had more tools at my disposal. At this stage of the game, there really isn't much my characters can do except shoot, but I have overwhelming opponents that massively outnumber and out gun me. There aren't many opportunities for clever tactics. Not even good positioning can convey much of an advantage, because the level design in MYZ places cover in random locations, rather than designing thoughtful and interesting combat arenas. This is another major failing compared to XCOM. So, I am giving up on MYZ. The setting and story had my interest, though the constant insults about humanity were starting to feel gratuitous and unfair. Why am I quitting rather than change the difficulty down to easy? Because as I mentioned at the beginning, it's the design of this game's combat that I dislike. The game would become more tolerable, but at that point I may as well fire up another campaign in XCOM 2.

There's so many things Terraria does right: It keeps the same confined world interesting for a long time, there's a wide variety of things you can do, lots of different enemies, gear, and items, you could give yourself a different build every time you play. That being said, there's some things about this game you need to be wary of: First off, RNG. There's a lot of dependence on it, and you're not gonna like it. Want that Ankh charm? be prepared for a lot of tedious grinding. Want a cell phone? You'll have to deal with the RNG hell of the Angler. Want a Slime Staff? HAHAHAHAHAHA! The unfortunate thing is just how much of this game you'll just be hoping that luck favors you. Then there's balancing. My first time playing the game, I decided I wanted to be a summoner. Well, Summoners are practically useless for most of the game, and the rare occasion where they aren't useless they're still more or less a burden. Playing with friends I found most of the time I was just trying to get back to where I died. On the other hand, you have yoyos. Ridiculously OP, and easy to get. Tried yoyos. Spend most battles camped in a small bunker or flying around while I let my yoyo do all the work. Melee in general just feels way more effective at everything ever. There's plenty of powerful melee weapons, and you really have to dedicate everything if you want to be the least bit effective as a summoner. There's also a persistent issue I've been having with the UI. It feels like all the buttons and text is too big on my screen, despite my 1920x1080 resolution, while at the same time, the cursor is WAY too small. In the heat of battle, I frequently lose it among all the explosions and giblets and bullets everywhere. The result frequently ends up being me throwing javelins at a tree or something else that makes me feel like a moron. So why am I recommending this game? Well. Despite all its glaring flaws, it IS still fun to play. It's really not good for building, and pretty much only for adventuring, so if building cool stuff is your preference, I'd say you're better off sticking with Minecraft. But if you want a grand adventure, here it is. It'll piss you off a lot, but it'll be fun. Honestly, I'm not really bothering with talking about the positives, because they're pretty prevalent in the trailers and other reviews. Expect to dedicate a week or two to a single playthrough, though. And don't be a summoner.

Yes. Sorry, I assume you were asking whether you should get this game? I assume you like 4X (and have a PC that can run it) since you were looking at the reviews and all you need to know on that front is "yes" you should. Stellaris takes Paradox's grand strategy feel into space and does it really well giving you a good deal of customisation of your race including, importantly, ethics that strong influence how you interact with other race (spiritualists don't like materialists and no-one likes a xenophobe). If I were to give it a score (out of 10) personally I'd like to give it a 9 but I can see a strong argument for an 8 based on a few bugs, unfinished features and gameplay plateaus that I am sure Paradox will fix/fill in a timely fashion. It's a great game, the only main issues are some bugs (mostly pretty minor so nothing to mention compared to most releases these days) and a fairly passive AI who plays war much more defensively than they could and a mid-game plateau where little of interest happens unless you are playing a very militaristic expansionistic empire. Additionally it is worth noting that the 'revolt' feature - particuarly important to slaves and races dependant on them, has not been implemented due to lack of time. Right now you can enslave away without fear of slave revolts and it is disappointing that this feature was cut froim release even if Paradox do intend to roll it out soon after. These are issue I have faith will be filled based on Paradox's previous titles (faith based on evidence - should have probably used a different word, oh well) and the game itself is still incredibly fun even for these failings. Now something I have to sing massive praise for Paradox for doing is the accessibility. Stellaris is incredibly easy to get into - there is a small advisor bot (who is helpfully voiced and is even amusing on occasion) who asks how much guidance you want when you start your first game. This alone with the early game 'missions' that walk you through some basic empire growing steps really helps push new players in the right direction. If you have ever had issues getting in Europa Universalis IV or Crusader Kings II you are fully justified - those Paradox games offer no manual, no tutorial, no guidance and are downright obscure at times (apart from Paradox's ever helpful dedication to tooltips which I love) - Stellaris however just works. You can pick Stellaris up and play - no YouTube guides or LPs needed (although you'd be remiss if you didn't watch my excel- ahem, where was I?). Stellaris is likely to be the Paradox gateway drug for players new to their titles. If you love 4X or Paradox games, then this is certainly the game for you. Does it have some flaws? Sure, but not too major and ones I do believe will be fixed in the near future. Does it have some bugs? Sure, the lack of upgradeable warp drives on troop transports is particularly egregious. But these are issues that will be gone within the month most likely and Paradox has a long history of supporting their titles with updates, fixes and optional DLC. Get it. -EE (p.s. Yes I focus on negatives more than I should with great games but that's because I want them to be perfect so bad!)

Dawn of War 3 is the spiritual successor to Dawn of War 1, with a modern twist. The objective based gameplay on the map prevents early cheese strategies that I believe have always plagued the RTS scene. This, however, doesn't mean that you can't lose the game in the first 5 minutes by making serious play mistakes, your opponents will just have to capitalize on your errors and failing to do so could let you back into the game. The elite system is a fresh way to use a race's premium units without a complicated tech tree and the emphasis on unit tactics and elite abilities rather than resource gathering micro/APM gets to the core of what Warhammer 40k is all about: the combat. Resources are still important; there is enough of a tech tree that you can get special abilities for certain units and upgrade their damage and health. However, you can easily transition between unit types unlike other RTS games of the past where you were heavily punished if you teched into the wrong unit type and it was incredibly expensive to transition. Each unit has its strengths and weaknesses, but the developers want you to be playing tactically and be able to respond to your opponents actions with a specialized squad rather than playing rock, paper, scissors and hoping you picked the right kind of unit to mass from 5 minutes onward. This open tech tree also allows you to build any unit in your arsenal and have them be effective, which enables more balanced armies, specialized squads for certain situations, and a variety of units reminiscient of the tabletop. The engine is fantastic as the game is beautiful to watch and its performance is exceptional without a reliance on top of the line hardware to be that way. Dawn of War 3, however, is not without a few problems. Things that stuck out to me is that there are only 3 races in a franchise highlighted by how many races there are, there are very few maps to play on with only 2-3 maps for each of 1v1, 2v2, and 3v3, respectively, and there is only a singular game mode instead of annihilation and others being included. These issues are not long term problems as other races will be released (as has already been confirmed), maps are an easy thing to add and playing the same ones currently in rotation doesn't feel as repetitive as you'd think (because it is more important what is happening on the map), and game modes are a simple thing to add as well. As a consumer, I am well aware that Relic has made multiple fine RTS games and 2 excellent entries in the Dawn of War series prior to this game. Both of those DoW games launched with only 4 races. Yes, 3 is a little bare bones and is similar to the racial trinity in SC2, but more races will be coming (probably quickly) and Relic has done right by this franchise over the last 13 years. Overall, the issues with this game lacking races, game modes, and maps are overshadowed by an innovative unit building and economic system, and outstanding engine that is breathtaking and performs admirably, and a game that feels like it is channeling a path to the future of RTS games. I applaud Relic for making changes and attempting to push the genre forward. It would not have been enough to simply reskin Dawn of War 1 and sell copies or to make a functional mimic of SC2. Dawn of War 3 is its own game with a development team that is committed to the franchise and will be resolving the issues with regard to racial, map, and game mode variety, but those issues pale in comparison to the outstanding body of work that has been delivered to us with this game.

For the Glory of My Manhood! 26 GBs to download, €30 to buy (on sale), and 40 hours to finish. And my immediate reaction: Well, that was weird! Let's start this review by addressing the (naked) elephant in the room. Japan has a centuries-old tradition for 'miniturization'. This tradition permeates all aspects of Japanese society, from bonsai trees and electronic gadgetry all the way to 'erotica'. If you DON'T know what a netsuke figurine looks like, then I'm not going to tell you. If you DO know what a netsuke figurine looks like, then you'll know exactly what I'm talking about when it comes to NieR: Automata (NiR), developed by Platinum Games (PLG) and produced by Square Enix (SQE). While PLG studiously try to avoid any gender-based questions throughout the entire game (Pascal is clearly a male, yet his voice is that of a 6-year-old girl), they couldn't resist a hint of sex when Adam/Eve taunts 9S if he ever wanted "to f**k 2B" - complete with asterisks! This of course only makes sense if both androids are equipped with reproductive organs, which 9S clearly isn't. Admittedly, as far as I know, this is the only time PLG will acknowledge the above-mentioned elephant. With that out the way, let's move on to the basics (for PC using keyboard/mouse): 1. The dialogue is beyond embarrassing. For all the artsy-fartsy, pseudo-philosophical observations (the purpose of existence, the human condition, and the constraints of human morality), the result is an endless barrage of stale, carbon-copied platitudes and one-liners from every American third-rate comedy show ever written, all ending with "Huh". Japanese story-writers need to understand that nobody - and I do mean NOBODY - actually talks like that! Or maybe SQE just ran the Japanese original through Google Translate... The Evil Within is just as bad in this respect, but it somehow manages to morph into comedy (unintended, of course), and at least the dialogue is delivered with grown-up voices. Employing the shrill, and very disturbing, voices of 9-year-old schoolgirls totally undermines any aspiration NiR may have had to be taken seriously. But le'ts be serious for a moment. 2. Fallout 4 (FO4) offers the exact same Man vs Machine (MvM) debate, especially in the Far Harbor DLC, but it ultimately emerges as a much more credible and engaging discussion primarily because: a) The dialogue is delivered by grown-up people, not a bunch of Junior High students desperately trying to impress each other by name-dropping every philosopher known to man. Even down to friggin' Kierkegaard! Really?? Just how starved for attention and recognition do you have to be to name-drop Kierkegaard? b) The MvM debate is seconday to the story-line, which is very simple and straightforward: You play as Nick/Nora in search of your baby son Shaun - and that's the story in FO4. c) The MvM debate emerges from the choices you (the player) make every time you choose between 1 of 4 response options, i.e. you take an active role in creating this debate. On a few occasions you can actually choose "Does it really matter?" which may ultimately be the most relevant, and honest, option. That's why the debate works in FO4, and that's precisely why it doesn't work in NiR. Mankind has pondered these questions from the moment we first looked up at the night sky, and we've basically known the answers since the days of Socrates. We've also known for ages that morality is a human invention that makes absolutely no sense when imposed on non-human entities, tempting as it is. But another thing that sets mankind apart from everything else is the power of imagination, and that has offered us the opportunity to play endless 'What-if' games, such as NiR. This means that despite the extensive background text and user-prompted conversations between Pods, Adam/Eve, and Popola/Devola - while certainly amusing to read - it never makes it off the ground because the whole thing only makes sense in a human context. And since we learn early on that mankind was actually wiped out centuries ago, the rest of NiR boils down to 'What if refrigirators or hair dryers had feelings, huh?' An amusing proposition if you're a Junior High student, but not one that makes any sense, because we already know the answer. One final reason that FO4 works and NiR does not, is that FO4 takes it cue from the perspective of fear. NiR, being a Japanese game, mainly confirms the underlying stereotype that the Japanese do not fear technology or robots - they consider these a means to an end (e.g. a more comfortable life), not the end itself. In FO4 every encounter with or reference to synths reflects this fundamental fear, but the fear is born from the humans. Because there are no humans in NiR, we are left with inanimate objects (simple machines and sophisticated androids) just copying human behaviour, which is simply a question of programming or circuitry, not one of morality. 3. At this point, you may be wondering why I recommend NiR. So here's why: a) If you can see past the pompously contrived and ultimately irrelevant story-line (not to mention the horrible dialogue), NiR is actually a very entertaining game. Some of the mechanics are new to me, and I deeply hate 2D platformers, but even so it's been many years since I had such a good time. €60 is definitely 'Not Recommended' but €30 or less certainly is. b) On that note, just because I'm a casual player with the motor skills and dexterity of a dead person it doesn't change the fact that NiR is very varied and quite generously laid out (quests and challenges). The graphics seem a bit odd, but that may be a Japanese thing. Technically OK, but where did all the colours go? And NiR is actually more of a GPU hog than GTA V. c) And finally, if you are a sex-crazed teen-ager with 99 per cent of your brain devoted to obsessing about boobs and butts, OR if you are a middle-aged, single guy who is too embarassed to create a user account on a proper p**n site, then NiR is the perfect game for you!

There are few games on Steam developed in full by just one person, and even less that manage to be something more than small indie titles easily passed by. Banished is one of those titles and benefits from its ground-up design which results in unique survival elements in a fresh take on city building. Bigger titles have more variety in terms of buildings, structures, technology and scale, but this game can stand on its own and is still very much worth checking out because of the tangible, residing-in-memory nature of citizens and other assets which gives them lifetimes, seasonality and the ability to affect each other, creating for a subtle but immersive ecosystem that you wont see in other titles of this genre. [h1]Highlights[/h1] All the delight of this game comes from it's memory storage of everything as objects. This gives life to everything from chickens and citizens to trees and mushrooms, and adds consequence to their lives or seasons coming to an end, which ultimately ends up in a more cozy, but deeper and genuinely reactive world and life cycle that doesn't exist in other city builders. It's also what produces the survival elements of the game. A bad season, for example, will mean not enough food being generated which can't be collected and stored, which might result in your citizens having not enough to get some of your children or old-timers through the winter, which affects the birthrates in future generations, and a whole street or village might die off too soon, which in turn affects the amount of workers and everything else, and the cycles and trends all weave and mix and affect each other. It's a rich and very interesting thing to witness and feel the affects of, and forces you to keep track of multiple different things to understand what's happening in the different parts of your town. * The great User Interface and tracking deserve special mention. Finding out population changes, food and resource statistics, work information and more is all very helpful and also very easy to understand. * Feelings of struggle and survival, and a network of subtle dependencies are rewarding when solved and help keep you engaged. * Gorgeous assets and engine make your town really relaxing to just sit back and watch at times. [h1]Mistakes[/h1] Similar to Dust: An Elysian Tail, Banished was developed in full by a single person, and really benefits from it, but it also hurts a game like this by limiting it's updates and scope, and taking feedback from the players. Little things like the achievements, for example, have been broken for most of the time this game has been available on Steam. The other big problem with Banished is the lack of end-game content and wider approach. There's great mod support in here which adds a plethora of new foods, animals, buildings and more, and helps extend Banished's life, but as with the core game, there's nothing new once you've explored everything and no means of alternative play other than hardcore survival. All city building sims suffer from this problem to a degree, but they help alleviate it by offering things like monuments and a larger variety of building types and interactions so that there's always a slightly different take but in Banished, once you understand how everything works and how the networks interact with each other the game becomes fairly straight forward and building becomes more labour and less love. * An awful lack of end-game or content for enthusiasts, though this is somewhat mitigated by good mod support. * It's very limited in scope and even small things like map generation options or more tech upgrades would go a long way. [h1]Recommendations[/h1] As a city builder, Banished doesn't have a set playtime, but you'll likely get at least 20 hours out of it before you're likely to feel the need to move on. It's available for £14.99/18.99€/$19.99 on Steam and that feels very fair for the playtime involved. It's also available (and sometimes slightly cheaper) on GOG and Humble Widgets, so shop around. * The developer created an informative and interesting Devlog which is worth a read from start to finish here http://www.shiningrocksoftware.com/2011-05-16-the-doors-are-open/ if you're remotely interested in game design and development * Banished has a great, and very useful sub-reddit which is full of information http://www.reddit.com/r/Banished

One of the best games I've played, ever. I was gifted the money to buy it by a friend and, gosh, I'm so happy they did. Sorry if I repeat anything or if it's a little messy, this is my first time writing a real, in depth review and I love the game to death. Before I begin, this game will be so much better if you don't know much about it. Have you seen one or two trailers and are interested to look at more? Buy it! Don't delve deeper into anything outside of the game. Hop in now. Though I have tried to keep this review completely spoiler free. If you already know tons about the game, then play it anyway, because the gameplay will make up for the loss of some mystery. Pros - This game has a stunning artstyle and lovely characters. Even some of the enemies I just want to stop and appreciate. You can see the love and care that went into the backgrounds and animations. Clean, fluid, and despite how different they all are, they all fit the aesthetic of the game, especially the animations. As someone who has dabbled with animation in the past, I've seen how tough it can be, but the animations here are perfection. It's masterfully crafted and a joy to see. The gameplay is endlessly fun, simple but unique. It's easy to pick up, but as you get more powers through the game you start getting more intricate with how you control. I play with a keyboard because I don't have a controller, but I've been told it's a lot better with the latter. So far I haven't run into trouble with the controls, though. Only dumb mistakes on my part because I hit a wrong button or something similar. You'll have to get used to mistakes like those in your first few hours, but take care and you'll improve in no time. Hey, can I talk about the characters again? They're all charming in their own way, and they're all very memorable. I'm always excited to run across familiar faces while exploring, they feel very alive and are very well written, you can feel their unique personalities, even after talking to them maybe once or twice. Each area has its own aesthetic and, most of the time, colour. This makes them very distinct and easy to tell apart, sometimes they even leak into each other and you know they're leaking in because you see enemies or background props from them, or you know if you're approaching a new area because the colour scheme has changed. This struck me when I had only entered three areas. That's how distinct they are. And they're all as beautiful as each other. I didn't play the game before the DLC was added (besides Godmaster) but I didn't even realise the DLC content was DLC until I checked because of how nicely it was crafted in. Perfectly placed and blended in, though I haven't run into much of it. But that's fine, just means I have more to explore! On that note... So much content! The map is huge! I'm 16 hours in (though by the time anyone reads this I'll probably be much deeper!) and I've discovered so much more than I thought I would when I first started playing, but from what I can tell, there's so much more to discover, so many more characters to meet, so many more bosses to fight... I want to see it all! The soundtrack (and sound design!), just for this review I'm listening to it outside of gameplay for the first time. It perfectly captures any emotions you're meant to feel. Peace, tension, fear, adrenaline, wonder and horror, and so many more, the amount of feeling the game mixed with this music can bring out is unbelievable. Everything is made expertly and placed in the right place, but it's still amazing on its own. Props to Christopher Larkin for making and adding something beautiful to the already beautiful game. The game has steady progression and you'll never feel like you haven't discovered something in a while, unless you're really stuck (more on that later). Each major boss gives you something to use in the future (at least so far) and discovering new areas is the best feeling, possibly one of the best in the whole game. Just when you think you've found the most unique one, you find another! The lore, the lore, the lore! Or, the mystery of the lore! Both! As an arachnophobe, I never thought I could enjoy a story about little bug things. But I am. So much. Every time I see something minor, a statue, a name, a new item, I want to see everything about it! I find myself making little theories on the go. The way it's laid out is.. the best. I love games with mystery in them but you rarely see it done well. Here, though? It's some of the best storytelling I've ever seen, possibly in any medium. Not so vague you're confused, but not so in-your-face that it's not a mystery. Always looking forward to more. This is the midpoint between pro and con; the difficulty. If you're not one for difficult games, then it's a con. But if you like a good challenge? It's a definite pro! The bosses (at least from where I am) aren't so painfully hard it's impossible but aren't so painfully easy that it's just "oh. that's over.". It's the perfect level of struggle, and I've felt amazing after defeating every boss, whether it took me one try or ten tries. Cons - The only con I could possibly fathom was sometimes you'll get stuck or lost. The map is large, which is amazing, but also sometimes hard to navigate if you're mapless. You may have to use a walkthrough a few times, but it's no large trouble. I have endless respect for everyone at Team Cherry and everyone that helped make this game a reality. It's one of the best game experiences I've ever had and I'm so happy I was given the honour of playing it. I'm always excited to do more. I very, very highly recommend it. Now if you don't mind, I'm going to go play it some more....!

Since I am a big fan of the older titles of the Assassin's Creed franchise, it's hard for me to write a review like this. But sadly the franchise is dying with each new title. There is almost nothing left from what the games used to be. That doesn't have to be a bad thing, if you make changes that actually improve what used to be good. In this review, however, I'll try to explain why that isn't the case with Origins. My first problem with the game was the new level system. While it theoretically has potential it just doesn't really work well with the immersion in the game. When I play ASSASSIN'S Creed I expect to have a fighting system which is focused on stealth. Yet most of the new features are only useful if you go into open combat. Stealth in general just got harder and at some point it is actually easier to just don't go stealth at all. Also annoying is the region, difficulty. Instead of making the different types of enemies having different difficulties, everything just gets stronger as you continue through the game. That way a standard guard at some point becomes stronger then former BOSS fights. In my opinion its just not fun and doesn't feel right. Next on my list is the story. In my opinion the developers spent far too less time, caring about the main story and the characters. I wasn't really able to connect to them and that way, big plot twists didn't exactly have impact on me. While the insane amount of side missions, just kept annoying me. The game actually has an option to skip levels so you can continue with the main story. That just makes the side missions feel like fillers even more and we all know how loved fillers are. In the end I'm just disappointed. The game looks very beautiful and if you love grinding levels, it may even bring some fun. But in all honesty and to those who are fans of the old games I can't recommend it at all. I do not mean any disrespect, I'm sure there were a lot of hard working people on this project. I just think that it may be a good thing to stop continuing the franchise someday.

English review (po polsku niżej...) One thing before we get started: this game may welcome you with wondrous graphics and a cute tiny beetle – knight. Mind you, as it progresses it mercilessly exploits your every single bug fear. Giant centipedes – check. Spider legs tapping in the darkness? Of course. Weird, moist, unpleasant sounds – sure. Wicked howling and screeching – there. Fungal plague infesting your body and possibly controlling your brain? Parasite induced body horror? Would anyone be surprised that creators come from Australia? Probably every single one of the above makes my skin crawl (including Australia, although, I’d love to visit), but I pressed on. And it’s not like I’ve been starving for a metrovania. Just recently I’ve been playing Sundered, Usurper and Valdis Story. I have also finished another very solid 2d soulslike – Salt and Sanctuary, and while I still wholeheartedly recommend that game, I must say that Hollow Knight is, in my opinion, a peak of 2d metrovania perfection. It’s also the darkest and the ‘soulest’ of the games I’ve mentioned. Let’s consider an example: which game lets you, after you kill one of the bosses (the first ‘large’ boss, no great spoilers here) slaughter his defenseless brothers (and as you do, read their thoughts of how terrified and defenseless they feel...) crying over his dying body and then actually dive into his dying dream and kill him again? Yep guys, that’s your bug’s everyday life. But my rambling has taken a significant chunk out of the Steam’s word limit so here’s what Hollow Knight may offer; an incredibly well painted and written world with tons of locations and lore (easily 30hrs of game), numerous free DLCs, insanely good combat and platforming physics (and I DO mean, the platforming in this game feels perfect), vast possibilities of modifying your character with skills and charms (and, in a fashion similar to The Binding of Isaac – charm synergies), countless secrets and tiny little details to discover and lots, lots of love and effort put into the creation of this gem. If you can accept this game being darker than it actually looks like in the first place, and can take somewhat high difficulty at times (still, always fair) there are only minor gripes this game has. First, rather large distances that need to be covered between the save spots and fast travel stations – you need to prepare for a lot of trekking back and forth, but hey! That’s metrovania for you. Second, map chunks need to be bought from a cartographer you have to find in every single section of the dungeon and even then map only updates on your visits to safe – zones so you have to be prepared to do a lot of memorizing whenever you visit a new area. Finally, I found that, while beautiful and charming, the game’s music feels too upbeat and slightly too magical for some parts of the game. I suggest playing something of your own collection in the background. If you look around Hollow Knight’s world, you can (but don’t have to, I’d say at least half of the game is entirely optional) find a broth… I mean a ‘Pleasure House’. For bugs. Littered with the said bugs’ corpses. And you know what? It actually feels more fitting than 78% of the mature themed content from the first Witcher. It makes an impression of a coherent part of the world’s lore and not something put in to make the game seem more adult, or because the audience expects that. In case you somehow didn’t notice, I’m utterly charmed with Hollow Knight. With all of its content and heart put into it, at the full price this game is a bargain. And discounted it’s a must. At least if you are into ‘Souls’ or 2d metrovania games. Polska receznja: Jedna rzecz zanim zaczniemy: Hollow Knight wita grafiką jak z Disney’a i uroczym chrząszczem – rycerzem, ale wierzcie mi, po jakichś 10 godzinach bezlitośnie wykorzysta każdą fobię związaną z robactwem jaką możecie mieć. Wielkie wije i stonogi – są. Dźwięki pajęczych nóg uderzających o podłogę, podejrzane szelesty, dziwne, nieprzyjemnie ‘lepkie’ dźwięki – pewnie. Skrzeki i piski od których cierpnie skóra – jasne. Plagi grzybów atakujące ciało i przejmujące kontrolę nad mózgiem? Pasożyty wijące się pod skórą i pożerające cię od środka? Czy kogoś w ogóle zdziwi, jeżeli powiem że autorzy pochodzą z Australii? Przyznaję, każde z powyższych przeraża mnie (włącznie z Australią, jako siedliskiem bodajże wszystkich, ale i tak bym pojechał), a mimo to nie zrezygnowałem z grania w Hollow Knight’a. I to nie dlatego że brakowało mi dobrej metrovanii. Ostatnimi czasy grałem w całkiem sporo: Sundered, Usurper i Valdis Story. Skończyłem też inne bardzo solidne ‘2d Soulsy’ Salt and Sanctuary i z całego serca polecam tą grę. Ale jeżeli chodzi o gatunek dwuwymiarowych metrovanii, Hollow Knight to perfekcja i to praktycznie pod każdym względem. I jak na coś, co wygląda jakby wyszło z najgłębszych otchłani współczesnego Disney’a jest zaskakująco ciężka i mroczna. Weźmy taki przykład: po tym jak zabijesz jednego z bossów (pierwszego ‘dużego’ w sumie, więc nie jest to jakiś drastyczny spoiler), możemy wrócić do lokacji w której odbyła się walka i wypatroszyć jego bezbronnych braci opłakujących ciało (jakby to nie wystarczyło, możemy jeszcze odczytać ich myśli – jak bardzo są wtedy przerażeni i bezbronni). A potem, moja ulubiona część tej historii, zanurkować w ostatnim śnie umierającego bossa którego wcześniej pokonaliśmy i zabić go jeszcze raz. Ot, życie chrząszcza potrafi być zaskakująco ciekawe czasami… Ale gadam i gadam, niebezpiecznie zbliżając się do Steamowego limitu słów, więc teraz na szybko: Hollow Knight oferuje cudownie narysowany i świetnie napisany świat z potężną liczbą lokacji, spójną i wciągającą historią i dbałością o szczegóły która zwyczajnie zadziwia. Kampania single może bez problemu zająć 30 godzin a dochodzą do niej jeszcze liczne, darmowe DLC. Mechanika gry to czysta doskonałość, zarówno walka jak i ‘platforming’, a jeżeli coś nie będzie ci odpowiadać to zdolnościami i amuletami da się zmodyfikować chyba wszystko (szybkość poruszania, zasięg skoku czy ataku, spokojnie można z bohatera zrobić postać walczącą zaklęciami na dystans, a jakby tego było mało, zdolności dawane przez amulety łączą się, nieraz dając zupełnie nowe, niespodziewane efekty). Są tu też niezliczone sekrety do odkrycia, na każdym kroku widać niesamowitą miłość i poświęcenie jakie twórcy włożyli w stworzenie tej gry. Ze złych rzeczy: świat jest wielki, a miejsca zapisu gry są od siebie dość oddalone. Stacje z których możemy szybko podróżować do innych lokacji są jeszcze mniej liczne, więc przygotujcie się na dużo biegania w tą i z powrotem (jak Hobbit, tylko że tu na każdym kroku coś może odgryźć ci głowę). Mapę każdej lokacji na początku trzeba kupić od kartografa który znajduje się gdzieś w lochach, a potem uaktualnia się ona dopiero kiedy dotrzesz do ‘sejwa’ więc będzie też dużo zapamiętywania labiryntów. Muzka jest śliczna, ale trochę jakby zbyt heroiczna i radosna czasami. Tyle. Jeżeli poszukasz, może znajdziesz w grze (a może nie, przynajmniej połowa Hollow Knight’a jest zupełnie opcjonalna) bur… to znaczy ‘Dom Uciech’. Dla robaków. Z korytarzami zaścielonymi zwłokami tychże robaków. I wiecie co? Pasuje on do świata gry o niebo lepiej niż 78% ‘dorosłych’ scen z pierwszego Wiedźmina. Nie wydaje się wciśnięty na siłę, jest po prostu częścią spójnego, dziwnego, dojrzałego świata. Pewnie zauważyliście już że Hollow zupełnie mnie oczarował? Moim zdaniem, ze wszystkim co ta gra jest w stanie zaoferować, kupienie jej w pełnej cenie jest okazją. A po zniżce koniecznością. Przynajmniej jeżeli pasują wam ‘te klimaty’.

This isn't by itself a bad game, but there are many parts about the game that might be a turn off for a lot of people. It is a great game for a small group of people. Pros: -I think the best part of this game is the weapon variety. There are many types of weapons, all with different specs, so everyone can find a weapon that best suits their play style. -Another part of this game that I really like are the boss fights. Each boss is different, and there are specific ways that you need to strategize against each boss, so each fight feels refreshing and different. -The progression system is very good, like most other MMORPGs. It is quite a grind, but its very rewarding when you reach a high enough level and start getting some op stats. -You can make your character exactly how you want. There are specific status points you can upgrade your character with to suit how you want to play. Cons: -The story is garbage. There is probably a total of 10 hours of text bubbles and cut scenes if you were actually to read them the way they are supposed to be read. It's a very low quality story, and has the typical Japanese anime visual novel vibe. The story/gameplay ratio for the first play through is probably about 70-30 depending on how good you are at the game. -In order to get really good weapons, you are forced to play through the exact same story again. Why don't they have a separate story for once you beat the game the first time? Why don't they let you get high quality items until you replay the story? It feels so useless playing through the whole story again when you have already played it. -The actual combat is mediocre at best. There are very few skills you can use at a time, and there just isn't much variety when just grinding NPCs. It doesn't help that literally every dungeon looks the same, so you can't even tell the difference from your last dungeon grinding session. You just kinda shoot and that's it. I can't really speak for the photon blade mechanics, but the gun gameplay is just meh. -The AI in this game is horrible. Your squad mates will do absolutely nothing for you, and the NPCs you have to face will one shot you right when you enter a room. It's so bad that sometimes you just have to take a break so you won't flip out in rage. -After you beat the game and have the items you want, there isn't really much to do. The online is completely non existent, so it's not like you can get some friends together and grind super hard dungeons with your op gear or anything, you just kinda have this gear but nothing to do with it. -The gear is kinda underwhelming at times, there isn't really a crafting system, there isn't any armor, the legendaries aren't really much better than commons, and there's nothing you can really do to base items to make them more powerful. Overall it is a fun game to play, beat the story the first time, grind it again in extreme mode, but after that there's not much to do. It is a single player game, despite the MMO tag, but it does for the most part play like an MMO. If there was a "Mixed" option for "would you recommend this game" I would pick that, because the number of people this game is targeted to is very few. If you're looking for an MMORPG that plays like FF14 without the crazy price tag, just pick up TERA instead.

20xx is a decent rogue-lite game, but since i'm a huge mega man X fan, it makes it all better, otherwise, not sure if I'd like this game a lot. The way it works is pretty simple, you choose one of the two basic characters, and start your run. you play stage after stage with a boss at the end. Each tileset has its own platforming gimmick or hazard element. in the stages you'll find items that upgrades your stats or armor pieces that give you different abilities. Like a Mega Man game, you obtain the powers of the bosses you defeat. [b]Pros[/b] [list] [*] The controls are really tight, the dash feels good just like in the X games. [*] Has some good music [*] Really like the idea of a Megaman roguelike game [*] Each tileset has a few cool gimmicks that do a nice job of spicing up the level [*] You can use special weapons from bosses to disable certain traps or gimmicks, making the stage easier [/list] [b]Cons[/b] [list] [*]All the items you find are mostly stats boost, which is kinda boring, compared to binding of isaac's various synergies and crazy items [*]The bosses are super easy and pretty forgettable [*]The game is pretty easy up until the final stages. I reached the first final stage on my second run, playing at the highest difficulty [*]There could be a few more tile sets, for the 8 main stages there's only 4 different ones which is pretty disappoiting. [*]Sound design isn't the best. For example, the sound for taking damage is kinda weak, sometimes I'm not even sure if I took damage [*]You rarely find a weapon item during runs, I've only found 1 weapon item in my runs, sometimes 0. (weapon items, are items that change your basic attack) [*]I wish the DLC characters were included in the base game but locked behind secrets or challenges, that way I have something to work for. (imagine having to find 4 armor capsules for each character, to unlock them.) [*] Some layouts for the stages navigate pretty poorly, and often you will get stuck on things, as you try to jump around traps and tiny platforms [*] The special weapons that you get from the bosses aren't super interesting, some are ok [*] Boss weaknesses don't make any sense, you literally have to try things at random until you remember them, but because they make no sense it's impossible to remember [/list] Overall, it's a pretty decent game. However, I'm really not sure if this is a game that non-mega man fans should buy. The game has some flaws or just things that aren't super good.

Now I know that I am writing this review a bit late since the release of this game. That being said, I do have a few things to say that have probably been said already. Rome II is the not long awaited sequel to Rome: Total War and though the game has been created in a era where better game mechanics can be made and better graphics can be created, The Creative Assembly has not made very many improvements to the original game. Many of the changes that you will see in this game will be in the campaign section, where TCA has decided to put much of their work on by making it simplistic as possible, and while I see that they are trying to expand their audience by making the UI of the game much easier, it ends up becoming a flop since they make it too simplistic. By making it too simplistic, you as the player cannot make very many changes to a specific provience and even finding the problem for the specific region can be difficult. Another problem that is in the game is the AI, and even though TCA has created so many game in the Total War series, they still have not tackled the bad AI issue. Much of the AI in the game is terrible, both in the battles and in the campaign section, on the campaign side the AI might put up some fighting chance in the beginning of the game but when you actually gain a large empire the game does not become fun due to the fact that the AI does not form any sort of coalition or federation to destroy you and you can just simply steamroll though the entire game by attacking them one by one. Also the balancing of the AI in the campaign map is certainly a huge problem, as the faction of the Roman Empire can easily be crushed by a single northern barbarian tribe or the mighty Egyptian empire can be destroyed by a random faction from west Africa, and many of the AI is very stubborn when diplomacy comes into play, when a large portion of the factions will not have any contact with you unless you give them several thousand gold coins. As long as it has been in the Total War series, the battle AI has always been a considerability huge issue where TCA has never seemed to fix over each game. Various bugs and problems always seem to riddle the game where the AI will never play smart and most of the time will try to rush straight forward towards you or the units will stay in place regardless if you are on the defending side. The bugs in the game make the units might even just walk into walls or just run in circles, which saddens me because these problems are never fixed or are "patched" way too late in advance. As usual besides problems on land, the sea battles are just as awkward as ever as units sail through the land or cannot keep a single formation straight and even sail around the place just to board a ship that is right in front of them. The sieges in the game are an issue as well as the one centerpoint in its past games have been scraped and multiple points have been put in place where you have to defend from multiple sides. So in retrospect, instead of consolidating your forces into one last stand, you have to divide them up into two or three groups to fend off oncoming attackers, which is annoying and frustrating to me. *Side Note: When on the offensive side, throwing sticks at a gate is not a logical way to take it down!* As much as I could rant about the game there is only a small handfull of things that I could say that is a good thing about it. The graphics of Rome II do look beautiful and makes the landscape and its nearby cities look amazing, as well as the look of the soldiers but unfortunately it does make the game lag alot and makes load times unbearable. Another good thing about the game is it's expansive campaign map, where there are at least over a hundred proviences that you can take over which makes you feel like that you are creating a empire, which is nice since in other games (besides Empire Total War) you feel like the world map is very small and condensed. Though I could go on and on about the bad (and very few good things) about Rome II I feel like I have spoken enough about this game. Even though TCA will patch their game to fix many multiple problems and bugs, continuing to release games with a poor polish and huge problems will not help the Total War series in the long run. It is sad to see such a great series crumble like the fall of the Roman Empire, but if TCA continues to make these games in this terrible of state then the longevity of the series is doomed.

review: This game is delightful. I'm a big fan of strategy games and I like Northgard for it's accessability, and variety of maps and victory conditions. I think the biggest strength is the map design. The world is divided into zones such that they have a particular number of resources and finite building room. There are probably other games that do that but I can't think of any. This creates a tangible urgency to super good zones and requires forethought as to what you will build with your limited structures which is where most of the strategy lies. Additionally, there are neutral threats in the land which I love. Some you can destroy for fame or to win, others you can befriend through trade. But they're always relevant to the game since you can't control their land without dealing with them. I really like this game, I think you'd be well within your right to say it's easy, but maybe that's because I've been playing Paradox games for years. But I like a low key strategy game. Can't wait to see how it develops.

Paradox continues to deliver top shelf Grand Strategy, this time a Space Opera. Where to begin? It looks fantastic, and sounds incredibly good with its spacey soundtrack ranging from feel-good to being simply majestic, Interstellar style. Using the Clauswitz engine like Crusader Kings 2 & Europe Universalis 4, it plays much the same; realtime with speed slider and pause features. Unlike previous Grand Strategy titles however, the Tutorial is brilliant. This, combined with starting out small with a single star system and a handy 'quest log', it eases you into the game concepts and never gets overwhelming. UI is very sleek like always with paradox, and it feels very cohesive having everything from technology to combat done directly on top of the beautiful map. Races are varied and cool, and the palette for aesthetics and ideologies is rich. I started my campaign as the good ol United Nations of Earth, being Democratic and starting out with Warp Travel tech and old-but-effective Nuke weaponry. After learning the ropes I soon managed to colonize the Alpha Centauri system, with felt great. I havent had much time with the Diplomacy yet, part from getting to know and soon forming an alliance with a neighbouring species of Righteous Bird people. Then we went to war together and managed to liberate part of another nearby system, from their plutocratic and evil overlords. So far so good :) What more to say at this point? Get it now!

[i]You begin as most of us came into the world: naked, washed up on some beach, with a large rock and a torch. Or maybe I just had a really odd childhood.[/i] Here's the deal: there's no pro-strats. No tutorial. No hints. No friends (this one is especially important.) Everything in Rust is out to kill you. The weather, the water, the other players, the glitchy animals, the radiation, falls, trips, slips, cacti, militarised militia, everything. Your only goal is to survive as long as you can, and even then the servers get reset monthly (on average). If, like me, you like the challenge of a game without any difficulty setting, if you liked DayZ for a while before you realised it was actually quite dull, if you liked minecraft but really wish it had better graphics and you could see your own (and other people's) glistening naked avatars briefly shining in the midday sun before they bashed your head in with a rock and ate your fleshy corpse, you've found a great little game here folks. If that doesn't sound enjoyable, tough. Life is hard and existance is pain. This game teaches you that better than anything. Oh, and you thought you'd be fine if you just log out in the middle of a field? Have fun logging in as a corpse.

Planet Coaster is THE theme park builder of the modern era. The game is a spiritual successor to RCT3 as Frontier, the RCT3 developer, broke their shackles from Atari and created their own IP. The first thing you'll notice upon turning the game on is the brilliant soundtrack. It reflects the developers love and thought for each aspect of bringing their world to you. The peeps and staff are full of life, mascots bring joy to the park, and staff's mood reflect in their work performance. The graphics are absolutely stunning and the lighting engine truly brings the best of it out at night. The sound design not only shows in the brilliant sound track, but each ride is brought to life with true to life sound effects that make the park feel even more real and alive. It feels like a miniature world created by your fingertips. My biggest gripe with the game does not have to do with the game design itself, but its performance. It is not optimized very well and as soon as you reach a medium sized park, you'll notice it stutter badly. A large sized park will crawl no matter your specs. I wish it was a more pressing issue with them, but its clear they decided that looks were more importance than performance, and after seeing the end result, can’t say I blame them. Overall the game blows the competition out of the water game design wise, and developer wise. Frontier truly cares about creating THE ideal theme park game and we finally have someone we can trust to achieve that. If you have even the slightest interest in theme park or rollercoaster design, this game is for you. The game does not excel management wise as it does creativity wise, but that aspect is there in force for those who are interested in that area as well. I wholly recommend getting this game and truly hope you enjoy it as much as I have! :)

Dead by Daylight is a game I hate to love, but a game I love to hate. For starters: The community for this game complains a LOT when things don't go their way. Killer players AND Survivor players will constantly say their roles are underpowered, or that the other is overpowered when they don't perform well, or they get killed by something they deem "Unfair". Just learn your Killer and their perks or the basics of being a Survivor, and try not to listen to anyone in post-game chat if they flame you for doing bad. You WILL perform pretty terribly for a bit of your games, but that's okay. Survivors Goal - Repair 5 / 8 Generators on the map, open an exit gate, and escape whilst being hunted down by the Killer to be sacrificed to the Entity. Killer's Goal - Kill as many Survivors you can before they all escape in any way possible. It's extremely fun alone: When playing Killer, or trying random perk builds in solo-queue (You + 3 other random players.) OR In a group of friends by: Bullying the Killer, trying perk combinations with your friends, trolling each other. Whichever way you decide to play the game, you WILL get your moneys worth out of Dead by Daylight. The game-play loop, though unbalanced is very simple to understand, allowing you to pick it up quick and stay with it if it's something you enjoyed. Some general terms you should know. Slugging - Leaving survivors down to pursue other chases or to avoid flashlight saves. [b] Camping - Staying near a hooked survivor until their timer goes down, ensuring a sacrifice. Tunneling - Focusing 1 of the 4 survivors for the whole entire game / until they inevitably die.[/b] ^ These 2 are usually referred to as "Toxic" from the killer side, but you should play how you want. Gen rushing - Generators getting done extremely fast, usually 2+ in 1 chase. 3 Gen / 3 Genned - 3 close generators that are easy for the killer to patrol, making the game extremely difficult to win. Looping - Running the killer in circles using windows / LOS (Line of Sight) blockers / pallets to keep him distracted from your team whilst they do generators. Kobe - When you successfully get off the hook in stage 1 by attempting escape. Thanks for reading, and enjoy!

I have been a huge fan of the AC series and have legitimately enjoyed every single game except for the Chronicle games. I have been known to be leniant toward the series about things that a lot of other people are usually much harsher about. Here's why I am absolutely loving AC Origins so far. It is completely and 100% seamless, where the only loading screens (that are pretty short on a HDD btw) are when you fast travel and going in and coming out of cutscenes. Unlike in the previous games where there's a loading screen anytime you leave a city and such, this game has none of that. The size of the world and the seamlessness reminds me of the Witcher 3's world. The controls are a bit confusing at first because they changed it from the previous games so veterans of the series might be put off at first HOWEVER there is an alternate control scheme that is basically classic AC controls. The modern era stuff, which a lot of people dislike, is very minor like in AC Unity and Syndicate. Hunting and wildlife is a lot more immersive and well done compared to AC 3 and Black Flag. There is microtransactions in the game HOWEVER they are actually completely unnecessary and a nonfactor in the game, you can get any outfit, money, etc. all on your own in the game at a reasonable pace. MT's are there, but please do not let that deter you, because you definitely don't need them. This also seems to be one of the best optimized games in the series as well. I have a 1080Ti and an Intel i7 Quad Core and at max settings I get straight 60 FPS. Your mileage may vary obviously if you have a weaker system but from first glance and the amount of possible graphics options available in the settings, it is very much optimised well, way better than Unity, Syndicate, and even Black Flag. Also, for those who care about Steam achievements, its also the first AC game to have Steam achievements which is nice. If I had one complaint about the game so far, is that like previous games, in the beginning parts of the world are block by story progression. It doesn't last long, but its there. If I were to give it an arbitrary score out of 10, it'd be 9/10. EDIT: I forgot to mention, but another major plus is that they have gotten rid of optional objectives, allowing for much more freedom with missions and much less frustrations. However they have also gotten rid of the memory sequence system, where you could replay missions and the like. EDIT #2: Do not sit on this game. It really is THE best in the series and that's from someone who already loves the series.

The tombs, the pyramids and just the sheer landmass is a beauty to traverse. Sadly, as with most Ubisoft games, thay fail to make that world feel like its actually livable. In early production they said they wanted to make a 'Witcher 3' kind of a open world game, but they fail to make it believeble. People just stand and walk around. Don't really act like real human beings and all scream to each other. Every time you encouter a guard somewhere he seems to be angry at you and screams some insults. This is totally gamebreaking because the gaurd in question has no knowledge about you whatsoever. Small irritations like this is Ubisofts hallmark. They create vast world but lack the finesse to really expend on them and make them feel believeble. When you get past this point the game opens up. The story picks up and really sucks you into it. Bayek, the main character, feels like a real person with strenghts and weaknesses. The main quests feel like they have gravity and are a bunch of fun to play through. If you have a love for old history make that double. Its great to feel involved with real world history and have a hand in shaping it. Very well executed. Side quests are a mixed bag. Again i will be refering to the Witcher 3. All the people that give you quests feel real and believeble and have awesome dialouge. Not here sadly. A fixed camera angle and a not so interesting sob story dont get me in the mood at all. Turn off. The open world map is way to crowded with points of interest and side quests. I dont really feel like its soemthing for me but i do understand the appeal. A LOT of hours can be spent and thats a real good investment for your time. Combat has been revamped and is now somewhat more then jsut pressing 'attack and counter' like the previous AC titles. [h1]Overall score: 6.5/10 Did I get my money's worth?: Yes Recommended input: Controller[/h1] With the majority of the reviews for South Park: TSoT being from fans of the show, I'm writing as someone who has never taken interest in South Park, critiquing The Stick of Truth for what it is: a video game. [h1]Overview[/h1] TsoT is a turn-based RPG with the primary selling point being that it takes place in the world of South Park, a show known for its crude humor. You play as a new kid moving into the town and are able to select from one of [i][b]four classes[/b][/i], Warrior, Mage, Thief, and Jew - yes, there is a Jew class. From what I understand, the game is more or less the same regardless of your choice of class, but your equipment and abilities will vary depending on your choice, which is cool. In battle, you will usually have a buddy of your choice, each one being very different and some of them having uses outside of combat. Playing comfortably, [i][b]the main story has about 7-8 hours of gameplay with probably about 6 hours more of side content[/b][/i] in the form of missions and other activities, like searching for collectables. [h1]The good[/h1] The Stick of Truth's combat system is pretty straightforward and [i][b]just about anyone should be able to pick up and play the game[/b][/i]. I find the combat to be most [i][b]comparable to Legend of the Dragoon or the Mario & Luigi RPG games[/b][/i] for Nintendo handhelds, both being series' I've enjoyed. TSoT features many things that RPG fans can expect to see from an RPG, like [i][b]different classes, abilities, items, and choice of strategy[/b][/i]. Most of the game takes place outside of combat, which is just as enjoyable. The area that the game takes place in is densely-packed and there's [i][b]plenty of incentive to explore[/b][/i] the world and talk to NPCs. I can happily say that [i][b]the use of buddies is one of the best things about the game[/b][/i]. Each one was very well made and fun to use. In order of unlock, you're given Butters the paladin, Kenny the seductress, Stan the warrior, Jimmy the bard, Kyle the war chief, and Cartman the wizard. Each buddy brought their own tactics to the battle and they were fun to experiment with. Butters was the buddy I used most of the time, due to his ability to heal, damage many enemies at once, and deal reasonable damage to armored targets. Deserving of its own paragraph is the fact that TSoT is [i][b]one of very few RPG games where grinding isn't necessary[/b][/i]. Personally, I enjoy grinding, at least to an extent, but many complaints about other RPG games is the need to grind or the impossible difficulty of the story missions without completing some side missions for added rewards. [h1]The bad[/h1] TSoT is a bit [i][b]spoon-feedy with its difficulty curve[/b][/i]. With the lack of need to grind, I never found myself in need of anything. My level was where it needed to be or higher, I always had great gear acquired normally through the story, I was never in need of potions (very often reaching capacity limits on many of them) and I ended the game with waaaay more money than I needed. In most turn-based RPG games, you can either attack or use an item. TSoT allows you to do both as well as doing the same with your available buddy. With resources being nearly free, being able to heal to full health AND attack twice in one turn leaves very little for challenge. Going a step further, your buddy can both use their ability and attack, giving you free healing, stat boosts, or added damage every turn. With having Butters as my buddy, I could heal to full health with just one nearly free item and still get both attacks or abilities. To make things even easier, once you have at least two buddies available, you can use a buddy's turn to switch them out. Once your buddy is low on health, you can have them switch to another buddy with full health and mana. Your main character is already very strong as it is, everything I mentioned here is [i][b]just to make the game even easier[/b][/i]. The Stick of Truth gives you a lot of options to cheese your way through the game, [i][b]reducing the overall enjoyment[/b][/i] of the game. At this point, [i][b]I'd rather have to grind[/b][/i] than just be handed the win. Fans of South Park go absolutely nuts over the humor, but I found it to be very hit-or-miss. There were some jokes about Jews or black people that made me smile and I gave the occasional chuckle at how wild the game got at certain points (like fighting giant nazi zombie fetuses), but half the time the humor is just "haha poop and FARTS xD" which made me sigh quite a lot. I don't expect this type of humor to change and I'm positive I'm in a minority here, but [i][b]the game as a whole really wasn't that funny[/b][/i] due to these constant dips in quality. [h1]Other things you should know[/h1] At normal price, TSoT [i][b]costs $30 which is way too much[/b][/i]. Fortunately the game gets marked down for as much as 75% off during sales and TSoT was a featured game in April 2016's Humble Monthly Bundle, which is how I got it. I enjoyed the game, but it certainly isn't worth regular price. If you are thinking about buying TSoT, I urge you to wait for a good sale.
