Ever since 2.0, something started going terribly wrong with the AI in stellaris. It has became worse in pretty much everything...from economy management, plantery building, ship and fleet building and general decision - making. For me, this has got to the point that in EVERY game I start the same scenario repeats itself (this is on max difficulty and max aggression with max everything else i missed), and this has becomes twice as pathetic now in 2.2. ​ Game starts, borders are formed, allies/rivals are made, anomalies are scanned and exploration is done. AI stops brain dead in its tracks, 30 year in, can't build any proper fleets let alone customize its ships to be even relevant in space combat, planets are poorly managed and the AI falls behind very fast compared to the player. Since all of the AI empires are equally pathetic, wars are uncommon, even in high aggression and the results from them are barely noticeable at all. the galaxy turns stale before the mid game even starts. Me, the player, yawns at the screen, building stuff and counting years for some fallen empire to awaken or crisis to pop out before I give up on the playthrough, occasionally I wipe some empires here and there when I feel like expanding my borders and clear some leviathans. Crisis starts, if its on the other side of the galaxy, by the time I get there I usually get bored out and stop playing, if its somewhere nearby then the game turns to be interesting for some time. Crisis ends, player economy, military and power gap is 40x times than the AI empires.. Exit to main menu > start new game. ​ Give you an example of my current devouring swarm play through in 2.2. By year 2303, half the galaxy formed against me, nobody bothers to declare war. 70 years earlier I wiped out a neighboring empire with a 5k fleet. Since then, nothing interesting happened in the galaxy, no wars, no interaction except endless defense treaties. BY 2303, FINALLY, I get declared by a federation......10 min later, i see a "Red aircraft" symbol approaching my border and my eyes grow wider...the federation fleet comes at my first space port and..... Its a 7k combined fleet, composed of destroyers and corvettes ARMED TO THE TEETH WITH AS MANY POINT DEFENSE AND FLAK AS THE AI COULD MUSTER. That, EPIC federation fleet got wiped by my 5k total power space port + domesticated space squid I parked there 50 years earlier. This, combined with the god awful micromanagement introduced in 2.2 by, essentially, removing sector functions from the game (and the camera stutter...) , forced me to just say "Fuck that", exit the game, write a negative review and post this wall. Don't get me wrong, I'm all in for those kinds of re-works, and I believe they were necessary and I gladly learn new mechanics and all...but stuff like that just sucks any enjoyment from the game for me. I play Stellaris since 1.3 and this is the first time that I just can't get myself to play anymore. I remember in 1.9, as a fanatic purifier-type empire i was fighting for my bloody life 20 years into the game. AI empires were freaking relentless at trying to wipe me off the face of the galaxy and action and tension were inevitable every time the 10-year war pause ended, I was glued to my chair. Where has it gone? what happened? why is the AI so incompetent now? ​ Giving the AI a 1000x economy boost and adding 10 more difficulty levels is not the solution to the problem. Unfortunately, I cannot with good conscience recommend this game at this stage in its development. PROS: ++ Graphics are beautiful, save for some animation and clipping issues, and the music is great, despite not being played very often. ++ The first moments of scavenging for items feel very appropriate for this game and set a fitting mood. ++ The possibility of finding recipes and experimenting with food crafting and different cooking stations adds a nice depth and immersion, should you want to expand on your chef qualities or roleplays. + Seeing islands slowly show up in the horizon adds a very Wind Waker-esque feeling. CONS: --- An extreme lack of content. --- The game ends up being as empty and barren as the vast ocean it's taking place on. -- Mere hours into the game, every task and event ends up being repetitive, from the shark attacks to the cooking and smelting of resources. - Actually approaching and exploring islands is very limited and disappointing. Overall: 3,5/10 - Potential in the future, but the present is barren and lacking. Playing this game with friends is absolutely the best way to experience this game, but even so, the game is so severely limited and empty that it gets repetitive and boring within hours. It has the feel of an open world exploration game, but ends up being strictly a resource management game, which can feel frustrating in the beginning, but quickly ends up a task too easy to handle. With a raft filled with chests with every possible resource imaginable, there's nothing left for the game to provide, with no actually interesting events or enemies. Everything you see in the game feels like a new discovery, like something you'll enjoy exploring, but actually approaching them up close gives nothing but a deep disappointment. At the end of the day, the most exciting parts of the game are building the raft - a task which ends up being very frustrating because of frequent shark attacks - and recipe experimentation - if you enjoy cooking in games, for whatever reason, be that roleplaying or just to discover and exhaust possibilities. The endless stream of debris and the surreal nature of the shark often took me out of any immersion I had found myself in, and for presenting itself in-game as an open world exploration game, it never rewards exploration and for any actual progress, the game forces you in specific directions. There's no open world or exploration in this game, at least none that feels exciting or rewarding. The game is currently way too empty to be thoroughly enjoyed, despite having an interesting idea and nice potential in theory.

So nice I bought the game twice. Once for the PS3 and once for the PC. Saints Row 3 is a masterclass of absurdity, for better or for worse. It's often times on discount and I recommend it over GTAV any day of the week. The plot revolves around the Third St Saints, a street gang, once hardened criminals have found themselves selling out. They have become so popular that they do photoshoots and sign autographs during bankrobberies. And that lies one of the major problems with Saints the humor can get gratting at times. Not every joke lands. A Star Wars title crawl over stars while "Thus Sprach Zarathustra" by Strauss is especially eye-rolling. Strauss's compistion is from 2001. There is no reason for it to be there. It's a reference for references sake. The core problem with the writing is with it's satire though. It wants to make fun of consumerism or capitalism or something but the absurdity overtakes the original joke and therefore it becomes muddled. A street gang that become celibrities is a interesting concept but it has no real message overall. In fact, none of the characters really seem too introspective about their situation. None of them grow. None of them care. Nevertheless, the characters really do bring you into the world and are incredibly likable. The scene in which the player and another member of the gang sing along to Sublime's "Where it's At" is especially memoriable. Sadly, you can't replay missions and must reload old save data which you have to back up manually. The main draw to Saints Row 3 is undoubtably it's appeal to your inner most childish id. Missions vary from driving with a live tiger, to shooting up bad guys falling from a burning airplane. As for weapons, the gangs all here. Pistols, machine guns, rocket launchers, and energy weapons pack your arsenal. Alot of attention in the games advertisments has been placed on the bat shaped purple dildo that you can wack people into next week with. I recall they gave out real life replicas of the weapon to influencers. Personally, nothing is as viseral as the chainsaw but the dildo bat has definitly earned a spot of favorite video game weapons right beside Half Life's gravity gun and Goldeneye's RCP90. Vehicles both land, sea, and air are accessable across the weird and wacky world of Saints Row. Navigation is done better than almost any other open-world game to date even almost ten years after it's original release. Holographic arrows point to you directing you where to turn on each corner. This allows the mobility and freedom to explore without restraint of guiding walls common in racing games, while not forcing you to look at a mini map at the smallest corner of the screen and taking your eye off the road common in most open world games. The soundtrack is top notch, Kanye West's "Power" is the perfect theme to mow down rival gang members to. Zombie's make a appearence much to the dismay of many critics at the time. Zombie fatigue was setting in at the time of this games release. As the game has aged the trope seems less contrived but still seems somewhat out of place and superflous. As far as gameplay goes Saint's Row 3 remains one of the greatest open world games of all time. It has held up to the test of time and is relativily cheap.

Monster Hunter: World is a multi-faceted game I have a blast playing and it fits perfectly to my gaming tastes. After 200 hours playing I feel I have to make a review for it. I would recommend this game to you: -If you like the idea of toppling behemoths and big beasts. -If you want an RPG where you can play as multiple "classes" with 1 character and not have to create an arsenal of characters just to enjoy the different styles of combat the game has to offer. -If you like fast paced action combat with many strategic layers built into it (example: hitting monsters weak points and positioning properly to avoid getting hit) -If you want a nice co-op experience as the game is built for teamplay. -If you want a game you can also play alone if your friends are not online or existent. -If the concept of skinning a beast of its' hide and making clothing for your character is appealing to you. -If you do not care intensely for an amazing story, as the story is somewhat of a tutorial to the actual game rather than the game itself. -If you like cats, as you have a cat-like creature as a companion. -If you want a game that can make good use of your good graphics card. Now the game is not perfect, there are many issues with it such as: -Crashes which may result in loss of progress. (Might be fixed in future) -Lack of appearence-altering mechanic for armor, thus an end-game character built with specific statistics in mind can look like a gypsy instead of awesome. (Might be implemented in future). -Lack of a clear statement from the company wether modding the game is allowed or not. -Existence of mods that can "break" the game or skip crucial part of game (The end-game farm) making a thousand-hour worth title a weekend experience where you have all builds for all weapons ready very quickly. -Existence of cheaters. I have encountered 1 in my 200hours so far. For me, all those negatives are deal-breakers on an average game, but Monster Hunter: World, being my first Monster Hunter game, is THAT good, that I can overlook those, and recommend this game for you to buy, on the premise that the gamebreaking crashes will be fixed. Until they are not fixed, I can understand you wanting to stay away from the game. Overall I'd rate the game an 7/10, but with crashes fixed and an armor appearence altering mechanic in place, it'd be an easy 9/10. Sadly the game can never be a 10/10 as the story is lackluster at its best.

I played this game during early access back when it had the base bosses and no cutscenes. I've watched it grow to what is today and can say that I'm proud to have paid full price. The game is just all around great when it comes to the platforming design. Lets get into what I like and dislike about the game. (For a quick and rather lackluster summary, go to the bottom) Soundtrack: I absolutely adore the soundtrack for this game, and can't help but sing along to each area's bgm when I play. The only problem I can think of when it comes to the soundtrack is the fact that there's not that many tracks. This is mostly because of the lack of different levels which I will get into now. Level Design: Each tile set is dependent on the level you enter. There are two fire levels, two ice levels, to ?ruins? levels, and two sky levels. The final boss zones each have their own tile sets as well. Each tile set is randomly generated depending on what order they are on your advancement; an example being level one has simple traps and easy platforming while level eight has numerous traps and difficult platforming. The levels also get longer the further you make it in your run. The randomness is nice if you're a person who enjoys skill based platforming and never needing to memorize each level's layout. All together, there are about six different levels that each have their own random tilesets. Gameplay: The game is very similar to the X series. There's wall sliding and wall jumping, and dashing as well. However, while the game plays like a Megaman game, it also pulls a similar item system from Binding of Issac. Instead of finding each item to unlock it, you have to get these in game collectible type currencies (called soul chips) that stay with you after death or completion of a run. You then use these things to buy new items and expand the upgrades you can get while progressing through each level. It takes time, and you'll probably end up dying many times before you beat a run, but once you get enough upgrades unlocked, you'll find that the game gets quite simple. It is also nice that it tells you what each item does before you pick it up, so you don't end up wasting your time or money. Speaking of money, there is also another type of currency that only appears in a run and does not travel with you after death or completion. This stuff (called nuts) is used for purchasing the upgrades that you've unlocked with the soul chips. You will end up getting a lot more of these because they only stay with you for each run. Characters: Without the DLC, you have two playable characters; Ace and Nina. Nina is very similar to X when it comes to movement and combat. She uses an arm cannon that shoots lemons (hooray!) and a charge up that fires a nice big blast. She's much easier to use than Ace simply because she has ranged attacks. Ace is a lot like Zero in the fact that he uses melee weapons. They do more damage than Nina's weapons but put you at risk because of how close to each enemy it puts you. He is also unable to double jump so it effectively makes him just a close ranged version of Nina. The DLC characters are a bit strange. Hawk is based around using your abilities while draining energy from enemies to fuel them. Her drain ability is actually just her basic attack which is a close ranged whip, while a good number of her other abilities are longer ranged. Draco is also somewhat of a closer ranged character as well. He's more focused on dealing lots of damage while also being a bit more versitile in his abilities. All in all, Hawk and Draco are relatively similar and challenging to use, but they add a bit more diversity and playstyles than the base characters have to offer. Dislikes: I don't have many dislikes for the game honestly. It does a very good job of feeling like a Megaman game while also incorporating other types of gameplay to spice things up and make it it's own game. I suppose if I did have to say some negatives about the game, they would be these: The game is heavily centered on having multiple runs to unlock every item and try to see how fast you can finish a run, but after you've gotten every item, or you've run through the game hundreds of times, there really isn't much to do. I suppose this is generally how most Megaman games go, in my opinion, but it just doesn't have much substance after you get everything. I guess it is something you can just come back to and do a few runs every now and again, but not something you'll sit down and play everyday even after getting all the items. There isn't much of a story either. While they do have a few simple cutscenes and a little bit of story, it's nothing that you can really sink into. The game is really just all about getting items to make each run easier and faster. The characters are also a bit iffy. Nina and Ace are rather similar to each other and the only real difference being their main weapons. The DLC characters are also a bit bland as well, although they do have a bit more complexities to them. There are also not very many actual levels besides the four main ones and the two final boss levels which also means there aren't all that many songs. In the end, I'm sure I missed a few things, but these are all the things I could come up with off the top of my head. I love the game and how it feels. The controls are tight and feel responsive and the levels are randomized so you won't play the same map every time. The soundtrack is also great even though there aren't that many songs. And the characters are fun to use, some more challenging than others although in the end still somewhat similar. I would deffinately recommend the game to anybody who likes the Megaman franchize and also like the randomness from Binding of Issac. Even then, I would still suggest giving it a try if you just simply like platformers because of the feel of it.

Ori and the Will of the Wisps is like coming home after a few years. You walk in the front door, and there's what you left behind, nearly exactly like you left it. Sure, some of the furniture's moved about but overall the same people, the same feelings that you loved are there. The longer you stick around for though, you see that there's more than nostalgia is letting you see. The old creaky door to the upstairs bedroom is finally fixed. You're amazed that it got better, you never even expected it to get fixed before because it was "FINE" you guess but... dang, that's some good door. And everything starts to feel like it's going to be perfect. But you get this feeling that something's off. You're not sure what but, it's someth- and then you're staring at the treehouse in the backyard. It was the best, wasn't it? Just to go on up there whenever something was wrong, because something would ALWAYS, always end up going wrong... and then the small little 8x8 foot space with a roof that was always just the right height for you to stand under lets you in for however long you need. Until everything's blown over and you get called back inside for the night. And everything's OK again. Everything's perfect, a happy ending. Now you're about as tall as the ladder that made you feel like the king of the world, like you were untouchable. You can't even stand inside the treehouse without bonking your head on the roof. It really kind of bums you out that THIS part of everything had to be the thing to change, the ONE THING that doesn't feel right. And it sucks. Until a little later, when you see your little sibling climb up that ladder with a friend of theirs from a window in the house. You see them smiling and laughing and just enjoying their moment like they thought it would never end. And you come around to the idea that the changes aren't bad. They're good... great even. It IS still perfect. Maybe it's not exactly perfect for YOU, but nothing ever is. You realize that things couldn't have ended up better any other way. And you're content with that. As you hug those people you loved like nothing else goodbye and head back to where you're really needed, you're glad. You're glad you got to see that old house again, and got to see the door get fixed, and got to see that the old treehouse is still one of the best goddamn treehouses you've ever seen. Ori and the Will of the Wisps is like coming home. It brings the same emotions of happiness, sadness, excitement and satisfaction Moon Studios brought with Blind Forest. And I can't wait 'till I visit again.

The basic premise had been touched on by pretty much everyone; it's Mega Man with rogue-lite elements added in. There's power ups, a ton of them, various weapons, and then a bunch of bosses with their own unique weapons you gain some limited use of. There's also two different core characters, one of whom uses a gun and one of whom uses a sword as their primary fire. My only real complaint is that there's not enough variation to the randomization of the levels or enemies; they basically take various premade chunks and fit them together, with later levels having harder versions of those same chunks (extra lasers or fire or whatever, for instance). Eventually, while the order varies, you start to recognize each individual part. Still, much better than doing the same static levels again and again regardless. Similarly, there's not as many different enemy types as you'd hope, after a late run through any given level, you'll have seen all of them. Still, overall, it's a great game, well worth your money if you like this sort of thing, especially when it's on sale.

I already had the free version of Black Mesa mod and have been playing the Unforseen Consequences level back-to-back with this new Steam release of the same mod with added polish. So how does the paid version of Black Mesa compare to the free mod? It's a bit early to tell, but the overall scenes seem slicker with some nice atmospheric fog added to the larger rooms. New weapon models/skins are added to the paid version. More NPC voice scripting/nicer animations. But one thing noticeable was, playing on normal, the enemies took less ammo to put down. In fact, just a few hits with the crowbar was all it took to level a zombie, whilst 2 rounds of the pistol took out a headcrab. Another noticeable thing was crouch-jumping onto pipes, etc was a lot smoother. So is it worth paying £14.99 when there's a free version out there? To a lot of people probably not. The free mod is such a joy to play in itself, it hardly seems justified to pay 15 quid for the newer version. But here's why I did: Having loved Half Life 1 for so long over the years, I want to experience the very best it can be, complete with atmospherics, weapon balancing and NPC dialogue/animations. The original Black Mesa may have 'just been' a fan-made mod, but it turned out to be so well crafted. It has given me many hours of enjoyment that I feel I want to give something back to the devs in the way of paid support. I trust the devs to deliver the Xen level which I'm really looking forward to. And the multiplayer support. So in a nutshell. I'd say buy this game if you're a Half Life afficianado and want to support the devs, play multiplayer, but for others, I'd say stick with the free mod until there's enough difference between the two.

I hate to see so many negative reviews for this game. I know that there has been a lot of issues with disconnects in mutliplayer. Although I think it's bit better than it was. I've played Monster Hunter 1 & 2 on PSP, and 3 on Wii, and 4 on 3DS... so I'm a bit of a fan of the series. I was eager to get into MHW when I first heard about it, but was sad to hear it wasn't on any platform I owned... and I am done buying gaming consoles. But I was very excited to hear about it's release on PC! Finally! A Monster Hunter on PC! I've been wanting this for a long time! This game is a blast to play! You are a puny human that hunts monsters that are larger than life! You have to track them down and brawl it out in an epic heart-pumping battle! You really feel like you have the disadvantage and you really have to fight hard and strategize to bring the monster down. It gives you a very satisfying sense of accomplishment when you are victorious over a particularly nasty monster. The areas are very diverse and the monsters feel almost real. Some monsters will have turf wars that can be so entertaining to watch, it can be easy to forget your mission objective! Even fighting the same monster can still be a very different experience because you never know what will happen. Will another monster come in and stir things up? Will something happen in the environment that will throw a monkey wrench in your plans? You never know. And the fun and excitement is multiplied when playing with friends. For those that have played the previous Monster Hunter games, there are some changes in this one that I see as improvements. Some may disagree, but I'll list some so you can decide for yourself: [list] [*]The areas are one big seamless map now. They are still divided into zones by number, but you don't wait for loading between zones. You can just run from one zone to another without interruption. It makes the world feel more real. [*]You can have multiple camps per area (and you can choose your starting camp). You can fast travel to camps (unless carrying something like a wyvern egg), and while in camp you can access your item box, your equipment for you and your palico, and you can eat a meal in case you forgot to do so in town or you lost the effects of your previous meal by being carted off to camp. [*]No more having to worry about pickaxes or whetstones. They are items that are always with you now and the pickaxe never breaks and the whetstone his unlimited uses. [*]No more having to worry about different sets of armor based on if you are melee or range. So you can wear the same set of armor when wielding a hammer or a bow. You just get a physical damage resistance boost if melee and an elemental damage resistance boost if range. [*]No more paintballs or paint shots. Instead, everything is based on tracking. You look for monster footprints, scratches, droppings, etc which will give you more information on the monster you are hunting. Once you have enough information on a monster that you know how to track them, you can use "scout flies" to point you in the direction of the monster. If you get good enough at tracking a particular monster, you can even predict the monster's destination when it is on the move by finding a big X on the map. [*]Using the "scout flies" mentioned above, you can track other things that aren't even monsters. You can select a resource you want to gather on the map, and the scout flies will point you there. Or you can select another player and the scout flies will guide you to the other player. [/list] All of that said, there are still some multiplayer issues from time to time. There's nothing more frustrating than starting a multiplayer investigation with a voucher only to be kicked off and be stuck in a mission scaled for multiplayer. At that point you can either tough it out and try to fight monsters that are not intended for single player... or you can give up and accept that you will lose the investigation and voucher. But in all, I think it's worth it. It's currently my favorite PC game.

I'll be honest: I've always been a bit of an AC fanboy. But by the time AC Unity and Syndicate rolled around, I really felt like the games were running out of steam. I still loved Syndicate, and never lost faith in the AC games, but I was slowly getting bored. So, when I saw how different AC Origins was, I was both excited and apprehensive. The idea of a reworked AC seemed like a huge gamble, but I can confidently say that it was worth it. AC Origins is a masterpiece, and something I absolutely recommend to all. If you haven't played any of the other Assassin's Creeds, then this is a great place to start. It's not really full stealth mode like the previous installments, but the reason for that makes sense: The Brotherhood isn't created yet. I've only played this game for 17 hours since release, but have only completed around 14 percent of the game because there's so much to do. There are very few bugs, and exploring the world actually means something for once. The side quests are actually interesting and worthwhile to do, and although there is a little grinding from time to time, entering missions as a bit underlevelled isn't completely impossible and really tests your skills as an Assassin. Origins first felt a bit like Far Cry 3/4 in the whole liberate-the-camp bit, and it's fair to say that the game was somewhat inspired by the Witcher 3, but the rest of the game is completely Assassin's Creed. 9.5/10 must play

If you want to play a short, xcom style turn-based combat game then Mutant Year Zero: Road to Eden will not dissappoint. Taking place in post apocalyptic Sweden, all that is left are rogue robots and talking animals called Mutants. You roleplay as a group of Mutants whose job is to be a Stalker, scavengers of the rot infested wasteland that search for scrap and resources. In order to sustain their hideout called the Ark, the Stalkers must embark on a dangerous quest. Regarded only as myth, a place called Eden rumors to hold humanity's last civilization. What was once a quest to find survivors becomes a quest to find truth. Visually the environment and NPCs are stunning. Exploring the world space felt rewarding. The unique visual style suits well with the comical characters and their corny jokes. Gameplay consists mostly of roaming around in search of items, and engaging in combat whether stealthily or loudly. And there is something so satisfying when customizing gear and weapons to your liking. I recommend playing on highest difficulty if you are looking for a challenge. For its price, I'd say only fans of turn-based games will especially enjoy this. Or maybe if you're just itching for a well made indie game.

Unfortunatley, it's not without its faults, default 1 Turn per Year Campaign and the very limited city construction makes the Campaign Map a bore, not to mention the wait times after ending your turn (Although they've improved they still suck) But apart from that, it's a very pretty game, with very fluid combat, although it does end abruptly. Another problem is units rarely stay in formation, putting Hoplites in a phalanx will often result in the units and the front of the phalanx running out of formation and getting their asses kicked, unlike in Rome 1 where phalanxes were unbeatable unless you flanked the unit. Siege AI is also still retarded as hell. All the units feel unique in their own sense as well, and rarely feel like clones of each other, with most units having their own specail abilities to accompany them. The Battle AI on land battles is usually pretty smart as well, although it still does the same shit it did in Empire where the enemy would refuse to march at you when you were on the defense, so unless you wanted to wait 60 minutes for the battle to end, you had to charge the enemy. This is especially annoying playing as a Hoplite reliant faction like Athens or Sparta. The voices are excellent though, and I'm glad that leader speeches are back in the game, even if they aren't cinematic. I'd love the leadership speeches of Medieval 2 to return at some point, those were swell. Also the combined naval/land battles is also great, and having your navy save the lives of your broken and ragged land army running from a 5000 strong Parthian horde is amazing. Although the game is still flawed in several ways, it's a great game at the core, if you don't compare it to Rome 1 and its expansions, and still better than the monstrosity that was Empire.

Okay so I have this game for a while now, and for some reason I'm writing a review about it right now. It's a pretty fun game, but like most games it does have it's pros and cons. It's definitely easy to pick it up, but in my opinion it does have a pretty steep learning curve. For example, you'll learn quickly how to control your car on the ground and also how to aim when hitting a ball, but after that things become a lot harder and take more time to learn. Since this game is multiplayer only (I don't count playing with bots or practice mode), you might not like this game if you get frustrated about teammates easily. Furthermore there are not really a lot of cons. Some people do complain about the ranking systems, since it really feels like you barely rank up when winning several matches, but derank after losing just one match. I never really had this issue, so I don't really have anything to say about it, but don't be surprised if this also happens to you, you're not the only one. Now about the pros: it's easy to pick up and really fun to play, every game feels like a new and fresh experience and there are several different gamemodes which you can try [i]if[/i] you're getting bored with regular matches. (you probably won't) You might think you would get bored after some games, but just like a lot of people have with mobas, every match feels differently since different people have different playstyles and your playstyle will have to adapt to that. The game is fluent, there haven't been any frustrating bugs as far as I know and even if there is a small bug it's mostly not a problem for the game. In my experience you barely have toxic players, as long as you don't completely mess up for your team. This however does depend on how good you are, because on lower ranks you'll find more toxic players than on higher ranks, obviously. The cooperation between Rocket League and Monstercat is also quite nice because you can listen to "normal" music instead of random boring menu music. Furthermore I don't think I have anything else to say, I can only say that it's a great game which you should definitely try out. 10/10 ~Monsieur Lenny

Probably the closest thing that us, the general population, has towards a realistic military simulator/game. I suggest that you do not buy this if you are expecting a linear fast paced action game like CoD or Battlefield, this is much more in-depth then that. This is not simply, running around 360 no scoping people. Squad Managment and effective communication is necessary. There is also something that you can't experience in the said titles above, which is long-range combat. (An example of this is preforming an assault on a base/camp with armor, artillery and other assests from varying distances from your own base. However, this is still a game and should be taken lightly from time to time. I suggest learning how to do tricks in the littlebird (MH9-Hummingbird) and exploiting the terrible physics. This game has multiple different gamemodes and tasks that could be simulated. So you'll never have the same experience twice. Pros: -Very Realistic. -Great Graphics (If you can run them). -Interactive Environment. -Realisitc Vehicals (Most of the time). ------------------------------------------------------------------------ Cons: -Physics (You will hear "Arma Physics" referred to multiple times). -Muliplayer Optimization. -Very steep learning curve but you will appreciate it over time. (More of a learn as you play) -Occasional Crashing. -Controls will more than likely conflict your normal keyboard setup, I suggest using the Arma 2 setup. Overall 10/10 Even if you don't think this is for you, trust me, the teamwork involved in this game is beyond amazing, the amount of co-op I've played counts for 95% of my game time. Great game with a lot of promise and clever concepts. Like SC survival maps, but with more resources and complexity in terms of land development. Great art and sound, visuals, etc. The problem is that it has either some serious balancing issues, or just isn't the right game for some people, depending on how you're looking at it. Basically, 90% of the game is babysitting resources. The top level players admit the game isn't really a true defense/survival game, because it's about expanding and building an economic empire, rather than focusing on zombie combat. The resource system is super-duper punishing and strict, resulting in few opportunities for inventive strats and emergent gameplay. More or less, there are certain build orders that are objectively better, and, like SC, you have to memorize and execute them perfectly, perhaps even more so than SC. The fact that zombies infect buildings just by touching, and not actually desroying them, exacerbates this issue. (I mean, seriously, if ONE zombie gets inside your base, its game over. Not even tower defense is that unforgiving!) It doesn't step as far back as SC in terms of micro, but you still have to do a lot of it, enough that, combined with the other ways the game is designed, make it unfun if you're looking for a turtling defense game. Which is where the source of my primary gripe comes from. A lot of effort was put into marketing this game as a zombie defense game, not only by the developers, but also by websites like Kotaku, which called it (to paraphrase) the game for people who like turtling and have played lots of SC defense maps. This is a huge misconception, and its frustrating because on the surface of it, the game REALLY seems like it is a pure zombie survival defense game. Early deaths and economic struggles are more likely to make players think that they're doing it wrong, or that the game is unbalanced, rather than realize that it simply isn't the game for them. I can't help but feel like this was deliberate, but maybe I'm wrong. In any case, a lot of retrofitting needs to be done to make sure that people properly understand that this is a Venture Capitalist RTS and not "the best SC survival map but with more complexity and its also steampunk". You'll like this game if you want really strict rules and having to do resource calaculations, if you want it to be all or nothing: die instantly or become invincible. If you want emergent gameplay, this game is not it. To reiterate, there's nothing wrong with this, its just that this game is really misleading. Like with most RTS games, the community is super toxic. I'm not thumbing down for that, though. And I will switch it to an upvote despite my personal distaste for the game design if significant effort is made to properly sell the game based on what it really is. I will also consider checking out the game again and switching to an upvote if the campaign mode makes significant improvements to the formula. It's possible that survival is not representitive at all of how the campaign will actually be, and I do feel like with tangible goals instead of "endless resource expansion with some survival", it could be a lot more fun. That remains to be seen, though, since the campaign has not been released yet. It's also possible that the devs may indeed pick up my vision of what this game was going to be, which could explain why what it says on the tin is so different from the contents. Survival for hardcore, campaign for fun mode. Starting with the ladder is obviously an odd foot to lead with, but I'm holding out hope that that may be the case.

Void Bastards is a cosmic, FPS rogue-lite that encourages planning ahead and tests your ability to make quick decisions. Its gut-blasting action mixes in well with its dark humor and cartoony, yet creepy atmosphere. Not to mention the game's flashy, comic book art style which is just the cherry on top of an already great game. As to be expected from the director of Bioshock and System Shock, the game has many similarities. Trap placement, map control, environmental hazards, and weapon combos are valuable tools in this game as well. The combat is as fast paced, or slow and stealthy as you want it to be, which was a factor that really drew me in. You'll have a client (a new one on every death too) with random traits. Your main task is simply flying from ship to ship, gathering parts to build weapons or the items you were specifically sent out to retrieve while making sure you're always snagging enough fuel and food. The ships you board have random enemies and conditions like frequent power outages or a better atmosphere for more oxygen. All together you'll have to weigh risk vs. reward, and if you're like me, get greedy and die a couple times. Definitely one of the best things I've played this year, but I still think the $30 price tag is a bit much. They are adding more content soon so it might be worth its asking price after that. If that's not a problem for you, then I can't recommend it enough.

I am conflicted about this game. On one hand this game has an amazing premise that is a lot of fun to play. The units are fun and balancing resources is difficult but not impossible. Particularly at the beginning this game keeps you on your toes and really has you planning ahead and frantically trying to both expand and not die at the same time. It's intense and rewarding when you succeed. This game has a glaring issue that makes me not want to try again. The beginning is fun, and the end is ridiculously difficult, but the middle is just a boring slog. Last night I spent two hours basically just waiting for the time to go down and quickly expanding out to the edges without any difficulty. I thought for sure I had won because everything was so easy. And then the final horde just bulldozed everything down and I lost. Now that in and of itself wasn't really a problem. I am OK with a challenge. What I am not ok with is spending another 4-5 hours total to get to that point. I feel like I have the early game down on normal (adequate?), but it is still fun and I'm willing to try it again. What I'm simply unwilling to do is waste the time on the mid game again just to either win or lose the last 2 minutes of the game. If I could reload my game from maybe 10 days before the end and try again, I probably wouldn't have such a problem with it. But the requirement to completely restart from the beginning and go through all of those hours again just to see if I can beat the end horde is too time consuming to be worth it. I honestly don't think the solution would be to lower the end horde. I think that the difficulty just needs to ramp up more linearly. It shouldn't go from killing the second to last horde basically without trying to getting steamrolled without even putting up a fight. Maybe it should go third to last with 2 hordes and second to last with 3 so you get a feel of what is going on? I also feel like towards the end of the game keeping constant streams of zombies coming at you would keep the pressure up and would make it more fun. I don't want to make it impossible but I just wish the mid game wasn't so long. Overall I don't regret this purchase. I feel like I got my $20 worth out of it. This game is still in Early Access so there is a lot of room for even Survival Mode to expand. I am really looking forward to the upcoming Campaign mode and will probably play the crap out of it. I would suggest everyone just try it because this issue bugs some people but not others, and at $20 it's worth just trying out to see if you like it or not. The addictive part of it is hard to describe and you should just try it for yourself.

I definitely liked the game more than I initially expected based on all the Steam reviews. For me, Far Cry 3 was still better than this especially regarding story-telling, but I had a lot more fun with this than with Far Cry 4 (never played Primal). The missions are fun and diverse so that it nevver really gets boring; not even for the few collection quests that can be done in quite a reasonable time frame. What I did not like though is that I felt like game/character progression was very lacking. In the very first hour when you don't have any weapons yet, I felt like my character was very vulnerable and I had to sneak though the woods very carefully and not attract any enemies, sneaking up on them an knocking them out. But only about an hour later I already felt like running around with different guns and shooting everyone down; nothing from these anxious moments were left. Also I felt that after clearing the first third of the map, I already unlocked everything I needed for my character. I had the "best" weapons and I did not feel like my character was advancing very much anymore. Once the armed helicopters become available (with auto-repair), clearing out outposts really become a piece of cake. Ammo is never a problem and after a while there is a "mobile gun shop" almost around every corner. I would have wished the game to be more challenging and much slower in progression, forcing you to be carefuly and sneaky for a longer than than it is now. Nonetheless, I enjoyed the game and having spent ~50 hours to complete the game and clear out all three regions 100%, I am happy with my investment.

This is a genuinely rewarding experience for players who enjoy resource management, Stronghold-style base construction and turtling. It needs work (hence the early access) especially around the map generation area, but it sets a very solid base for one of the most fun games I've played in ages. Some people seem awfully quick to complain that the game is too difficult and some scenarios are completely unwinnable; which is completely true, but those who persevere through a few rounds of unmitigated failure will find a good defensive location spawn and take the fight to the horde. This game needs: - Campaign Mode. - Map Editor (Dev supported. There is an unofficial one). - Choice of random or fixed starting location. - Vehicles (scouting & war-ready) - General expansion (Another advanced tech state?) If you are the kind of gamer who throws down the controller because a camping sniper ruined your streak, just don't bother. This is not a stress-free experience. If you want gentle serenity, try Banished. This is stuck-with-what-you-got post-apocalyptic survival which, more often than not, will not see you surviving until the end.
The core gameplay is much more refined and fun, this definnately a step up from XCOM 1.

Rocket League is where elegant design is combined with an engaging theme, resulting in a terrific gaming experience. The rules, objectives, and controls are simple enough for almost anyone to pick up very quickly. However, due to the physics at play, there is a surprising amount of depth to the maneuvers you can pull off using just the core set of moves (jump, boost, powerslide). Also, like any good sport game, positioning and awareness are key components that players can expore and practice with as they progress in experience. The theme is the icing on the gameplay cake. The bright colors and sound assets (roar of the stadium) further elevate the bombastic gameplay into something that will have your adrenaline pumping throughout the game. I haven't played a game in a while that has made me cheer out loud the way this game can (I'm sure my neighbors appreciate that). I recommend this game highly and will also be picking up the console version when it comes out.

its like the game knows, hey this fall will kill you, you cant use the hook now. and as stated from so many others, taking the hook from you in certain places in the story, cause youre exhausted. too exhausted to use a grabbling hook, but nowhere near to exhausted to parkour your way up a skyscraper, dangling from the sides of the walls jumping like a mutant upwards to the top. the human enemies, are as said, supervillains, that can dodge, deflect and parry just about all attacks, other than gunfire. they often dont get fased by a dropkick in the torso either. there are survivor encounters/events every so often. its fun to parttake in helping/saving them. problem is, often youll have to save them from a Goon, two Toads and/or a Demolisher. meaning, theyll die before you kill the zombies. eventho they fight back. and some of them looks like somewhat trained people. the story.. cliche, okay what did we really expect. well i became increasingly annoyed by the fact that youre reduced to nothing but an errandboy, youre the only "runner" in the city that can get things done. how people survived before you get to the city, is beyond my knowledge. and you get boned, over and over, you get called a monkey, imbicile and the likes. and you still just eat it all, and go yes sir let me do this incredibly dangerous meaningless task for you, you promised me loot. only to be bend over and dry docked in the bum bum. i get that youre the "good guy" but come on, more than a few times i wished i could just raise my weapon and smash their teeth out, telling them to shove it where the sun dont shine. but no no. youre Kyle Crane, the messiah. you get annoyed, but you still do everything they tell you to. three people die thats, somewhat big to the story, and none of them gets killed in any cool fashion, two of them turns zombie, where you think, hey i would love to kill them, but no a cutscene of you snapping their neck, and thats it. and the end boss is a QTE... no fighting, just dodge dodge dodge dodge dodge punch, stab. and then you get pushed over the side of the building, cause your protagonist is an idiot that lets the baddie live, hoping the gut would leave him bleeding to death, QTE again, stab him in the neck. done. thats another problem. i had a big problem getting invested in the main character. because you get so tired of hearing people boss you around calling you everything from a monkey to a moron. and you still help everyone out. you take all the abuse. youre nothing but a dumbed down lackey. and the game tries too hard to get "dem feels" up in you, that you need to feel bad for some of the survivors or those who die. the coop is fun, spite the fact that youre all playing as Kyle Crane, why not the host being Kyle Crane then the others were random runners? plus you cannot take quests or go through specific doors or places. without everyone being there. so if one is walking around killing zombies and another wanting to speak to npcs, that one cannot speak to, open specific doors or get quests, until the other player(s) either run to him/her or port over (pressing and holding B) and my god... you cannot complete the last quest coop, youll get booted from the hosts game, cause its singleplayer only. thats so damn stupid, why make coop when it negates the mode in the end. plus why have two skills tied to the same button? i had slam, when in mid air press and hold C to perform a slam attack, and a skill that allowed me to press C when i fell to save myself from damage. 9 out of 10 times, i would slam instead of safely landing. sprint + space and then e makes a dropkick, but if you have vault, youll often do a vault, cause thats sprint + jump when youre near and enemy. both skills require you to be, somewhat close to the enemy. lockpicking is super random, i get to a lock, i turn the pick around, look for the sweetspot, very carefully. i dont find it, i break around 3-5 picks. then i find the sweetspot, in an area of the lock where ive tried numerous times. other times i find the sweetspot, but its a bit off, so the pick breaks, i try again, now to find the sweetspot is not there, its in the oposite side now. i know many of these things has been said before, and its more of a spoiler, negative reveiw. With development on it starting way back in 2010, StudioMDHR's Cuphead is finally here. Officially announced in 2014, its been a hotly anticipated game for me and boy did it deliver. Punishingly hard at times but incredibly satisfying once you master the many bosses and levels it has to offer, Cuphead will both frustrate and please you. Thankfully, the game offers unlimited lives and you don't lose upgrades or coins upon death. The story is pretty simple, seeing as its inspired by 30's cartoons. Cuphead and his pal Mugman go to play dice but ultimately lose to the Devil and thus are forced to collect souls for him in the hopes of him sparing their soul. Given powers via a magical potion gifted by their friend, they set off to save their very souls. Cuphead, apart from playing at 60fps, genuinely feels like you are playing a cartoon from the 1930's. Full of vibrant colours, fast-paced and hectic music, and some truly imaginative enemy design, the game is bloody gorgeous. I felt like I was playing out a classic Max Fleischer or Disney cartoon, waiting for Betty Boop, Popeye, or Mickey & friends to pop out at any minute. With animations and colouring done completely by hand, its not hard to see why Cuphead took so long in development. Every single boss feels unique and has their own pattern to learn, with multiple phases to work through, getting intense the closer you get to the climax. The game even shows you how close you are to the end of a fight, as if to taunt you for getting so close (or nowhere at all). The screen can get incredibly busy at times with all the enemies and projectiles flying at you, causing you to die if you lose focus for even a second. Its not all bosses though, there are a handful of run and gun levels, featuring classic platformer elements. These are optional but by doing these you can collect gold coins to then purchase different weapons (especially Chaser, that upgrade will make your experience easier, trust me) and charms, such as one that auto-parries when you jump or briefly makes you invincible upon dashing. Super arts can also be acquired, requiring all 5 special meters to be charged, these vary in effect going from a ton of damage or brief invincibility. You also have flying sections where you control a plane that can shrink in size to dodge more easily but deal less damage, and later on, you can use bombs to deal more damage but have to be much closer to do so. These flying sections in particular were the hardest fights for me, having to dodge in all directions while having flying projectiles to deal with is really not my forte, but I eventually managed. The music, both in terms of theme and the actual sound quality of it, could be placed over one of the classic cartoons and it would not sound out of place. Particularly the King Dice song that plays between islands, I loved that damn piece. There are three islands that you'll be working your way through, but to move on to the next one you have to beat all the bosses, either in the simple mode or the regular mode, but to fight the final boss you do have to beat them on regular. So keep that salt handy, because it will flow. Initially, you have a mere three hit points with no means of restoring health during levels. You can get an upgrade that bumps it up to four but as you can only equip one charm at a time, its up to you whether you want that one extra hit point or something like brief invincibility. Co-op is local only, which is unfortunate. Keep in mind though that this makes bosses even more frantic as both of you have to dodge attacks, and, while you can revive each other, you still have to manage to stay alive to do so and reach their ghost in time. I should note that when it comes to platformers, I am pretty bad for the most part. This took me much longer than I expected to actually beat but once I did, I felt like a great weight had been taken off me, Cuphead lured me in with its gorgeous art style and music, then kicked my ass until I finally beat it. Both a work of art and a phenomenal game, Cuphead has already secured its place in my top 10 this year.

[h1]10/10[/h1] I have played this game since I was four years old. I have so many fond memories of playing Age of Kings (which we called the "red CD") with my brother and my father back in '99 and '00 and then the "blue CD" (the Conquerors expansion). I don't have any competitive experience but this is the only game I have always come back to. When I learned in 2013 that they would release an HD edition compatible with the new and recent operating systems it was the happiest news I received for years and made up for some of the sorrow I still felt for the loss of our wonderful Ensemble Studios, the awesome people who brought this game to life, back in 2009. It is a very solid RTS and I would still prefer it to any other I have played (AoE3, SC2, WoC, etc). And with the scenario editor you can create your own maps and shape them how ever you like (well you can't choose the shape, it will always be a square on the tip but you can choose whichever terrain and elevation you want). Plus you can publish your own maps or scenarios on the workshop and share them! With the Rise of the Rajas expansion released recently, the game offers more civs than I ever dreamed possible. The campaigns (especially the first ones from Age of Kings and the Conquerors) are well-made and the voice acting is wonderful! The game even offers a mini encyclopaedia on the Main Menu for both civs, mechanics, and history. The game community is wonderful and I recommend you follow killer_b_aoc, ZeroEmpires and Spirit of the Law (to name a few) on youtube for good insight on both in-depth analysis of mehanics and civs as well as upcoming community events, streams, expert gameplay and tournaments. The developers have been slacking off the earlier part of 2016, leaving a buggy and relatively unstable game on the same patch for many months. Out-of-sync have been a common issue. But it seems they've gotten a thumb out and fixing stuff now in the autumn. If you already own AoC on CD, you can play on voobly instead which is arguably more balanced and stable (but the average skill level is much higher and people are more competitive there in my experience and you will miss out on all the neat new expansions they're making now)

As an outsider, the extraordinary character design and their expressions did not appeal to me in the slightest. But I don't want to judge a game solely on its cover and I'm glad I didn't, because I had a good time playing the game. I am conflicted on how evidence is gathered and how little of a detective you actually are since everything is mandatory, but people have told me that's not the main appeal of the game. Instead, the actual trials themselves are the main appeal which are a joy to experience. They're fast-paced and full of twists that throw you off-guard. You might think you know everything about a case, but the trials may very well prove you wrong. Other characters have found evidence as well, and it's up to you to debunk their evidence and come to a conclusion together. Besides, I might have said earlier that evidence and all is mandatory, but that doesn't mean you can just blindly go into the trials; you do actually need to pay attention to what the evidence is, where is was found and how; the whodunnit as to say. They are amongst the most successful teens, being dubbed ''Ultimates'' even. Yet here in this school, they are all the same; humans trying to escape despair. And you can learn more about them through campaign dialogue, but also bonding scenes a la visual novel style. This is further explored in the ''school mode'' which is unlocked after the main campaign, but honestly that mode is only good for one run. If you want everyone's ending though... prepare to go at least 4 times. It's a brain-dead resource management mode and you do always need to pay attention unless you want even more playthroughs to happen. Fortunately this mode is just something extra for people who enjoyed the main game and want to bond more with characters, as the main campaign is good enough for anyone looking for a good Mystery Visual Novel. My 2018 ‘Game of the Year’ Before MHW I was very cautious of the series. It was always something I was very interested in playing but when I did it was little things that kept me away. Less the gameplay knowledge curve and more dumb things like multiplayer questing systems, handheld exclusivity (terrible game series to have isolated to a cramped PSP/3DS imo), and other tiny issues that added up which I didn’t have time to mess with. Monster Hunter World solves 90% of these issues while amazingly keeping the core game itself intact. It has seemingly satisfied both the pre-World MH fans and the casual/new players alike. I dropped just under 300 hours into the PS4 release in early 2018 and plan to follow suit with the PC port. It’s amazing how you can put hundreds of hours into the game using a single weapon type and changing that weapon alters the game feel completely. Can make the entire experience fresh and new again. Post-launch support has been pretty great. Capcom has been adding multiple monsters, seasonal events, and armor completely for free. The only bits they charge for include things like emotes (both character animations and sticker emotes) and some minor things like Ryu layered armor for example. The upcoming expansion (G-rank) “Icebourne” will pump even more content into the over all core package (will be a payed xpac). The only gripe I have with the post-release content is that a good portion of it is set to rotating timed events. I think that style of distribution is an excellent method to keep the game more alive but if you don’t have a ton of time or you rotate off to other games a lot then you’ll often miss an event. I’d rather just have all the added content readily available to play at anytime. The PC port has been spectacular for a team that has had near zero experience with the platform in the past. The post-launch content on PC is slowly but surely getting closer to parity with the console releases. They *should* hit that target before the expansion. Very pleased to see that the team will be adding 21:9 ultrawide support in Q1 2019. That was really the only last request I had for the port itself. Well that and I’d like proper DS4 icons but it’s not a game killer. This isn’t really a review of the core gameplay itself. If you want that please look online for those types of overviews. I just wanted to drop this on here because the game itself and the PC port is well worth your time. The folks who love to review bomb this are usually unnecessarily salty about update parity with consoles and/or they are trying to play this on a junked toaster. Seriously give it a shot. Odd review here... its a good and atmospheric game. Loved the storyline. I could even live with the clumsy combat. But there are two awful flaws to the game which combine together to almost ruin it. Firstly, there is essentially no signposting for most of the critical decisions in the game. That sounds okay at first because choices are supposed to have impact right? Well not really as in Vampyr the choices are utterly contrary in nature - if you learn from your experiences and adjust... nope what worked last time provokes an utter disaster this time. Theres also no way to recover from those disasters. Without leaving any spoilers the decisions around the "pillars" of your community are critical. Its the only game where I've ever recommended people to deliberately read up on the encounter results - charm/embrace/spare BEFORE reaching the encounter ... which will of course ruin the storyline for you. The other choice of course would be to reload even at the cost of a hour etc play.. Which brings us to problem 2 and one of the worst game design decisions I've ever had the misfortune to experience. The game has a single overwriting autosave slot with no manual save option. You got it there really is no way to recover if you make a single mistake in your entire game. My first game I ended up restarting from scratch after 21 hours. Hindsight taught me the hard way - take a copy of your save in: C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\AVGame\Saved\SaveGames You may think its unecessary but believe me it changes the game from awful to good. Anyway - overall I'd say its a very flawed gem of a game. 5/5 if it had a manual save facility. 3/5 despite its great storyline as it is.

I'll cut to the chase. This is easily a 10/10. CONTROLS [9/10] - Easy to grasp, first 15-20 mins is all you need to master the controls. - Those that have played RE7 will feel right at home. - Quick Turn (Q) does not seem to fully turn 180 degrees and leaves you instead of a vulnerable and awkward end position where you need to realign your aim. GRAPHICS [10/10] - RE Engine. What more can I say besides the game is horrifyingly gorgeous. - I'm rockin a GTX 1050 4GB with 20GB RAM but still enjoyed consistent 60 FPS (given you have optimized the settings). Heaps of Youtube videos to help you with that. - If you have a PC with awesome specs, definitely max everything up and enjoy the gory details. - You can literally dismember zombies limb by limb. Too many amazing details of this game to mention. SOUND [10/10] - This game is best played with headphones. My goodness, the binaural (3D spatial) sounds on this game is absolutely terrifying. You can legit tell where all the groaning, screeching and growling noises are coming from. And do not get me started on Mr. X's footsteps. The sound design on that is PERFECT. It elevates an already tense situation and never lets up. - The environment sounds are nothing short of amazing. It is so immersive and eerie. - Voice acting is great. The protagonists have done well and their adlibs are great. The standouts for me were Chief Irons and Claire's "I'll get you, you f@cker!" line. I applaud the voice behind the lady zombies. No one's talking about her high-pitched screeches which is shockingly horrific when I first heard it. MUSIC [7/10] - Let's be honest. This can not hold a candle to the plethora of iconic themes the original RE2 has. If you want that experience, get the DLC that plays the audio from the original RE2 (This should've been free though). - The only memorable music is Mr.X's theme when he's around. VERY memorable might I add. GAMEPLAY [9/10] - They have brought back survival-horror. - Ammo is scarce. Care must be taken on when you need to fight or GTFO. - The undead have a hard on for noise. - Inventory management is easy. - Puzzles can be challenging on your first playthrough. They are not easy but somehow not frustrating which is a good thing. - Hide and seek mechanic is awesome. - I finished both scenarios. I started with Leon, just like I did in the original RE2. I have read about people complaining there are not much differences between both scenarios. While I get what they say, it didn't really bother me. I enjoyed both scenarios specially the second one with its more satisfying ending. Can't wait to play again and start as Claire in Hardcore. OVERALL EXPERIENCE [10/10] - As someone who has played the original, I totally enjoyed seeing the environments and characters that are masterfully recreated in full detail. I like that it is not a 1:1 remake but more of a reimagining. For those that have not played the original RE2, don't fret. This is essentially how the original game is told with today's gaming technology. - This is a highly tension-filled game and the reason why this formula is beloved by fans of the genre. CLOSING THOUGHTS - Back in 1998, I used to bug my older sister to buy me a Playstation and it's all because I saw my neighbor playing Resident Evil 2. I wanted to be able to experience playing as a pixelated cop shooting zombies. When I finally got my hands on it, it was by far the best gaming experience I have ever had. Almost 2 decades later, I am thrusted back to a city that I'm familiar with, characters that I know and love. It is like reuniting with an old friend. - Definitely buy this solely for the experience. Turn the lights off, crank the volume up and grab some snacks. It's a really scary game so beware. It is hands-down one of the best games in 2019 and a happy (or shall I say, a welcome) return to survival horror.

I thought I would write the update post 2.2, 'Le Guin" patch. I love the economic changes thus far. Some may call it "micromanaging", but I find the increased realism and improved dynamics of the economy much-needed. Prior to 2.2, managing the planet tiles was cumbersome, especially if you went above 7 planets. The galactic market is a great feature which requires some polishing. My current issue with the game is primarily balance and performance. Balance: — The addition of new megastructures is excellent, however you can still only build one at a time even if you get the Master Builders ascension perk. This limits you to really build one, at most two megastructures. — I find myself always running out of minerals towards the end game, this is while swimming in energy credits. The devs should look into the advanced manufacturing building and rebalance the mineral consumption for consumer goods factories and alloy foundries. This could be counterbalanced by decreasing the energy credit generation from trade, which is insane. — Tradition vs technology. The penalty of going above your administrative cap for technology is smaller than the penalty for tradition. — Strategic resources. Too difficult to find, too difficult to manufacture and the payoff from advanced building seems to be not worth it. — Corvettes are still overpowered, especially heading towards the mid game where it is pointless to build destroyers/cruisers since the corvette evasion trumps everything. I have been winning battles I shouldn't have, while the enemy has a superior fleet composed of larger ships. — Galactic Market — great feature, however it still requires major rebalancing and bug fixes. Performance: — Currently my biggest issue with the game. The late game is almost unplayable due to the stuttering/lagging. Does not matter what hardware you have to run the game, the issue is definitely with the game/game engine and the multiple calculations required with the economic changes. Once Paradox addressed these, the game will be an all-time great for me.

I love this game. If you're here on the fence looking for reviews; get it. There is a reason this is CAPCOM's best selling game of all time, by a lot. The only legitimate complaint I see in negative reviews is issues with disconnects. I have played for upwards of 9 hours straight without ever being disconnected, and yes, I was playing multiplayer the entire time. If you want a game where every thing is a bossfight, you and three friends can curb stomp monsters into the ground with an array of flashy, unique weapons and feel an amazing sense of character progression; this is the game for you. Iceborne is, in my opinion, the "most worth it" DLC/Xpack I have ever played in my life. Iceborne is meant to be more difficult than the base game. Most people playing this game spent hours upon hours in the game before Iceborne. (I myself put 300 hours in) The game is meant to get progressively harder. This is to not only balance around your constant power creep but also to continue to challenge and push your skills. I fell in love with the Dark Souls series because of the feeling I got from returning to a fight I once felt impossible and parrying half of the boss' attacks and utterly decimating it. This is that feeling but at an almost constant rate. Do not let anyone tell you this game is not worth your time. Here are some points I would give to try and convince someone to play this game: 1) It is one of the most fun games I have ever played with a group of friends. (4 total, you + 3) 2) You feel an amazing sense of progression not only in your gear and paper stats but also your own ability. 3) There are 14 different weapons and ALL of them feel very different to play and cater to different play styles. (The only exception I would potentially accept being LBG vs HBG) 4) Overall I feel the community is very friendly and extremely helpful. If you are struggling on any particular part of the game you are able to fire an "S.O.S flare" which allows anyone (who is able to do the quest you're on) to join your game. This includes endgame hunters who will obliterate whatever you are struggling with. 5) The design of monsters is challenging yet fair. I personally find every monster fun to fight besides MAYBE a few and that's only because I'm salty that I got comboed into oblivion. (Uragaan, MR Kush, maybe something else I can't think of) I could go on, but the odds of anyone reading this far are pretty low. Just buy the fucking game. I had never even heard of Monster Hunter until World and I have put 700 hours into PS4, 300 on Xbox One, and you can see how many I have here. This quickly became my favorite game of all time, and Iceborne only widened the gap between it and second place.

review: This game lies to you. The difficulty options, even if you have them set to "Easy", it is not easy by any stretch of the imagination. That bothers me. And furthermore, let's get this out there, I'm not a fan of zombies. However, when I looked at the screenshots and read the descriptions and reviews, I thought "This is the game I wish Stronghold 2 was." Don't get me wrong, I love Stronghold 2, but what you miss in that game is the pure joy of just building castles and defending them against stronger and stronger waves of enemies. Well, this game lets you do that, except it's not a castle, it's a colony. Whatever. Base building is fun, everyone likes base building. Difficult games like Dark Souls and such where you have to manage limited resources, those are all the rage too. So here's They Are Billions, the Dark Souls of RTS games. I wish it was Stronghold 2, I really do. I hate that it has to be zombies, and I wish it had a more complex supply-chain based economy with a bit of civic management thrown in (law and order, keeping citizens happy, that sort of thing). All that said, I can't deny it makes you want to keep trying to win. You might think your defenses are good, but they attack from all sides at random, so trust me, they're not. Then if the zombies do break through, every building they take will spawn more zombies, which causes the problems to just increase exponentially. It seems like the difficulty is artifically inflated, with what sometimes seems like unfair shortcomings in the control scheme and general setup. I'd prefer if some of that extra difficulty was transferred towards a deeper, more complex city builder / simulation, but I guess you can't have everything. I have a feeling that once I beat the game on Easy (if I ever do), I might want to check out one of the unlocked map types. But then I'll probably be sick of it and want to go back to something with a little more depth. But for the price, I guess you could reasonably expect to get at least 20-30 hours of entertainment out of it, which seems like a fair deal at $1 per hour.

[h1]After finish review[/h1] [b]TL;DR[/b] GOOD: 1. Great atmosphere, music, voice acting, graphics; 2. Engaging combat system (takes a couple of fights to get used to); 3. Social system. BAD: 1. Main character story development; 2. No manual save; 3. No quick travel; 4. Ending; 4. Social system. Yes, this game stands and falls on its brilliant, yet flawed, social system and the way it interacts with the main character. You play as doctor Jonathan Reid, vampire (or Ekon in this game) newly born into London ravaged by a strange plague you need to find solution to. There are several unique districts available in the game, each with its own inhabitants, one of whom is the so called "pillar". When the pillar dies, the districts goes into mayhem. So, naturally, it is good to keep the pillar alive. The citizens can also become afflicted with different illnesses that you can cure to keep the dictrict healthy and further from falling apart. In the end you are supposed to be torn between your duties as a physician and the fact that killing humans makes you stronger, therefore more efficient in saving the city. I engaged in conversations with all the inhabitants in every district, collected all or nearly all the hints that tell you more about them, finished their quests, handpicked who I "embrace" (kill), but in the end it just doesn´t matter. You see, I only killed people who were straight up bad, like gangsters, extortioners, bullies, killers and such. My reasoning was that I use the ones that feed on misery and create hardship to save the true victims. But, alas, the game is written in a way that this doesn´t matter. It doesn´t care WHO you kill, it only takes into account HOW MANY you kill. This led to the worst ending for me ([spoiler]my sort of forced love interest killed herself and I went on a killing spree, however not as a result of my love´s suicide, but because I embraced too many people[/spoiler]), which I did not expect to be honest. This is in sharp contrast with the fact that Jonathan is not an idiot, he is an open-minded SCIENTIST, who just has to have the ability to distinguish between different options and determine which action is the best one in a set of specific circumstances. So, if he determines that killing this gangster, who took lives of many people, is ultimately beneficial, it shouldn´t make him a rampaging monster. However, the game does a very good job in tricking you into believing that problems of such a diverse world revolving around a complex character are not going to be resolved in a straightforward way. It can´t be like this right? This is not how RPGs work. Well, unfortunately, in Vampyr it doesn´t matter how much you interact with the world and its inhabitants, how much you help them, how much you use their stories to decide who to kill, the ending will still be determined only by how many people you killed. So, quantity over quality. That is not a good writing. Anyway, if you go chapter by chapter, the main story is great, it has superb twists and well written characters. It just falls short as a whole. In the end for me it was 31 hours I enjoyed ruined by the last 10 minutes.

If you liked Tomb Raider 2013 (from now on TR13), then this game is going to be a disappointment. This game, although not as good as it's predecessor, still get's a lot of things right. I found the combat entertaining and enjoyable, as well as the atmosphere, scenery and the optional tombs. The initial Siberia maps were also quite nice. However, this game also really fucked up: a storyline that stops being interesting halfway through the game; a higher emphasis on exploration, inventory management with resources, a plagiarised ending, daddy issues, boring and bland secondary characters (except Anna), skills that you'll never end up using... I also played the croft manor, and it's bearable (but quite boring). But the worst part was the technical aspect. This game frequently lagged and stuttered for no apparent reason, and the loading times were horrendous. The cutscenes are actually slideshows in disguise. Every time I interacted with something there was a chance the game would stop for about 5 seconds and then continue. Sometimes it was longer, and I ended up force-quitting, which would cause my computer to stop and freeze, forcing me to restart my whole system. I upgraded my hardware halfway through, and that didn't do anything. This inevitably left a bad taste which might've carried across to my other points and ultimately affected my judgement. My final rating is a 6/10 (7/10 without the technical difficulties). It's not a bad game; it certainly gets a lot of things right, and I enjoyed myself frequently, it just didn't live up to my original expectations and ended up disappointing me. I might play it again some day, but not for the next 5 years. I'd recommend it if you're desperate, or if you're a TR fan (just be ready for a letdown). If you're going to play it, make sure that you can somehow fix those technical issues, because otherwise it's just not worth it. If you're going to buy it, just stick with the base game, without all the outfit, cardgame and bonus level add-ons, because no one really gives a shit about those.
