Vampyr is a game comprised of wonderful ideas exectued with extreme mediocrity - A fun, immersive game drowning in a pool of its own untapped potential. Given a bigger budget, more time and more experienced devs, this could have been a Witcher 3 level game, but it falls short on many fronts. That is, of course, not to say the game is not fun, but the lack of depth becomes more and more evident as you progress, and by the end I found myself just pushing through just to see how it ends. And yet, I do recommend it - but it's not for everyone. If you are looking for a souls-like well-made combat system with great boss fights and a huge variety of abilities and enemies - Don't buy this game. The combat is pretty fun, but like all the other mechanics, it lacks depth and gets quite repetitive after the middle point. Now, if you're looking for a dialogue-heavy narrative-based game that does a wonderful job of creating just the right feeling and atmosphere, then this would be more to your liking. I should mention, though, that the story is very linear, and whatever choices you make may affect the world around you, but will not have any significant impact on the story. In more detail: Things I liked: - First and foremost, the NPC-embracing and experience system. This mechanic is the most well done of the game, and possibly the most brilliant vampire/victim mechanic I've ever seen. Basically, the amount of experience you get from combat and quests is very minimal (just enough to keep the game from being impossible), and the amount of experience you can get from killing a single innocent NPC is massive. If you want to keep up with the level progression of enemies, you have to kill a few people. And here's where it gets interesting - In order to maximize the amount of experience you get from killing someone, you must first learn all you can about them. But the more you learn about them, the more evident it becomes that they are complex characters with connections and loved ones, and the harder the decision to kill them becomes. It plays on your conscience quite well, and I've let several potential victims go after learning about their struggles. - The atmosphere. The game portrays the melancholy of vampirism, as well as the desperation of the dying London, extremely well. The doom-and-gloom atmosphere can be really felt throughout the whole game. - Voice acting is wonderful. - Great soundtrack and visuals (even if the graphics are quite bad considering we're in 2018, the visual design is very impressive) - The lore and worldbuilding is very well done. I always wanted to learn more about this world and its history. - The story is, for the most part, very good. The ending seemed like a mess though. Things I was "meh" about: - The combat. At times it was fun, at other times I did all I could to avoid it. Some enemies are a chore to fight, most boss fights (other than maybe 1 or 2) feel really uninspired, and it gets more and more repetitive as the game progresses. - Investigations (side quests) are sometimes fun and interesting, at other times quite dull, and they are never of any significance. Do them, don't do them, choose to resolve them in one of the many possible ways - It will make no difference. The characters and districts will not change as a result. They're still mostly worth doing for the experience and, in some cases, for the story. - NPCs in peril - You can run into NPCs in need of help, who will not survive the night if you ignore them. Like most mechanics, it's a cool idea, but doesn't reach its potential. It's never NPCs you've already met that are in danger - You always meet the endangered NPC for the first time as you rescue them, and they never have connections or any importance to the district. Most of them won't give you any sort of quest afterwards either. The only plus side is that you can kill them yourself with minimal damage to the district. Things I didn't like: - Not much significance to choices, even ones made during the main quests. - No reason to learn all the hints about people you don't intend to kill. Other than increasing the amount of experience you get for killing them, you get nothing for it, and there's no way to use those hints to help the characters or make any sort of difference. The only action the will have a consequence is killing an NPC, and even then it will only have a visible effect if that NPC has connections to others. Nothing else will affect the lives of the citizens. - Healing NPCs. The more unhealthy the district is, the more diseases the citizens will get, and to prevent further deterioration you have to run between them all and heal them one by one. This is simply not fun. - No fast travel. Fast travel between hideouts would have been SO useful. It could be limited - for example, you can only fast travel to healthy districts, and that way you don't get disconnected from how dangerous a district has become. But please, get this into the game, devs. Walking across the city so much really sucks. - Bugs and crashes. Not gonna go into too much detail, but things like the game crashing if you tab out during a loading screen, the map adding markers clicking on the tabs at the top of it, used dialogue options appearing as unused and so on. Will hopefully be patched soon. Final verdict: This is a good game, although it's quite unpolished and a little pricey for what it offers. I love many of the art and design ideas behind it, and I really hope this game gets a bigger, better, more polished sequel. It would be a real shame to not develop these mechanics further.

They are tackling all the issues I mentioned again on 1/3/20 by going back over earlier levels with yet another layer of paint and polish graphically and aesthetically and have almost FINALLY fixed the HECU to act smarter and more like their Half-Life counterparts which is something I and many others have complained about for years. They didn't [b]have[/b] to redo all the earlier chapters but they [b]needed[/b] to and it's appreciated. The optimization is just terrible with the game desperately needing to be ported to DirextX11. At this point I am tired of announcing every year that the game looks kind of off and runs really badly but it shouldn't struggle to run still with on my PC with a RTX 2080 Super, i7 4790k Devils Canyon, a large speedy SSD, and 32 gigs of RAM. 5/25/17 Half-Life 3's story was revealed. 2/24/17 As of this date I have all of the achievments currently available: http://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198056186683/stats/362890/achievements/ https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1374882457&fileuploadsuccess=1 In it's current state Black Mesa is impressive. The singleplayer game still requires a little more polish as things are still a little glitchy and runs like ass on my over powered rig but it's coming along nicely otherwise. I haven't seen so much love go into a similar 1:1 remake since Resident Evil 1. The weapons capacity and handling really need to be exactly like they were in Half-Life because strangely (And in regards to Half-Life 1 this isn't that nitpicky I swear.) the small changes made to how they work just make almost absolute crap. The combat is usually kinda dull and weapons feel and work terribly. Before an update May 14th here is how I felt about two important enemy types you'll encounters remade incarnations: "What it really needs to do is fix the soldiers as they are not as intelligent or as fun to fight as their GoldSource counter parts...". While the HECU's AI in the 2007 release had a jaw dropping aimbot combined with an insane firing rate (which did get fixed in the retail version) before a recent update the soldiers still acted less like HECU (Flesh and blood humans) and more like reskinned Combine in terms of behavior by standing still and doing idiotic "death charges". As of the update currently the HECU have been made to run away, group up and spread out a lot more than before AND even make more hand signals which while an improvement is just window dressing and sadly they aren't as smart as their Gold Source and flawed Half-Life: Source counterparts. Head shots are basically worthless against the HECU and hit scan should be outright replaced with projectiles ala Mmod. The Vortiguants now have similar timing for charging and aiming their lazers where as before in the 2012 version they completely missed the point of their Half-Life counterparts having a charge up times. The only problem now is that you can dodge their attacks without getting behind cover like in Half-Life and can simply strafe right or left. On another dour note the Source engine is really starting to show it's age as these remade visuals are ( a wee bit) inconsistant in terms of quality and some maps have aged. My favorite chapter Surface Tension has terrible performance during the uncut sections because it's lacking a few more NODRAW textures and because it's pushing the engine past breaking point. It seems silly to say this after complaining about performance but I feel like some sort of Ultra option for textures and models should be added to uncompress the textures or use 2048x2048 resolution textures for the NPC's model and just have higher poly versions of the models in general. Some of the faces look great while others look more dated than the faces from Half-Life 2 which might I add have aged quite well even more so for 2004. Even with all of that said this is probably the best game on early access right now and this iteration improves greatly upon the 2012 mod version. In Early Access so far there haven't been many updates other than officially un-cutting Surface Tension and adding some more Deathmatch maps but it's a shinier version of Half-Life that none the less faithfully recreates it. Not everyone will be able to enjoy a game that's aged as well gameplay wise as Half-Life or get immersed thanks to the originals visuals like I was and still am which makes this a must play for newcomers interested in the series or without any new entries to look forward to. What a game. What. A. Game. You drop in, having no clue what's going on with a friend or a stranger you've never met before as you embark on one of the most painstaking, gut wrenching, fear instilling journies of your steam career. Surrounded by hordes of undead, various mutated creatures and apparitions, and pitted against your own flesh and blood, you are on a mission to hunt an elusive and competently strong beast. Your first time will confuse you, and only intrigue you further, as you learn how deadly the environment can become. Once you get your bearings you're on to the real challenge, taking down the most wicked target across the bayou. After the fight, you will have to banish the deceased anamoly (as well as safeguard it during this process), and then take the newly found bounties to extraction as the remaining players in the game chase you, with constant awareness of your location at all times. Between the rush of hunting players in cold blood with unparalleled precision and tactics with friends, to getting swarmed by multiple mobs and screaming in paril as you can only die, this game captures the highs and lows of a battle royal with all the right concepts, and puts an extremely alluring incentive on it with an aesthetic that is unrivaled by any game of it's kind. The real problem is, however, how few people read the game's disclaimers. Which for a fact, are listed multiple times throughout your menu navigation prior and post purchase: "Early Access Game Get instant access and start playing; get involved with this game as it develops. Note: This Early Access game is not complete and may or may not change further. If you are not excited to play this game in its current state, then you should wait to see if the game progresses further in development." Yes there are bugs, yes servers are kind of funky and it may take a few tries to get into a party with a friend, or you might have to wait till the servers aren't peaked, but this game is still fresh out of oven and cooling, it is not worthy of scrutiny just yet because the devs are still proving themselves. With daily server maintenances and consistent watch for when these bugs do break the game, I for one am so far impressed with the attention the game is receiving to counteract the many inconsistencies with such an impressive project. TL;DR People are actually too impeded to read the early access disclaimer and fully understand it. If you are considering buying this game but are hesitant from the massive wave of negative reviews crying about the bugs, do not waste your time reading them. The game is insanely fun, the devs show promise and for $30 to buy a game being developed by a AAA company, Hunt: Showdown is a cheap and extremely satisfying date.

Joining the Bandwagon here but for good reason. One. This game was never good. It looked sorta pretty, satisfied board members, and provided people with enough distractions to be led to think it was good. It isn't. Its not a good RPG, the voice work is a distraction to make the "safe" writing feel more emotionally waited. It detracts from the point of an RPG, the role play. You can't roleplay a pre-made character, no choice feels powerful or weighted. Your characters options are severly limited by the voice acting as well leading to cringeworthy threats and over zealous actions you thought were calm. Two. The combat is strange, the shooting elements are improved yes. But the melee is the same Bethesda trademark wet carboard feeling. Nothing provides resistance or feedback, enemies don't have enough reception to attacks. The cinematic deaths are buggy and just serve to remove from the combat in general. Guns while much more aproachable than previous games serve little purpose than to clutter inventory. The Pipe guns will take you through the game at normal and Hard difficulties will just chew up more ammo. If you do switch up combat becomes a breeze when everything you have cleaves 60% health or more. Three. The base building was enjoyable to me, not everyone's cup of tea but I get why. It serves absolutley no purpose, build a base to defend against raiders who come and attack a base. No incentive to keep that alive, its a time waster with no value or reason to care about it. There isn't any attachment to settlers and their isn't an endgame in it either. It ends up becoming a "Look what cool thing I made" generator. Perfect for PR screenshots. Four. This whole game feels like a cashgrab. I mentioned the PR but the DLC policy is downright atrocious. The Prices for essentialy 10% of a game with barely enough content to be worth playing. That and creation kits that might as well be free. There are modders who could have made this DLC. It would have been free. Which is where I imagine this Creation Club situation arose. It feels like some exec found out about mods and said "alright, how can we utilise this to turn a profit." Little thought has been put into the idea of it, nothing makes a lick of sense. What are the legal implications of it? Why have mods been uploaded to the nexus only for them to make the launch of the creation club? It feels scummy. It feels like an insult to the player base. I really tried to enjoy my time in this game. I installed mods to make the process more fun and it helped a little. The music is brilliant though lacking the variety of New Vegas and the Boston vibe is enjoyable and uplifting at times. Its just the very coporate attitude in the DLC and hence that show that the game itself wasn't intended to be enjoyed but sold. Its a real shame

Arma is a game that scales with your imagination. While not necessarily easy, users can create whatever mod they want for this game. Just recently I saw a video for a T-Rex mod. T-Rex aside, many of the modders for this game take it upon themselves to implement items and equipment into the game that the developers could not (most likely for legal purposes/trademarks). Missions are made constantly so there is never a worry of running out of something to do in Arma 3. With one of the largest maps, realistic ballistics, and a sometimes brutally hard AI, the game provides a sandbox for players to play whatever military simulation they could every desire. Games can be designed to have a small 4 man team infiltrating small enemy camps or they can be designed to have huge operations with several platoons, armored vehicles, and air support. My only warning would be to take your time learning the game and the modding community. When I first purchased Arma 2, I didn't play it for a year after my initial play through because I didn't quite 'get' the game. My brother also was not a fan of Arma 3 at first. Don't Starve's title is ironic because not starving is among the least of your worries. As you comb the environment for the necessary elemants for basic tools, you'll find food scattered about. Seeds and carrots are enough in abundance to get you by initially, but you'll soon be seeking more-filling foods. Unfortunately, the very environment is out to get you. As you travel, you'll encounter hordes of spiders, murderous tallbirds, roaming packs of dogs, shifty pigs, stalking trees, killer whip-vines, and pain-inducing wormholes. Honestly, I enjoyed the game more in its early development. It seemed as the game progressed in its creation, more and more difficult elements were added. Initially, you could trick the A.I. of birds and rabbits so that food wasn't a concern, allowing you to explore the envionment more readily and craft new items to your heart's content. New elements to discover were around every corner, and the unlockable characters only added more creativity to the game and encouraged you to try to survive again and again against the many creatures bent on your destruction. Eventually, the game became increasingly difficult as more and more foes were added and the A.I. exploits were removed. Life-sustaining meat became harder to obtain. Also, the addition of the Nightmare meter was wholly unwelcome, as the game took a huge difficulty ramp. Whereas before Don't Starve enjoyed a certain Tim Burton flair, the Nightmare meter bordered too much on the horror genre for my tastes. Can I recommend Don't Starve? Yes. It's a highly creative game that allows you to play as you will, with a basic goal of survival. There IS a way out of the grueling world, and your quest to survive will offer you many hints at escape. You can construct planks and stone and bulid yourself a refuge against the game's many enemies; you can don weapons and armor to slay the nefarious enemies that await; you can taunt the tallbirds by stealing their eggs and live as one among the herds of beefalo; you can use the Firestarter character to burn down whole forests; and you can shave Wilson's manly beard. Don't Starve has an awful lot of content to be found for a game that tries so hard to kill you. It's going to take a certain amount of endurance and ability to handle punishment to get something out of the game, but the persistant may find a world much to their liking.

I am 4 hours in and having a blast. I just recently finished my second playthrough of Dark Souls and have been aching for something close. This game pulls combat elements from the soulsborne games, mixed with the arkham series batman detective mode, with the movements and visuals of a good assassins creed game set in the bloodborne style england. I can't speak to what the rest of the game will hold but I'm having an awesome time and I absolutely love the combat. It can be challenging managing stamina/healing but that's sort of the whole dark souls experience. At level 8 I can beat level 18 enemies with a little bit of a challenge. (I'm not sure if there is an option to up the difficulty.) The game also rewards interactions with NPC's and if the player does the ground work the exp gains suit the amount of work put in. It's a neat social puzzle with shades of gray moral choices that impact the game and quests. I really enjoy the choice of whether to kill and get powerful or stay weak and do the morally righteous thing. It seems as if choices actually matter to one's playthrough. I also enjoy the well voice acted cast, and the main character Jonathan Reid (the fact that I rememberd his name speaks volumes to me) has the coolest voice. The music is perfect for the setting and it seems like the game setting was meticulously researched. The orchestral soundtrack is so ambient and the game's assets are high quality and gorgeous. I'm glad I overlooked the folks who spoke poorly of the game and decided to just jump in. Most of the reviews I read said the combat was dull and uninspired but I disagree. I've been thoroughly enjoying it. It reminds me of bloodborne a lot. But with better visuals, fast framerate, and unique outlook. It's a hybrid of a bunch of my favorite games and I just hope it's a decently long game. I'll see though I suppose. Either way I love it so far.

Let me start by saying I'm a paleontologist, and I own and/or have played almost every dinosaur and paleo game listed on steam. This game is full of bugs and broken models/systems/etc, isn't optimized whatsoever, and even at the highest graphic levels looks flat and undetailed, more becoming of an early-gen PS2 game or mobile game than a PC developed game. Its broken, difficult to play and the experience when you DO get to play isn't anywhere near rewarding enough to justify the frustration and roadblocks encountered in normal play. The game is currently in a state that isn't anywhere close to release-grade into EA. The framerate never goes above 25-30FPS even on a machine that's nearly double the requirements. The animations are very awkward and unrealistic, resulting in broken necks/tails and bow-legged gaits that make the dinosaurs appear totally weightless or toy-like. The sounds of the animals themselves are almost entirely unedited stock sounds and some seem to have been lifted from other sources (JP Utah roar, etc) that's ripe for copyright smackdowns. The sound system in general is extremely low quality; there's no directional hearing, sounds seem muted and muffled even when the source is extremely close, and for a game reliant on audio cues this makes for a terrible and frustrating experience. Most of the models are decent enough, but a few (like the Allo and Oro) are of sharply lower quality than the rest. Sounds and actions/animations aren't properly synced on almost every animal. Keybinding is difficult and only works half the time. The servers are highly unstable and crash repeatedly even when mostly empty. The lag is very, very noticeable. Half of all of the actions a player can preform come with no context or introduction, leaving to a confusing, conjested and disorienting experience that can span from the first few hours to longer. The maps are large but resources are spread thin and the topography is jagged and extreme to the point of annoyance; its insanely easy to fall and die or fall and get stuck resulting in waiting for death or a respawn that wipes the character. The skin system is neat but there are so few choices that its confusing and intimidating at times. [/strike] There are color options for parts that are completely invisible on the selection screen which makes customizing annoying. Bright neon colors are neat in theory but are jarringly out of place in a survival setting, and the lack of dimorphism makes grouping difficult. The different systems surrounding comfort are interesting and unique but can sometimes be so wildly out of the player's control as to be infuriating. Players can't control weather and other environmental factors, and for slower dinosaurs this means a long, drawn-out pointless death of vague "discomfort" just from being out in the rain or wind for too long. [/strike] Nvm The Isle doesn't have a working skin system to any extent. The camera is jittery and results in breakneck swings and snaps that can make combat impossible. The flying and swimming cameras are particularly terrible and result in accidental drowning or fatal crashes often. The larger dinosaurs are so slow that playing them isn't particularly rewarding in the survival game mode. Scent is functional but nearly useless at night and uses up ability that can leave a dinosaur bafflingly vulnerable. Sure, carrying food and forming packs is easy enough and useful, but keeping an animal within a ridiculously razor-thin band of optimum "comfort" takes so much effort and sheer dumb luck as to greatly diminish the overall fun from playing. There are very few dinosaurs and marine/flying reptiles to pick from and there are far less herbivores/prey than carnivores, leaving the player environment disasterously tilted towards the predator. Again, herbivores could be fun if they had more to offer from gameplay than a near constant need to eat and drink and few choices for socialization, interaction or goal reaching to reward the long, exhaustingly drawn-out playtime to grow them. Comparisions to ARK: Survival Evolved are inevitable, but I'd rather keep that kettle of fish well out of the home. There's obvious copying and mimickry of ARK: Survival Evolved present, but the game isn't solid enough on its own to offer much of a unique experience besides the "nothing" quantifier that is completely unexplained, vague and nearly impossible to fullfil. Just having less systems to keep an eye on doesn't make the gameplay more exciting or fun, it just makes keeping track of all of the lack of mechanics even harder and survival difficult and unrewarding. The complete lack of an introduction, tutorial or other key to ease new players in leaves most confused and disoriented and easy pickings for other players. It makes for a frustrating, unrewarding experience. Some of the dino models are okay, the foliage looks okay in places and horrible in others, the lack of a tide and monsoon/drought cycle is neat but can be annoying, scent is jarringly oversaturated and impossible to keybind off of key movement keys. The skin system is cool to a degree but then becomes wildly unrealistic, and there aren't any in-game rewards to favor players acting in natural or environmentally building ways. Its been a little over 4 years and there's always room for improvement, but the game doesn't deliver on the promises it made out of the gate. It should have been released later in a more stable, complete state, as playing for 30 minutes only for the server to crash and take all progress with it? Gets very, very old after the 13th time in a row.

Warhammer II is a game that you have to spend $200+ at retail price to unlock everything, but there's an incredible amount of content in this game. Whether or not it's worth that much to you is debatable, but about half of the factions now playable are unlocked by just getting the base game, so it's not expensive to try. Creative Assembly's new DLC policy is expensive, but I'd argue the games are complete without the DLC, and the DLCs themselves are usually worth the money, as they add a unique playable faction or a new campaign. Total War grognards will insist the earlier Total War titles were better, and they certainly had their charm, but this one has so many nice UI features, so many choices in army leadership with every faction, and more transparent combat mechanics. I would argue the vast majority of the differences between "old" TW and "new" TW are massively for the better. I love this game. Each faction is truly, truly unique and plays totally differently, and there's so many different characters and map locations. The map, especially the Mortal Empires campaign, has an incredible amount of sheer detail and scale. The graphics are beautiful, the strategy is engaging and fast-paced, and you really have tons and tons of breathing room to do all sorts of things that you want. My only two minor issues are that they made siege battles a bit too easy for the defenders in a lot of cases by making them along "two walls" instead of four, and the chaos respawns can feel poorly designed depending on what faction you play. Also (super minor), you're sometimes bombarded by generic loot notifactions when you get really big and win a lot of battles. I've played three factions fully to (short) campaign victory now, and the experience felt fresh every time. I don't even have all the DLC, so I know this is a game I'll be playing for years.

[h1]STOOORY OF UNDERTAAALE[/h1] I bought the game for 3.49$ during sale, pretty much the price of a videogame soundtrack dlc, so considering that you can't go wrong really. I should also state that i did the true pacifist run, so some story pieces and the overall experience may be different for other people who chose different routes. Let me start off by saying that i think the game is VERY overrated. It's pretty good, but not as good as some people want you to believe. [b]The story[/b] is good, but not really noteworthy. There weren't really any new ideas i haven't seen in other games, BUT it actually gets really interesting during the last area you get to explore. Thats the only part of the game that i actually went WTF and was super eager to explore and find out what really happened. I was a bit dissapointed, since due to the clues you receive (spoilers:) [spoiler]the empty coffin with the red heart, the mentions of the human in the labs, flowey's boss machine being some kind of hibernation chamber[/spoiler] i was led to believe that your character (spoilers, again) [spoiler]was dead and experiencing some kind of purgatory[/spoiler], though it was revealed that the developer actually settled for a more "safe" option, which was a bit of a let down, but it still was good, so props to that. [b]The characters[/b], which were supposed to be on of the main draws of the game, were pretty average. Some of them were sort of likable (Toriel was a weird mother type figure, Sans was pretty ok, though he felt like a 14 year old's self insert, Metatton was a pretty funny and a charming character overall, but i found his first, more likable form to be really reminiscent of Mike Myers' [i]The Cat in the Hat[/i]) some others kinda unlikable (Udyne was behaving like an edgy manchild rather than a respected and hardened warrior, that dinosaur scientist who i don't even remember her name was pretty annoying especially after [spoiler]metatton revealed her true motifs[/spoiler]), and then there is Papyrus, who was the only character who i found genuienly likable and charming. [b]The humor[/b] was mixed. It all comes down to personal taste, but even though i found some jokes to be funny (Papyrus' famous, special attack, how to end the buff unicorn/cat encounter as a pacifist), most of them were pretty averange and a lot of them were straight up frustrating (the pet the doggo/pupper jokes made me want to gouge my eyes out). [b]The gameplay[/b]. During your defending state, you have to avoid objects thrown by the enemy, like bullet hell games, but with variations between each enemy. The hitboxes are pretty generous, so you don't have to worry about the difficulty. During you attacking phase, you can ether attack or convince your enemy to stop fighting you by pressing the correct order of dialogue prompts each turn. You can also play some [spoiler]dating minigames[/spoiler] depending on your choices during the playthough, which are pretty much interactive jokes, with humor as the main focus (which is much better than actually taking them seriously). Having said that, there are also things i REALLY enjoyed while playing the game [b]The soundtrack[/b]. Oh boy, the soundtrack. It's actually one of the best videogame soundtracks i have heard! from the calming tone of "undertale", which game me such a comfy and nostalgic feeling, to "death by glamour" and "Hopes and Dreams" which made me so hyped that only a few other games managed to succeed, it made me believe that the game was made purely to showcase this soundtrack. Though some tracks aren't as good as some others, the ones that are good will undoubtedly stick with you for a loooong time. [b]The final bosses[/b] Although i found the boss fights to be average, The last few boss fights [spoiler]with Omega Flowey and Asriel[/spoiler] were actually some of the best boss fights i have played period. The idea of being weaker than the boss in the beginning of the fight, and actually building up your strenght during it even though the boss starts doing faster attacks is an AMAZING idea that is mostly overlooked by other games, or implemented poorly. The fact that at the end of the fight you end up being equally strong to the boss by [spoiler]the help of everyone that you have helped during your playthrough[/spoiler], which is super satisfying on it's own, and start doing crazy attacks at each other, while having an amazing soundtrack blasting on the backround makes you experience pretty much the hype that anime battles capture, but in the form of a videogame. I also have to give props to the developer, since even though the bosses attacks are insane, he managed to make them not as punishing as they seem to be, while the player is still tricked to think otherwise. It's hard to describe really, but these are some fights that you have to experience for yourself to see how well thought out and brilliant they are. [b]tl;dr[/b]Anyways, after all that i believe that undertale isn't incredible. It's pretty average during the whole way through, and only gets good towards the end. However, it does some things so incredibly right (soundtrack and true final bosses) that you have to experience them for yourself, and it's worth the purchase during a sale. Hope you found this review helpful, cause otherwise i wasted my day for nothing.

I find my feelings about this visual novel rather mixed. It's hard to talk about it without spoilers, so I'll keep my thoughts as brief and vague as possible. This is a well-developed visual novel from an otherwise unknown team. The graphical style is consistent and pretty to look at, especially for a Ren'Py game. The music, for the most part, is simplistic and catchy. On the surface, it looks to be a well-made dating sim-type game, and if it were only that, I would have loved it much better than how it turned out in the long run. You see, the writing for this VN is considerably strong, and the direction it took made it seem like an affectionate parody of typical VN romcom tropes. However, by the second half of the game, the pacing starts to drag as the writing becomes overly self-indulgent and, for lack of a better term, fun-sucking. I get that the story wants to deconstruct dating sims by playing with character tropes and their extremes, but after a while the shock wears itself too thin. The ending feels defeatist and unsatisfying, making the whole journey feel utterly pointless. Do I still recommend this game despite all that? Well...I didn't like it as much as other people did, but I still recommend playing it because how you ultimately feel about this game is dependent on your own experience. I don't want anyone else's enjoyment of this VN or any other game to be hampered by my own mixed or negative receptions. If anything, I think this work really acknowledges how difficult it is for aspiring writers such as myself to really express themselves. Even though I don't see the point of this VN's overall message, it has smaller, more positive messages woven inside that I think made the experience worthwhile. Also, coming up with my own poem in-game to woo girls is pretty cool. I wish more VNs had something like that. :D

review: TL;DR at bottom. This game is fun, chaotic and destructive, and there are certainly other games of the like that are much better. Just Cause 3 adheres to a certain audience of players, so be careful before you buy. If you're looking for a peaceful, island exploration game with cool vehicles and realistic NPCs, then do not get this game. If you're in to story-driven, adventure titles with relatable characters and a deeply developed lore, you may be a bit dissapointed. But if you're looking to blow off some steam after a stressful day and liberate hundreds of dictator-controlled towns and outposts on a copy and pasted map, then this game is for you! This game is like a stereotypical action movie, with a charasmatic main character equipped with a reel-in grappler, wingsuit (rocket wingsuit with DLC) and a missile-equipped high speed boat. If you want the ability to call in overpowered mechs, helicopters and weaponized cars, destroy an uncountable amount of fuel tanks or hijack an ambulance while the paramedic is performing CPR, then this game is for you. If you like over-the-top action with a paper thin story, then you'll like this game. I did. TL;DR: If you like chaos, destruction, liberating dictator-controlled towns and outposts and playing through an action-packed paper thin story then you'll like this game.

Got this on sale at greenman gaming for just over 5 bucks. First JC game I ever played. I wrote this review + 30 hours in, and will change it if so inclined through gaming experience. Game is a tad shallow and somewhat repetitive in certain aspects, but big fun with some interesting options at your messy disposal. Huge game world, decent to quite good general gameplay mechanics and some fantastic explosions - and a lot of crazy stuff to try out, not in the least thanks to the (imo anyway) cool and refreshing gadgets the protagonist works with. So far, I have experienced JC 3 mostly as a sandbox where I get to try fun stuff and liberate a small island nation, and eventually complete the game while doing so. Along the way, I get to ask questions like "why does that dude on YouTube have 4 cables?" or "why can't my rocket mines blast people up and away like that dude's?" - which leads to a series of challenges/missions I need to play to unlock upgrades. A simple scheme of creating an intrinsic need ("get to do more whacky stuff") and offering activities that are challenging, fun and feel very optional. Nothing new there, but for me it works more in JC3 than in most other games. There is a distinct feeling of freedom about this game that sits very well with me - but is described by others as a lack of direction or structure. Personal taste will probably decide here. Liberating Medici (the fictional island nation where JC3 plays) comes down to fighting the local militia/army while being backed by the rebels, and taking out/over their strongholds, like harbors, police stations and military bases. Lots of fire. Medici remembrance day will probably have more time for it's liberator than it will for it's oppressor, but that's shock and awe for you. You can give a people their freedom and make them eat it, in fact. They don't seem to mind that much anyway - Rrrrrrrico is a local hero who's actions are hardly questioned by the locals - a few years of oppression have really sorted these islands out. As for Medici - It's not the most beautiful game world you'll ever see (not bad by any means though), but it's probably the most beautiful burning and exploding one. There is not quite as much demolition going on as in Red Faction Guerilla, but what it does, it does very well. It's also quite big - I hadn't seen about 90% of the map 10 hours in - but I'm not yet sure how diverse this big world is. The gameworld is not quite the explosion of joy that GTA5 was for me, for instance - but more than holds it's own as a venue for the kind of death terror mayhem action I would have liked to see more of in that game. Many people experience RAM related problems with the game, for me it works fine in borderless windowed at 8 GB RAM (ddr4) on a G4620 with a 1050TI. Is the game worth 30 euros? Good Q. I wouldn't say it's a ripoff, and at any decent sale I'd call it a steal. Just understand what kind of game it is, and what kind of game it isn't. My last 30 hours playing games were spent playing JC3. And I just got back to the Witcher 3 right before I got this. One is a beautiful lady, the other is a partygirl. That makes for one lonely lady so far. PS. I can't help but think that there is an actual political message in this game, and some social satire even - and it's not Rico, but you and me playing this game that are playing the lead in that respect. But maybe I'm just getting old.

[h1]Pros[/h1] [list][*] Fishing system where the bait you use matters and you actually see if the fish within the water. [*] Cooking system where there is a little mini-game you play where you have to stop cooking at the right time. [*] You can catch and collect small animals and then let them loose within your house. [*] Tracking system which becomes more effective as it levels up for the specific monster you're looking for. [*] Gathering and mining system which is similar to MMORPGs. [*] Craft your own consumables, weapons, and gear, using resources from ores, herbs, and monsters. [*] Several weapons with their own unique attacks and playstyle. [*] Monster body parts can be broken and severed which reduces their effectiveness and gives you materials. [*] Armor skills which allow you to customize your character beyond just defense. [*] Cooperative gameplay, where you can easily invite randoms to help you with quests and monsters. [*] Expeditions allow you to reveal the map and do whatever you want at your own pace. [*] You can use environment to do specific attacks, benefit yourself, and trap or damage monsters. [*] You get your very own pet which assists you if you don't have enough players helping you with a monster or quest. [*] You craft your pets armor and weapons. [*] Not pay to win whatsoever. [*] The company provided a high definition texture pack for free. [*] Company added a whole lot of detail to keep you interested. [*] There probably is a whole lot more to mention, but I just mentioned some of the main pros of the game. [/list] [h1]Cons[/h1] [list][*] Many main quests make you fight a monster that is unknown to you instead of following the role of a monster hunter where you could track, study, and learn how to counter it before you fight it. [*] Alt+tabbing seems to cause disconnects when in online sessions. [*] Commonly you cannot connect to a session when you try and matchmake. [*] Terrible storyline, could of been way better and sometimes it was confusing. [*] Armors and weapons could of looked way better, some weapons look exactly like their upgrades. [*] Many monsters are reused and just re-textured. [*] NPCs don't have names, not even the main ones within the story. [*] Hassle to play with friends, since someone has to always post a quest and then everyone has to join it, rather than just adding each other into a group and doing quests together. [*] Most main missions force you to play solo before being able to invite your friends and sometimes they don't even let you at all. [*] Canteen system is annoyingly complex and once you figure it out, you realize it's a required tedious task that the game could of done without. [*] Building recipes at the canteen seems almost pointless, because fresh ingredients continue to change. [*] Armors are not upgraded in the same way as weapons, so low rank armor eventually get replaced. [*] Hammers need to be sharpened and more frequently than most weapons.

It's not a perfect game, but it's a damn good one. The storyline and atmosphere might not be as strong as older titles in the series, but as far as gameplay goes this is definitely the most innovative game of the franchise. The cover system is kind of clunky (and this is disappointing considering that the cover system in Max Payne 3 worked pretty well) but you can do fine without using it. The guns feel like they have force behind them, the driving returns to the arcadey style of older GTA titles but with more reliable physics, and the game world is so detailed and varied that not a single inch of the map feels copy/paste. Is it worth the launch price of $60? That's arguable, but if you're looking for a fresh third-person shooter this is worth a look.

Quick disclaimer: While this game was made by the same studio that gave us Dark Souls, it is not the same and may throw off anybody who is expecting the same playstyle that they learned from Dark Souls. Yes this game is very difficult and I can almost guarantee that you will rage after getting your ass handed to you by the same boss for the nth time, but one of the reasons this game is so great is the feeling of finally beating said boss. Sekiro does not have builds or anything of that nature, but that is one of the reasons you can play with such versatility, especially once you have acquired more tools for the prosthetic (a very cool feature of the game that I thoroughly enjoyed playing around with) and combat styles etc. I have seen many reviews negatively reviewing the game because it is too hard, and yes it is hard, but once you learn patterns and combat rhythm and learn how to deflect, counter, and dodge properly, its actually quite doable. Guys, its a game built around difficult bosses and a very punishing combat system, ofc it's going to be hard, at least try and get better at the game before you negatively review it for being hard with only 10- hours played on record. That said, the game has a very cool setting and I really enjoy the charm of the many enemies influenced by japanese culture and the overall feel of the game. There are some very cool moments and the fact that there are multiple endings that one can organically stumble on instead of having to search a wiki should be something the developers are given props for. I've seen people saying the controls are horrible, probably trolls, but still it should be talked about that no the controls are not horrible I play on m + kb and have not had one complaint so far. Plus I mean if you hate controls on it so bad, get a controller, if you don't have one lying around you can find pretty good ones for like $20 or $30. Great game, would recommend, excellent story imo and the gameplay is very rewarding if you take the time to learn how to play well before sh*tting on it. 10/10 would recommend. PS for the love of god stop saying it's bad cause it's not the same exact play style as Dark Souls.

Half-Life 2 is one of those games that everyone has at least heard of, perhaps only as a part of the meme, nonetheless the points stands. What about the first Half-Life game then? It would stand to reason that such a creature existed, so there could be a sequel to it, yet it has been overshadowed by its successor to the point at which the first game became almost obscure. Frankly, it’s a shame because back in the 1998, when Half-Life was released, it had almost single-handedly shown the world that FPS genre can have a story to tell. The notion is almost absurd nowadays but back when the genre was synonymous with Doom and Quake, FPS stood for raw gameplay and a text panel at the end to sum up your exploits. Using it as a fundament for presenting a complete narrative which on top of that was integrated into the gameplay seemed almost daring. Coupled with innovations in graphics and AI, it had created a formula that many games strode towards in years to come. Today, the graphics are obviously dated and the level design is confusing but otherwise the game still holds up surprisingly well. It came from outer reality Half-Life tells a story of Gordon Freeman, a prospering physicist working at Black Mesa – a top-secret research facility capable of using sci-fi literature as schematics for their next project. The player takes control of the mute protagonist and soon steps into the iconic Hazardous EnVironment suit (abbreviated HEV) to join fellow scientists for work on the faithful day. The day when a single experiment gone horribly wrong made a tear in reality sizable enough to allow for an alien invasion. Alas, the quest begins amidst chaos and alien life forms rampaging through the facility. Most of you are well aware what that struggle had ultimately lead up to. Until then, Freeman’s chosen field of expertise had just become the ballistics and there will be dozens of test subjects just dying to further your research. The extraterrestrial menace that player is about to face comes in many shapes and sizes, all equally deadly. Even the cat-sized headcrab is capable of turning their unfortunate victim into a zombified monstrosity. Much larger, acid-spewing bullsquid or water-faring ichthyosaur aren’t any more docile. Then there are deliberate invaders of Earth, the Vortigaunts capable of conjuring a lightning and their massive armoured counterparts, harassing the player with literal swarms of hornets. Then there are far more mundane enemies. Black Mesa survivors soon realise that the military relief force has arrived with orders to purge all life from the facility, alien or otherwise. This not only makes for a wide selection of enemies but also leads to encounters, where the player enters the middle of a fight between the two enemy factions, allowing for all kinds of tactical play. Crowbars per second Half-life’s wide selection of enemies is matched by equally diverse arsenal at the player’s disposal. Chief among them – Gordon’s trademark crowbar. This rather exotic choice for “mandatory weak melee weapon”, as the nickname implies is only useful in early stages of the game. That said, it’s far more practical than most melee weapons in FPS games. Freeman is simply ludicrously agile with it, being fully capable of bashing with the thing 2 times per second – according to the HL wikia. The noise it makes while doing so just adds in on the absurdity, making whacking stuff with crowbar a go-to downtime activity between fights. Jokes aside, HL means of murder do start off easy with, FPS standard-issue buckshot and bullets but then just keep on adding. Soon there is a scoped crossbow, trip-mines, lasers and entirely unique armaments – Gluon gun, which produces a blue beam that vaporizes targets after short period of contact or Hivehand, an organic artifice capable of firing infinite swarm of hornets. It’s not called sci-fi for nothing. If that wasn’t enough, many weapons have some form of secondary fire mode for a good measure. Physicists on ice Despite the game’s multiple strengths Half-Life is not all milk and honey. Title’s most glaring flaw is confusing level design. Half-Life is a mostly linear game, though it does allow a degree of exploration. That being said, perhaps “enforces” would be a more applicable word, as time and time again I was simply lost. Now, I would like to emphasise that I am not trying to criticise the game for not being linear. The issue is more complex and perhaps an example will picture it best. If you come across the door there are 3 options: it’s an obvious way forward, it’s a shortcut and the door opens from the other side or it’s a prop with no function at all. Except there is no text pan to tell these apart. Instead the game provides an immersive sensation of wandering around aimlessly. From this, parallels can be drawn to entire sections of the game – at times you can side-track to find extra supplies, and the other time you are supposed to side track, in order to turn a valve that clears an obstacle from the main road. The gnawing uncertainty soon sets in, since you could’ve missed an interactive key element at any point by simply not stepping off the beaten path. Then there are smaller things, such as Gordon being permanently on skates. The movement in HL is mind-bogglingly fast, to the point where the character keeps some of the momentum even after the player takes their hands off the keyboard, creating a “sliding” effect. While such rapid movement is very useful in combat, the game also has arcade-like platformer sections, where sliding is no longer welcome. Finally, there is a matter of bugs. Admittedly, whether they appear or not is a game of chance but Half-Life can get wonky when played on modern hardware. And I definitely lost that game. Every Ichthyosaur was going through a roid-rage, moving at double the usual speed and clipping through the environment – to the point when during the final battle it “jumped” out of the water and got stuck on the jumping pad. During the fight with Gonarch, the boss couldn’t be asked to transition to the last arena so I could end the fight. I had to literally breach the floor myself by stacking the explosives. Those are just the “highlights” of my HL run but the bugs truly inflated the feeling of confusion. There was no way of telling if it was me doing something wrong or the game. All in all, Half-life has to be taken with a grain of salt. It was a fun ride and when the game worked as intended, it has done so really well. The title is extremely playable for its venerable age. Half-Life may be at its core a simple story about the otherworldly invaders but it created a framework that allowed to implement all of the best qualities that FPS genre had to offer and more. Diverse cast of enemies, wide variety of weapons, visually distinct environments, all falling into one coherent whole. Valve even went a step further and had given many elements of the game’s convention a logical explanation from in-universe perspective. The enemies spawn out of nowhere – because of the resonance cascade. The supplies are lying around – because Black Mesa fulfilled military contracts and required armed personnel to man expeditions into another universe. The devil is in the details and Half-Life sure has those covered. The expedition to Xen makes for a tremendous final act and even the aged, edgy look does not make a dent in how strange and utterly alien it appears. I highly recommend the game to anyone who enjoys the FPS genre. Half-Life is as forthcoming as a 20-year old game can possibly be and if you can’t stomach the game being a little rough around the edges, there is a Source port or modern reimaging in the form Black Mesa as perfect alternatives.

What fantastic game! If you like the turn-based tactical rpg genre ( á la XCom) you will like this game. The world is wonderful, very atmospheric and feels alive. Filled with details of a post apocalyptic world where nature claims everything that once was hers. I absolutely love the style and designs of the characters and the individual levels, some more forest(y), some more city-ruins. I kind of felt some Simon Stålenhag (if you don't know his art, go check it please!) vibes in some levels due to the robots, the atmosphere and maybe also because the game has swedish roots. The story is also told in a very immersive way by one of the main-characters while beeing visualized in some nicely rendered and/or some comic-esk cutscenes. Aswell as a well done english voiceover during the whole game. There is even some humor in it, which for me was unexpected, but very fitting. Gameplay wise, its everything you would expect from a turn-based tactical game, with some additions in unique character-bound skills to switch up the fights and give them some new turns. I really liked the necessary switching between characters, upgrades (mutations) and weapons in order to win the fights on different locations. Also there is looting and leveling (on a small scale) involved - so what else do you need ? There is a kind of online-feature aswell, something like highscore-hunt ( idk, haven't tested it yet) Maybe it increases the replayability of the game - but even without I pumped easily 15 hours relaxed gameplay with exploring every nook and cranny of the levels and scooping up every piece of electronic garbage :) All in all - a visually very pleasing game with fun game-mechanics and loot. Love it! 10/10

I. Fucking. Love. This. Game. STORY ------- By far the best aspect of this game. The story and main characters (or even the side characters) are so engaging that it feels as if youre watching an interactive movie. So often with games that allow you to create your own character, it doesn't allow for a finely polished set of interractions due to how different YOUR character may be and how that character has to interract with the world around him/her. Being that you are one set character in this game, everything is written with that in mind and it is just a fantastic ride. I'll admit that the main villain of the base game feels somewhat underwhelming from a narrative standpoint, and doesn't exactly feel like the main stride of the game. Both of the Expansion packs' main villains, however, are absolutely AMAZING and I might even add that the First Expansion (Hearts of Stone) has a main villiain that may be my favorite character in any form of media that I've ever seen in my life. WORLD ------- In my opinion, the world is lush and filled with different things to do that aren't just repetitive nonsense or reskins of the exact same task. Sure, some things are repeated such as the loot caches but for the vast majority anything you do in the world will be different from what you've already done. Quests in the world introduce you to interesting new NPCs that you'll find yourself attached to even if it's just a brief interaction. The world itself is beautiful, with a variety of areas all being unique being convincing as an actual place in a world. I often find myself just riding around the world on Roach (the horse you ride in the game) and just admiring how absolutely gorgeous this game is. COMBAT/SKILLS ------- This is where some people have different opinions. Personally, I love the combat. It is a more casualized version of previous witcher games, yes, but it works. You can block attacks, roll, or sidestep as well as having heavy attacks and light attacks. You have two swords in this game, one for Monsters and one for Humans/Animals. You have a variety of bombs with different effects as well as potions. There are also blade oils which increase damage to specific types of enemies. You have 5 different Witcher Signs that you can use as well, which can all be upgarded in the skill tree and each has an alternative mode. Lastly, there is a crossbow which I'll admit seem slike more of a tacked on element than an actual meaningful weapon to have. It does come in handy for some flying creatures, however. ========================================================= PROS ------- +Highly detailed and vast world to explore +Amazing dialogue and believable character performance +Gripping questlines +Not repetitive and actually fun to play multiple times over +Choices that actually matter and effect the outcomes of the game +Multiple FREE!!! DLC packs +Cheap expansion packs which add upwards of 20 hours or more each to the game +Yennefer SUBJECT TO OPINION -------- +/- Some may not enjoy the combat or find it mediocre +/- The game is long (which I find a massive plus) but some people find this to be overwhelming NEGATIVES ------- - Triss - People who like Triss - People who think Triss is better than Yennefer - Dumbed down alchemy from previous witcher games - Underwhelming loot caches SUMMARY ------- Hands down the best game I've ever played and my favorite game that I've played to date. This game has set the new standard for RPG titles or even video games in general, with the phenomenal main story and gripping quest lines with none of the usual repetitive nonsense that plagues RPGs commonly. Is it perfect? No. It has it's flaws but they are few and far between and in most cases completely subjective to opinion rather than a definitive negative point in itself. Let's just say that I'm currently on my 3rd full playthrough of the game at nearly 300 hours and I don't see myself stopping any time soon.

This has more content than triple A games, and at a higher quality than most of them. It's $15 dollars. The controls are perfect, even on a keyboard. The story is perfect. The upgrades are perfect. While some bosses are better than others, they mostly ooze creativity, brilliant design, and orange infection all over the screen. The visual art rivals the likes of renaissance masters, and the music rivals the likes of classical composers. This is the best purchase I've made in years. If I had to find something bad to say, and it almost pains me to do so, it would be that some of the secrets are hidden a little too well to find without a walkthrough. That's it. That's the absolute worst thing I can possibly say about this game. Some people might have trouble with parts of it being too difficult or too easy at some parts, but that's almost entirely because of the incredibly branching path you can take. This means that some bosses are balanced for later or earlier in the game. I actually found this to be a good thing. It's prevented me from getting stuck on bosses when I personally had a hard time with the attack patterns, but it has also allowed me to dare to challenge bosses that I encountered early. Additionally, it adds a level of replayability, since each playthrough can vary so wildly depending on the order you do things.

An overall improvement in all aspects of Tomb Raider (2013). If you enjoyed that game I definitely recommend playing Rise of the Tomb Raider. [h1] Gameplay [/h1] There are still a ridiculous amount of collectibles, challenges and platforming as in the first. I'm not a big fan of collect-a-thons as it feels like a cheap to pad out the playtime of a game. I am a big fan of exploration and puzzles and this game was able to scratch that itch for me. While the puzzles are slightly challenging, none that I came across completely stumped me or needed me to look at a guide to solve, I would say the puzzles in the first game are harder than any I came across in RoTR. I really liked how in this game there was much less emphasis on quick time events (QTE's). There are less QTE's so I found myself dying a lot less and not having to watch the gruesome death cutscenes. The action sequences are much less over the top compared to the 2013 reboot, Lara DOESN'T get impaled and is then miraculously running around later on like nothing has happened. These make the story and Lara as a character somewhat believable and it doesn't feel like I'm watching a bad 80s action movie. [h1] Combat [/h1] The stealth combat in this game was really fun and reminded me of the stealth mechanics in the old Assassin's Creed games (but with many improvements). The stealth sections of the game were really fun and when you had the option to use stealth or run and gun, I chose stealth every time. The crafting and upgrading was also good and felt fair and balanced. The maps are bigger and there are more animals you can hunt (birds, deers, bears, wolves,..), I did hunt a few times and while you do need animal skins to craft pouches, upgrades, arrows it never felt grindy. The game throws so many resources at you, that you don't need to constantly hunt animals - you can just pick them up in crates or backpacks. There is also on the fly crafting for bandages (heals) and throwable weapons (like grenades and mines), which for me added to the immersion and makes you feel like an explorer and using the environment to your advantage. I do have one minor complaint about combat and that would be that the melee combat felt weird in this game. Although that may be by design as an axe is not great for hand to hand combat. The dodge and counter attack felt very unsatisfying in this game and the QTE for the counter window would not always show up. Dodging felt very strange as there was no enemy lock on or targetting, you could dodge and be facing with your back to the enemy leaving you wide open for an attack and you wouldn't be able to see because neither the camera or Lara would adjust to the attacking enemy. I also found using axe finishers would occasionally cause the camera to clip into walls. [h1] Overall [/h1] I did get a few stutters in the "open world" areas and occasionally the game would get stuck for about 5 seconds before going back to normal. I never had any CTD's or lost progress or had anything game breaking so not a major issue for me and I was able to look past that. It's a good game and if you enjoyed the first Tomb Raider from the rebooted trilogy, I recommend playing this game. [b] 7.75 / 10 [/b]

An excellent entry into the DOOM franchise, held back by the same recurring (albeit subjective) problems that have been present in many of its installments. The game certainly has its problems, but I've greatly enjoyed it regardless and would overall recommend. Pros - The new cadence they've established to the game is very fascinating in regards to weapon management and chainsaw usage. It's like almost like an established dance tempo to Doomguy's routine. I like it. - Production quality remains excellent. Animations, visual and audio effects are visceral and well done. - Every gun and ability has feeling behind it through sound, damage, and the resulting gore. - Slayer gates are some of the most fun you'll have in this game. Every one of them has been a satisfying roller coaster from start to finish. - BATTLEMODE (though subjective) was an interesting pvp mode I enjoyed, even if balance rides on a thin line. It really does feel like the ultimate stress test of reflexes and wit versus strategy and coordination. Cons - Early game is awful. Slow and lacking of any meaningful arsenal. After the first level or so, it picks up momentum and you actually have fun. - Platforming has very slippery control and feels like padding for game time. I didn't like it in previous DOOM iterations, I don't like it here either. - Goo sucks and is a lazy way to try and invoke discord in the player's movement. Marauder's design doesn't fit DOOM. Pain Elemental and Archvile are examples of annoying enemies done better. - Netcode is utterly atrocious in BATTLEMODE and is its biggest setback.

Rome II has a few nice features the original Rome Total War lacked, like cavalry being able to dismount for assaults on cities ; and a battlefield AI which, after patching, is reasonably competent and doesn't throw it's generals in immediately to their deaths to try to run down a unit of skirmishers. Unfortunately it not only drops many of the most interesting, enjoyable and atmosphere enhancing features that were in the original Rome, but also implements many features in ways that destroy game-play, believability and historical accuracy. It also seems unfinished The province system in which cities are grouped into provinces in which buildings in one city affect every city in the province held by the same faction is interesting, but the way buildings work is pretty annoying. You can research technology, but the starting tech isn't even bronze age - you need a tech advance for battering rams and ladders. The level of detail you can see in your settlements population, happiness/unhappiness, squalor etc is massively reduced as is info on where income and trade income comes from. The political system and 1 year turns result in generals being recalled or dying as soon as they get any significant experience or skills. Agents don't last much longer. The stylised icon interface is annoying and not intuitive. The AI and pathfinding bugs in assaults on walled cities are pretty terrible even after 6 patches and one beta patch. The AI still can't pick up, put down and use ladders, rams or siege towers effectively the way it could in the original Rome Total War ten years ago or Medieval 2 Total War 7 years ago. There are over 100 factions, but many are out of period or just made up, including client states like Carthage's two ; and they slow the AI turn down more and more as the game progresses. Worst of all are the instant super transports. Any army can create transports to carry it by stepping off a beach, for free. They're capable of fighting in sea battles and beating any starting fleet whether in auto-calc or not by weight of numbers. Every faction from Scythian nomad horse archers to Spanish and African tribes goes for a sail in the Mediterranean, with nothing much to fear from enemy navies. Factions which lose all their cities also take to the sea. They then either float there till they slowly die, or hover off the coast forcing you to place armies in all your coastal cities for dozens of turns until they slowly die of attrition, or else they take cities by avoiding your land armies and acting as vikings. What? Build fleets to hunt them down you say? But you can't afford to - ships for fleets take time and money to build and require pay. Instant transports don't - and your own field armies are tied down on land preventing them from coming back by sea. Bizarrely the game designers have decided that transports should be just a slightly inferior version of a large oared warship with the same hundreds of oarsmen and ram and sleek design as a warship. In reality in the Roman and Hellenistic period transports were usually commandeered merchant sailing ships, because they could carry enough troops, horses and food and water for them. Oared warships were good for ramming, boarding and raking the oars off of enemy ships - but all those oarsmen and the narrow hulls to make them maneuverable left them with no room to carry more than a few marines. They usually followed coastlines so they could land to get food and water for the oarsmen each day - and so they could land if there was bad weather as oared galleys were not very seaworthy. Yet insta-super-transports somehow fit hundreds of soldiers, horses and elephants. Unlike in the original Rome you can fight out sea battles rather than just autocalc them. The ships and marines in sea battles look great, but the way sea battles work is pretty lamentable. Boarding is made very easy. No need to use grapples (iron hooks on ropes) to get close to an enemy ship to board it, let alone use a corvus (rotatable boarding ramp with a spike on the end to go through the enemy deck) - bumping into them is good enough. Even more ridiculously, once one ship is boarding another no other ship or marines can touch either of them. Historically smaller galleys could outmanouvre and defeat larger ships - as at the battle of Actium. In Rome II small ships are incapable of doing much damage to larger ones, even where the large ship is a transport or some lightly built viking style ship. Historically a small oared galley with a metal plated ram could turn faster than larger ships and immobilise them by oar raking (shearing off enemy ship's oars using ram). Or they could sink them by ramming broadside and holing it below the waterline. Many major ancient cities such as Syracuse and Jerusalem, which the Romans had great difficulty taking by siege and assault due to their massive fortifications and inner and outer walls and citadels are in the game as unwalled villages and hamlets. This makes the game even more ridiculous and annoying for anyone who knows even the basics of the history – and makes no sense. Total War games can’t include every settlement, so they usually include the most important, largest or most strategically significant ones. By conquering a settlement you conquered the province it was in in Rome Total War. In Rome II this is called the ‘region’ with two or more regions grouped into a province. How could the most important settlement in an entire region be a hamlet or a village? Even ignoring the pissing all over history, this makes no sense. Giving three quarters of settlements no walls seems like it was another cheap, rush option to minimise costs and so maximise profits. Have working siege AI? Nah - just re-use the engine from Empire, Napoleon and Shogun Total War but take the walls off most cities. Some attempt to justify this as reducing the number of "boring" sieges / assaults. In fact it reduces the frequency and size of field battles compared to Rome 1 or Medieval 2 Total War because in those games the player or AI required at least 1 turn and usually more to build enough siege equipment to take a town - and in that time the player or AI usually sent an army to try to break the siege - resulting in a battle with the relieving army on one side and the besieging army and garrison on the other. In Rome II you get lots of incredibly dull and annoying assaults on the unwalled town square against some garrison militia units instead. Field battles or assaults on an actual walled town using siege equipment would be preferable. The myriad bugs a requiring endless patching and missing features suggest it was rushed out incomplete and without even beta testing. Rome II runs poorly and with poor graphics on many PCs and laptops unless the Graphical Enhancement Mod is used. Mistakes made in the ongoing patching process make the game currently not run with mods. Anyone thinking of buying should hold off for at least 6 months and maybe a year or two till patching is over and better mods finished

Worth a second go The first time I played Stick of Truth, I bounced off hard. Partly because I'm not a huge fan of the combat style, but also because the difficulty isn't well done. It's very easy in most places with massive spikes- particularly the fight that involves a former government official. That fight is totally doable, but it's head and shoulders above the difficulty level of anything else near that part of the game. In fact, that fight is probably harder than any of the end-level boss fights. But a few years later I thought I'd give it another go, because I did like the humor. This time I spent a little more time figuring out and reading strategies and had a much eaiser time, to the point where I breezed through on 'hardcore' mode. The game still has some pretty significant mechanical drawbacks, but the humor, plot, and stylization are worth it. First, the game IS Southpark. It's not a licensed game made with Southpark characters, it's much more like the actual show that just happens to be built to be interactive. Everything from character creation to abilities to missions just screams 'Southpark' and it's clear that the creators had a huge amount of influence, unlike some earlier SP games. The basic quest structure mirrors that of many episodes where the kids are having their own little game that happens to run into a 'real world' problem. The whole thing is styled after the 'Black Friday' episodes and fits perfectly for a game- so much so that I wish it was being continued in the next SP game, but that may be because I like the 'fantasy' setting more than superheroes. The game is set up to be about as '3d' as the series which is... not. This works aestetically but causes problems with getting around puzzles and sometimes makes it hard to even see the solutions. It also seems like the creators loved some of the ideas they had a bit too much- for example, the use of an alien butt-probe to get around is used way too much and serves less as a puzzle and more of an annoyance for the latter half of the game. The 'magic' (i.e. farting) to get through obstacles gets a bit old as well, though at least it often serves more as a way to kill foes out of combat. As I mentioned, I'm not a big fan of the turn-based fighting system but it's a matter of preference. The biggest drawback is still probably that the difficulty is not balanced well over the course of the game. The player can take one buddy with him at a time. Some are definitely more interesting and useful than others. Stan, for example, definitely gets the short end of the stick. In terms of classes I tried Jew and Mage, both of which felt very powerful- though Jew seemed to get very powerful near the end while Mage was comparatively powerful in the early stages. In the latter stages Cartman and Kyle become recruitable, and both have quite powerful attacks. Depending on which buddy is chosen, the new kid (player character) will hear a variety of banters at different times. Kenny, unfortunately, seems even more difficult to understand than in the show and again, stan just doesn't have much to say- but I guess if you're looking for comedic lines you wouldn't go for the straight-man anyway. In terms of plot, jokes, atmosphere, etc, I would recommend the game to anyone who likes the show- which it emulates, RPGs- which it often subverts, or poop jokes- which it embraces. I will warn that there are some lines and songs ripped directly from the show to the point where it feels less like fanservice and more like a bit of laziness. As a final note, even though I'm not 5 years old I really never got tired of the fact that the player can go up to pretty much anyone and fart on them or hit them causing a variety of comedic lines. Unlike some of the other gimmicks, it never felt old because the game never insisted on the player doing it.

Counter-Strike: Source is an amazing game. Not only that, but it is also a very competitive and very punishing. There is no health regeneration, nor is there any respawn until the next round. In addition, there is a certain amount of money you get each round, which you can save or spend on weapons. If you don't die, you keep the weapon until the next round. If you die, you lose the weapon and have to buy it again. Because of this, you have to think out every move you make to make sure you don't die and waste money to purchase useful and effective equipment and weapons. In each game, there are two groups, the Counter-Terrorists and the Terrorists, and there are two game modes - Defusal and Hostage Rescue. In defusal, the Terrorists place a bomb in one of the two bomb spots, and the Counter-Terrorists have to defuse it in a set amount of time. In hostage rescue, the Terrorists have to stop the Counter-Terrorists from rescuing four hostages. In either of these modes, though, you can also just kill all of the opposing team and the round is over. Besides these modes, there are also user-made modes, like Gun Game, Deathrun, and Surf. Every game mode that I have played has been a blast, and I've clocked over 400 hours. It's insanely addicting, and a lot of fun.

[h1] Innovation in a zombie game? This can't be true! [/h1] [quote=Wikipedia][i]Dying Light is a zombie apocalypse-themed game set in an open world. Players traverse an expansive urban environment overrun by a vicious epidemic, scavenging the world for supplies and crafting weapons to defend against the growing infected population with a heavy focus on freerunning mechanics, allowing players to perform actions such as climbing ledges, leaping off from edges, sliding, jumping from roofs to roofs and zip-lining.[/i][/quote] I'll tell you something right away. [b]Dying Light[/b] is something you'd never expect from a zombie game: innovation, smooth mechanics, a storyline, tons of tasks, variety and devs who listen to the consumers. So the story... The story is not the best thing you could hope for — it's quite cheesy with its stereotypical antagonists and doesn't succeed in making the important characters feel like they matter enough, lacking an emotional connection. The first half of the main story is promising, but after you get to Old Town, the tasks get quite repetitive and the plot starts falling apart, offering no interesting continuation or conflicts to prior events. Luckily, the game still has huge replay value due to the meticulously crafted gameplay elements and co-op shenanigans. The smooth mechanics of the game really make up for the lackluster story, since slicing and bashing zombies and jumping from rooftop to rooftop feels really fluid and it really is a blast. [b]Overall[/b], Dying Light is a great game, despite its flaws. I couldn't ask for more when it comes to gameplay, weapons and co-op. The only real con is the story — if it was done as well as the game mechanics, this game would be GOTY material without a doubt.
