Playing this game was an awful experience. I feel bad saying this, because there is a LOT of good in here. The combat and skill systems are unique and immaginative, most characters are distinctive, and the worldbuilding is original enough. If you like exploration, if you don't mind reloading time and again because something blindsided you without forewarning, if you like having to beat a difficult game and using your hard-gained knowledge to succeed on your Nth try... you'll have a blast. I mean it. But if you are like me, and you are coming here for an RPG... don't. On paper, the story sounds serviceable enough; but living through it is frustrating and a chore that strips the game of meaning. The big allure of RPGs, for me, is to make choices and see the consequences; here, nothing you do actually really matters. You spend hour upon hour trying to fix the problems of the first area? All those people will die as you leave it. Well, some will survive. For an hour, before a deus ex machina kills them all, which you survive only thanks to another deus ex machina. You go around the second area? Nothing has weight, only your training matters. So it feels like farming and little more. You finally get to the big objective the game has been building up? You get blindsided by a deus ex machina and saved by a deus ex machina, having accomplished nothing. Worse still, it's the same dei ex machina from the first time! I guess if the tone was meant to be bleak and hopeless, it could work. But it's full of colorful characters and talking animals and silly side quests, so the tone really doesn't work. It never feels funny, because the apocalypse is ongoing. It doesn't feel bleak, because you are helping turtles and mouses falling in love. It doesn't feel epic, because you get nothing done. Your victories mean nothing. There is also a lot of bookkeping. To stay relevant, you need to renew your loot every two level or so. On every character. There are ten gear slots on each, each with multiple attributes and requirements. It's a great system, intriguing and complex. But you have to spend so much time twitching it, you end up hating it. Looting the bodies litterally takes me longer than fighting the baddies, every time. This really breaks the immersion. And don't even get me started about fucking lockpicks. Also, it's a minor thing, but the combat system makes a huge deal about positioning. Which, you know, is awesome. Except you will almost always start the fight with your group walking together, unless you want to constantly be clicking them individually, while the enemies are always well prepared in position. So unless they wreck you and you have to reload, approach quietly and try to guess when the combat will trigger, the system will be something you fight against and not with. The game also makes a big deal about you being able to choose where to go freely in a given area, which sounds like freedom unltil you realize how much character and gear level factor into your ability to survive a fight. The quests have no suggested level on your journal, so this "freedom" means you'll have to spend tiem getting wrecked before finally finding a a quest you can finish. There is a lot of good in this game. But the bad really makes it an unpleasant experience. I doubt I'll ever pick it up again.

TL;DR : If you put over 500 hours in the game, quit whining. ARK is Awesome. And for perspective players, this is why. ARK: Survival Evolved, is a fantastic game. I could not believe it was still in Early Access when it first released on steam, and have been constantly wowed with the quality of their continual updates. It is truly a wonderful sandbox with incredible mod support to make this game anything you want it to be. The demands for playing on high settings are heavy, but the game is still very pretty and easily playable on low settings. One of our computers that got a 'cannot run it' on CanYouRunIt could play on low settings without any lag, and the player still had a wonderful experience with it until the computer was upgraded a year later. To hear recently (as of September 3rd) that it was STILL early access blew my mind. I was sure it had released as a full game. I paid $30 for the base game and have put in AT LEAST 500 hours of game play. That comes out to 6 cents and hour. I leave and come back weeks or months later and every time find something beautiful and new. 500 hours and I have still not fully explored the whole starting island. The center map, which is a full new map for free (done by the community) is absolutely stunning. Exploring it has taken my breath away several times. Scorched earth is currently $20 and promises to have much more growth to it but is a welcome counter to the dense jungles and lush beached. The harsh environment is beautiful in it's own way and the hidden marvels so far have lived up to everything the other two maps I have played on have lead up it. On the standard settings, taming takes a very long time. Taking down your animal (without killing it), fending off the other predators that wander by for an opportue bite, and finally having one on your side is a fulfilling experience. It can get old, and incredibly frustrating when you spend 5 hours attempting to tame something and a dilo or compy walks by and eats it when you arn't looking. But that is part of the game. Private servers or personal game can be set to tame dinos nearly instantly if you desire, so if the waiting game isn't for you, then you don't have to play it. What ever your play style, Ark has something for you. Just like if you don't want anything to creep up and eat you, you can set the difficulty very low and boost your health incredibly high and just go to town building your own cities or castles or what ever it is you want to do. You can simply sit and farm if you wish. You can spend all day breeding dinos to get what ever color or stats you want from them. You can paint them. You can use server commands to change their base color. You can paint yourself up, dye armor, paint walls and deal with the fashion aspect of the game. You can spend all day crafting recipes or creating your own. You can simply explore the island. You can scuba dive and explore underwater reefs and caves. You can be a pirate on a raft, or a trader, or have a dino based walking attack castle with automatic gun turrets. You can fly around and pick up dodos, strap them up with C4 and bomb Rexs and anything else you please. And if there something you that you can't find, Mod it yourself, or ask the amazing moding community to make your dreams come true. The ONLY thing I don't like about the game is the lack of player character customization. The base two gender figures are basically the same, though you can change the sizes of different parts of your body. Hair color and eye color mildly differentiate the player, as does the inclusive range of skin color, but it is extremely basic and needs improvement. But, let me say this. ANY game you have played and enjoyed for more then 80 hours well outranks the re playability of most AAA games. There is an extraordinary number of Early Access games that are borderline scams that cost $30 or more for less then 10 hours of full gameplay. Many of us gamers will play $50 for a game we hardly touch because we didn't like it. So if you got over 100 hours of quality entertainment our of a game, do not bitch about paid DLC for $20. Go play any of the many user made FREE maps, or FREE DLC or wait for more updated content that is continually coming to the main ARK game for FREE. Or play it on the FREE weekends. Or next time they release a FREE Survival of the Fittest Map. I'll be taking my $40s of 500 hours of game play and playing another 500 hours or more. And you won't hear me whining.

How long have I been playing this game? 2 hours? 300 hours? 4 years? It's hard to keep track. Let me elaborate: Character creation is solid and straight-forward. There are a LOT of choices. People who have played D&D 3.5 may be a little overwhelmed. The closest approximation I can make is to have all of the 3.5 supplemental books and access to all of the prestige classes, but they're available at level 1 and balanced accordingly. If you start this game with an idea of what you want to play, you're still not going to be ready for all of the options available to you. So I made my character and started a new game. Immediately my lore-hound senses start going off. The history of the world is insane, and there are more dialogue options than I really expected. Tracking down every little detail will be a daunting task for even the most seasoned of completionists. On top of finding information about the political landscape that you'll be navigating, there are also books upon books of stories from individuals (some that you'll meet, and some that you won't). Everything is well-polished and adds a level of immersion that really sucks you in. Managing your kingdom puts a sense of urgency to your exploration, as things keep moving at your capitol even if you're out adventuring. You'll want to make occasional return trips to check on things while you're out looting (and pillaging, if you're so inclined). Completing tasks in your capitol can affect your other gameplay, so pay close attention to what you're advisers are doing. For instance, trolls may start harassing your people until something is done, and you'll start seeing more trolls on your adventures until a solution is found. When you combine all of the game's elements, and really give yourself over to the environment, the characters, and the story, it's easy to lose track of time. Playing for two hours feels like playing for four. It's an odd sensation when you're used to the opposite.

A really fantastic game, with practically infinite replayability. Paradox gets an awful lot of flak for their DLC policy, and many have complained that they feel they are being robbed of the whole experience of the game. However, what is all too often ignored is the fact that expansive free updates accompany each DLC, and that this free content would not exist were it not for the DLC policy. People may say that they feel robbed by Paradox, but were it not for their DLC policy then the game would be a mere fraction of the gem it is today. Someone who bought this game at launch, and hasn't bought any DLC since, will have hugely benefited from the DLC, as it will have supported huge new free content expansions that add depth and fun to the game. While you don't need any of the DLC to enjoy the game, and I speak from experience here, I would still suggest that you pick up some of the key ones during a sale. It's worth bearing in mind though that a great many of the DLC, such as unit packs for instance, are purely cosmetic, and in no way affect the game. Furthermore, there's no need to worry about the lack of DLC affecting your ability to enjoy the game with others. Whoever hosts a multiplayer game essentially allows players to use their copy of the game, granting access to the effects of new DLC in your campaign. EU4 is a game that has received many times more development, polish, and attention to detail than most games will in their lifetimes, and it shows in the enormous strategic depth and complexity the gameplay has to offer. Whilst intimidating to newcomers, soon enough it becomes intuitive, and I would strongly urge people to play multiplayer with their friends in order to rapidly hone their skills. When I first got this game, I didn't have that pleasure, and partly out of laziness, partly out of my love of Crusader Kings II, I sadly neglected Europe Universalis IV for far too long, and I really wish I hadn't. So take the plunge, buy it in a sale, jump right in or watch a few guides if your nervous, and have fun! It's a true joy to play. If you like it, then grab some of the DLC on sale too if you fancy.

This game has had so much potential but it has failed to become the great game I thought it should be. This is because of a few things. 1) Balance 2) DLC 3) Stupid leave game system 4) Botched alliance and favour system 5) Coalitions First of all the balance, this game has the entire world for you to play as but most of time will be in europe. Why? Well faster gameplay stronger units on average as well as more and bigger events than anywhere else. This leads to the balance complaint. First of all if Castille decides to it can easily conquer most of Northern Africa then inherit Aragon and possible Naples very early game. Meaning they can quickly expand into Italy and lower parts of Africa. This then leads to the alliances complaint as it is entirely possible for Castille to have both Austria and France as allies meaning the main defence for Africa (Ottoman Empire) is not going to last very long especially with Poland and Lithuania glaring at them as well. A united India would struggle to push back a European power as well. The DLC in this game while it did come out very slowly and only the host needs it is a gauling ammount. Another complaint with this is the unbalancing that Common Sense originally brought with it which if not purchased allowed the AI to develop their provinces making them much better while you couldn't without the DLC. The alliance system in the Cossacks was a step in the right direction for curbing the use of powerful nations for rapid expansion but it does not seem to have an option for 'I am attacking your rival, please help me curb their power', which I have found it to be rather annoying. Some of the features do feel like they should have been in the base game anyway such as the ability to swap occupations which came with the art of war DLC. More of an annoyance than an actual complaint but the game shuts down briefly and reloads if you quit the game you were in. At least it is a step forward from the previous method of locking you out of multiplayer if you were going to go play with a friend. The alliance system as mentioned before does need some work still. This because you can have all the powerful nations in the same area all allied with each other which basically means game over. I have seen this with Scandanavia - France - Commonwealth which was proberly the most annoying, Russia - Ottomans - Austria - Papal State, this one was daft. Britain - Austria - Castille - Aragon, is a more recent one I have seen. I would say this makes it interesting but they will quickly become immortal and just keep expanding everywhere. The coalition system, now this is a huge pain. Largely because the AI never seem to get them. I have seen France take over huge portions of land in Germany in single wars and not have any back lash for it. Normally it is measured through development but since it is Germany the average values are quite high and can easily cause a coalition. I have had this game since 2016, but I never got very far with it. I recently played through the full game with a group of friends (5 of us in total) and it was honestly a really fun experience. The gameplay is simple; Find a spot, build a base, explore the world, hit a wall, find a way to overcome said wall. This was enjoyable, as we found ourselves backtracking a fair amount, to find something we needed to continue forward later and finding lots of little secrets on the way. Building a base was priority one for us when we were in our first few nights, but as we progressed, we spent less and less time at the base, so it felt like wasted time and improving it just wasnt worth it. This feels very true post-story too. The building mechanics themselves are great however, and the most creative of people will be able to make some really great creations. The combat was fun, but somewhat frustrating at times. The game does a great job of dropping you into a world without explaining things, so the enemies really do pack a punch until you learn how to deal with them (which is the frustrating part). I can imagine solo being especially hard, as you dont have a friend to revive you. Overall, the game is great, and I hope the sequel is just as fun, but with some tweaks. More emphasis on the base(s), terraforming and survival is all id ask for.

Dropping the tag of a covert ops group looking to defend Earth, [b][i]XCOM 2[/i][/b] sees you reinvented as a Guerrilla fighter unit, battling an occupying force of Snake Men and robotic foes. Whereas before you had to enter the battlefield blind, [b][i]XCOM 2[/i][/b] adds to the formula by providing you the chance of sneaking up on your enemy. Concealment acts as mode where you can avoid enemy fire and set up your own ambushes. It means you can take on a whole wave of foes and enjoy finishing them off in one foul swoop. The battle system remains the same, challenging players to move their fighters across blocks of movement spaces, finding cover to help them survive through the AI’s turn. From the start, it feels like you're against the clock, be it on the ground or in the air. The isometric battlefields throw-up procedurally generated maps and mission objectives, meaning the problem of constant grind has been dealt with quite effectively. [b][i]XCOM 2[/i][/b] also does a good job of tying its story with real-world events, you must wreck Advent's plans at every turn to pushback the inevitable chaos that will consume humanity. Building the right rooms and facilities will mean reducing healing time, however that will also remove the chance of something else that could provide better weaponry. This gives rise to a multi-layered adventure that follows a different course each time you play. One thing you can never factor in, however, is luck. While the game does seem a little less random than Enemy Unknown, you are still faced with times of joy and frustration. Luckily, [b][i]XCOM 2[/i][/b] single-player offers a great deal of content for its price tag and can make for quite a thrilling ride. UPDATE: With Denuvo Anti-Cheat removed in the recent patch, I am giving this game a thumbs up as per my original review. The original post is still below from the time when Denuvo Anti-Cheat was included. This was the only issue I had with the game, otherwise it is a well rounded experience that truly challenges me. ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Old Post Below ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Bought and enjoyed the game since launch, but with the new Denuvo Anti-Cheat update, my enjoyment immediately died. I installed the update without realizing that it would install Denuvo. My game that used to run consistently at least 90 FPS dropped to 60 FPS and would dip from time to time. Performance wasn't the only concern, since Denuvo runs on ring 0, where it has access to portions of my computer that only the OS and drivers are supposed to have. While I do understand that this runs only during the game, the damage that can be done while it is active can be irreversible. If there is a bug or false positive detected, the anti-cheat could cause unnecessary damage to user files. This is even worse for an exploit, as hackers can use this to compromise a user's system, all they need to do is wait until the anti cheat is in use. I enjoyed this game, and my main issue has been with the inclusion of the Denuvo anti-cheat. Not sure why I would need an anti-cheat for a primarily single player game with only 3% of its player base playing more than 25 matches of multiplayer. Once (and if) Bethesda remove the anti-cheat from the system, and continue to show that they are taking steps to fixing this issue, I will change my review to positive.

LOOTBOXES ARE STILL IN THE GAME. WHAT WAS REMOVED WAS THE MARKETPLACE / PREMIUM CURRENCY. I've seen too many reviews, articles, and blogs touting that lootboxes are "removed from the game," which is just completely uninformed and patently untrue. With the removal of $$ microtransactions (once again, this is NOT the removal of lootboxes; there are still various "crates" earned or bought with in-game currency, except now you can't directly purchase captains, instead just "training orders" that customize captains), the game shows marked improvement. However, multiple facets of the game design were specifically modeled with microtransactions in mind. These still feel completely out of place in a single-player game. Additionally, the AI in the pit-fighting is STILL a complete joke: most times a literal coin-flip as to whether or not your captain will decide to initiate an animation that makes any sense or does any damage. This game is simply not as good as it could be, purely because predatory, anti-consumer, corporate greed heavily influenced major elements of the game design and narrative structure. These systems and mechanics have been tweaked after the removal of the marketplace, but are still a net negative and detract from the experience. Get it on a 75% off sale. ORIGINAL: I had fun with the combat and story, but the orc pit-fighting is garbage, the lootboxes are ludicrous, and the "true end" is locked behind a repetitive grindwall designed to bore you to the point of spending money for higher level orcs. What I cannot understand is people leaving positive reviews who didn't enjoy the combat/story, instead lauding the nemesis system. Any iteration of any pokemon clone over the past 20 years will give you a more rewarding experience in terms of collecting/leveling your army than the awful pit-fighting in this game.

Death Stranding evokes a feeling I haven't felt in many other games. It is at times both tense and relaxing, flowing between the emotions it pours out at its audience much like a relaxing, albeit slow-moving, river. The soundtrack, gloomy and serine, kicks in at opportune moments and never overstays its welcome. The game's presentation is solemnly artful and gorgeous, even while the world it depicts is so dreadful and empty. Death Stranding plays with the void it portrays by emphasizing gameplay features that have the players explore the concepts of connection and existentialism. The story is high concept and difficult to follow at times, but it's an enjoyable ride all the same. All in all, Death Stranding is an experience worth having and though I believe the reception it received upon its original release to be valid and not entirely unfair, I feel many of the opinions shared were shortsighted and not willing to give the experience its proper chance.

I love a good vampire story and this game really nailed the vampire mechanic. Usually I like to role play my character in games if possible and normally this results in me being the "good" guy that saves everyone. Not in this game, it's too tempting to give in the temptation of blood - so I already killed a few more or less important characters. Dotnod really nailed the whole execution of "embracing" those humans. The screen turns all red, the music gets much more dramatic, sometimes there is a short cutscene where your "prey" tries to get away - but they are left without a chance. The more you embrace humans the stronger you get but it comes with trade-offs: you can potentially lose a district and any potential quests from the person. This is a very clever mechanic on the one hand side it allows for great replay value on the other hand it gives so much character to this mechanic, you can really feel how more powerful you get when you embrace humans. The game also shows you how much XP a human gives you when you embrace them, which makes them almost look like tasty dinner to me - haha it's a really great mechanic for a vampire game. The game is very text heavy and not all dialogs are very interesting in my opinion. That for me is the biggest downside. I am only in Chapter 3 so far and I like the game, might buy it again for console to play with different choices. I can recommend it and I think the price is fair - I do think in general $50 is a fair price for a video game, given the resources it costs to produce them. I had no technical issues and the game supports Ultrawide properly which is a plus.

Straight off the bat, I'd like to say that this is by far the best game I've ever played. Even though I dont have too much of a gaming history when it comes to JRPGs, the game is just phenominal. To sum it up in a couple of words, its a roller coaster ride of emotions with otherworldly music and memorable characters. I'm just going to provide here my personal opinion of the positives and negatives of the game that I can think of: PROS: - Fun, action filled gameplay - Large open world with lots of places to explore - A variety of different weapons to chain together fun combos - No need for any knowledge from previous games to know whats going on (but the lore is interesting) - Good graphics and quite smooth* (I'll talk a little about this later) - THE EMOTIONAL BAGGAGE - THE ENDINGS (this just broke me on the inside... but in a good? way) - Difficulty settings for all skill levels (Easy - Very Hard) and you can change it anytime - THE MUSIC - 2B[spoiler]'s butt ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)[/spoiler] - The game's change in playstyle (ie. it can go from 3D open world to 2D platforming or a top down view) *While I've heard that other people seem to be struggling with the game being weird with its graphics, I personally didnt have much of a problem with this (except for one time where the game had to render a lot of things, and since my PC is actually a potato, it couldnt handle very well so FPS dropped a bit) CONS: - The controls on keyboard and mouse could be a lot better (double tap evade? ew. but you get used to it) - Hacking is the bane of my existence (the mouse aiming killed me on the inside [spoiler]low-key hint, if you cant beat a hacking game you can just set the game on easy mode and equip auto-evade[/spoiler]) - The map is kinda confusing - You cant really do much in the debug room without a controller - Despite being state-of-the-art fancy androids that can sand surf in high heels in the desert, STUMBLING IS YOUR WORST ENEMY Honestly, what I've said is only a very basic summary of the game. While I understand that this is not everyone's cup of tea (and considering its hefty price, it may not seem worth it to some people), I would honestly recommend it very much if you're interested in good (mostly orchestra/classical-ish type) music, killing enemies with flashy, fast paced combat, and good storytelling. All the while sprinkled with a dash of bullet hell. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to go back to my dark hole and ponder about my life again. Gosh, this game gave me a major case of the black-hole-in-your-heart feeling that you get whenever you finish something amazing..... (though Im not quite done yet, I need that 100%) PS. If you dont want to be severely overlevelled and basically one shot everything in your playthroughs.... dont be like me and do all of the side quests.... (you can leave it after playthrough 3 where you unlock chapter select.) [You did your best.][But][don't give up here!]

Fast forward five years into the future - and the series transformed itself into the RPG. A shame that it plays even worse now. It does not even feel like an open world game anymore. Let me explain. Every zone on the map is assigned with the level requirement, and if you are not meeting it then every enemy, and that includes even the local wildlife, will kill you in a couple of hits. You would assume that it's where the stealth comes in but no, even stealth assassination attack remove no more than a quarter of a health bar from the enemy. On the other hand if you are overleveled for a zone, then the experience gains are so vanishingly small that you can safely neglect them. What that means is that at any point you can only explore a single location on a map, effectively making this game a linear experience in an open world map. What is even worse is that you can't just do the story missions only. Because they also have a level requirement and don't provide you with enough experience to continue. So after every story mission there's a grind of doing sidequests so you can do the next story mission. And don't forget that for a long time now a moment to moment gameplay in every Ubisoft game is effectively you doing a checklist: collect X amount of stuff to upgrade Y, kill A amount of enemies to do B, do this insignificant nonsense just so you can perform that. It is all plays so very mind-crushingly boring. Absolutely monotonous, lifeless game.

Even if Huniepop’s selling point lies within its lewd aspects, it’s a fun puzzle/dating sim game that rewards memorization of details and strategy. You interact with the characters by talking to them and buying them things, which rewards “hunie”. This “hunie” is used to improve your stats, which might be needed for harder dates. As you talk to the characters, you will learn certain details about them, only to be quizzed about those later for extra hunie, so either having a decent memory, or Steam’s screenshot function really helps. When you choose to go on a date with a character, a game of match-3 begins. To win, you are required to obtain a specific amount of points (the required minimum becomes higher as you progress), with a limited number of moves. During dates, you use “date gifts”, which provide effects and perks to help you win. Even if you lose, you obtain money which you can use to purchase more stuff for the girls, so unless you’re going for certain achievements, or get emotionally hurt by the girls’ sometimes mean responses to your failure, you got nothing to lose for trying. While this game doesn’t have what I would refer to as a story, there is still an objective, and that is to make love to every “pretty girl” in the neighborhood (plus certain unlockables). I found the characters to be fairly loveable and varied; projecting certain archetypes with some being more obvious than others, and the dialogue managed to get a chuckle out of me a couple of times. Overall, very fun puzzle game, with the addition of lewd. Definitely looking forward to the sequel.

Half Life was one of my childhood defining games (which is probably a terrible thing, but I digress). I thought, that even with a remake, I would always prefer the original. For example, Pokemon Red/Blue could never truely be replaced by Pokemon FireRed/LeafGreen. The graphics were improved but the feel was just different. Black Mesa is better. It captures the EXACT mood and feeling the originals evoked while improving and giving character to the small nooks and crannies that the average player probably wouldn't even think would need touching up. Additionally, I actually really appreciate the game being made in the original Source engine as it, as well as including characters like Kleiner and Eli, really helps glue HL1 and HL2 together, something which I always thought was a bit of a problem storywise. It'd also be awkward to have the first game look better than the second (ala the Star Wars prequels). The tedium and confusion of some of the original levels has been straightened out and just overall, Black Mesa IS Half Life just better, plain and simple. Can't wait for the Xen levels! Xen was a complete mess (imho) in the original, especially against the Nihilanth. Really hoping for some fantastic overhauling and a wonferful finish that does Half Life justice. (P.S. Half Life 3 confirmed.) ________________________________________________________________________________ Some minor complaints or bugs I noticed in my initial playthrough: - HEV Suit Charg Station SFX were so cool in the original, there was no need to change it. - Explosive Satchels clip through the floor sometimes. First noticed this in the outdoor portion of "Questionable Ethics" - Scientists' ties flail around and clip through their torsos upon reloading. - Vortegaunt corpses will resume a T-Pose upon reload sometimes, especially in early levels up through "On a Rail". - During the opening section of "Surface Tension", the distant structures and pipes against the canyon vista could use a little blurring/fog as they appear closer than they should. Otherwise, this version couldn't be more perfect ;)

I'm just about the biggest fan you can find of Megaman X. This game is a phenomenally executed tribute that captures all of the elements that made the X series a thoroughly enjoyable playthrough. Certain trade-offs are apparent, but in my opinion are reasonable given the need to create something both familiar and innovative. What I miss: Bigger build up and boss rush at the end of a playthrough The feeling of a story. Megaman has always been a little story-lite, but this is pretty thin. What I love: The roguelike elements give this game a wide skill gap that you can enter at any phase- memorization of maps won't save you. Difficulty ramps up as you progress. Customize your character as your progress through each playthrough. Co-op! Overall, the game delivers on an emphatically fun experience that does a good job of keeping from getting old. I've poured more than a dozen hours into this thing so far and have no interest in stopping anytime soon. It's more or less everything that Mighty Number Nine should've been.

Many games in their Early Access stages aren’t worth the money that’s being asked for them. Northgard however, in my opinion, is worth the asking price already. That isn’t to say that it can’t be improved. Absolutely every game in existence could be improved in some way and Northgard is by no means an exception. However it’s already got the same level of content as many larger, fully developed games have. In some ways, I actually prefer this game to a fair amount of Triple A games out there. Northgard opened up and the first thing that I noticed is that it looks very professional. It looks like a fully finished game that a large company could have designed. The menus are easy to navigate, and everything is clear. It currently has no way of customising key bindings that I can find, but that isn’t an issue for me as the controls seem pretty standard and were what I was expecting. It’s not very demanding for my computer to run at all I get a solid 50-60fps. The graphics are minimalistic, but that works in favour of the game. Most RTS games are fairly cartoon-like and their graphics are meant to be a bit fun. This is definitely something accomplished in Northgard. I think the art style is incredibly fitting for the game. A lot of people go for hyper-realistic when it doesn’t greatly suit the game however they know what they wanted with this and they got a good result. I like the music in this game. It adds something that improves the gameplay a lot. As far as the setting goes, it’s quite refreshing to see a game based on Norse mythology. There aren’t many out there and there are even less of them that are Real-Time Strategies. I think there is still a lot to be desired in the gameplay though. A lot of the time, it’s just luck as to whether you’ll do well or not. If you start off nearby to 2 enemies, you are going to be destroyed fairly quickly and even if you don’t get taken out, you’re other enemy has spent time building a stable system and has likely gotten halfway to a trade victory or wisdom victory. I think spawning needs to be a bit more balanced because sometimes you have an unfair advantage/disadvantage and that makes the match less fun. The tile system can sometimes be a bit of a pain as well. The entire match is set on tiles which make the game interesting because you have to scout ahead to be able to expand at all, but they also add an element of annoyance into the game. You can only place a set number of buildings per tile and I’m pretty sure it’s a near-random number between 1 and 5 that determines the building count. This was likely added as a way of forcing expansion to stop people from turtling, so it’s a good idea for that reason, but I was taken aback by it when I wasn’t able to place buildings without spending a large amount of food on a new bit of land. I really like the fact that domination isn’t your only route to victory, but rather you can have wisdom, trade, fame, and whatever appears on the map help you to achieve victory as well. Not only do I think that’s a great idea, but you can enable and disable them for the different matches so you can make more interesting games. Overall, I think this game is great because it hasn’t tried to do too much too quickly. It’s a nice economy-building game and it gives you a fair amount of choice as to what sort of match you want to have. I like that no unit is less important than any other so there’s a lot of balancing involved in unit assignment. In the future, I’d quite like to see the game progress so the matches don’t take place on an island, but instead maybe have Viking Longboats to take units between different lands. I’d give this game a 9/10 as an Alpha, but in comparison to fully developed games, I’d award a 7/10.

So I'll admit I'm still working my way through the game, but seriously? This is the game to bring down the big AAAs? One of the greatest games ever made? Winner of over 800 awards? If I wasn't already convinced that video game awards mean shit that would cinch it for me. Full disclosure I came into this game with low expectations. The first was unplayably bad and the second played like a shitty console port. I got maybe a combined 4 hours into them before giving up on both. This one is merely mediocre. Honestly if Steam had a "Meh" rating this would be perfect for it. The graphics are nice, but not 'one of the most expensive games ever made according to Wiki' nice. The music is decent. The voice acting is alright, other than I can't unhear Geralt talking like he has a stuffy nose. But the controls make it clunky to just walk around. Melee combat is bland and repetitive, even on higher difficulties. Non-melee combat is effectively non-existent since your spells only work at point blank range and your crossbow has about the same range as a four year old throwing a teddy bear, and roughly the same effect. And as for the much vaunted story? Well again, I'm not very far in to the game, but after 20+ hours the quest for the baron's family is the one story I've found that's not straight out of Generic Dark Fantasy for Dummies. Every quest is just "hunt down random generic monster and kill it." How many times do you play the "this thing eats children" drama card before it just gets dull? Ultimately I intend to keep playing and see if the story gets any better, and I can certainly understand why some people would rate this as a good game, but it in no way lives up to anywhere near the hype and I dread that a game this mediocre is apparently going to shape the industry for years to come. Update: So after 140+ hours of gameplay and completing both DLC and as many side quests as I could find that didn't involve racing, boxing, or gwent I can offically update my opinion of this game from mediocre to shit. The combat's pathetic, both in terms of quality and difficulty. There are a grand total of two bosses and one generic enemy that require any level of thought, all from DLC. Fucking bears, generally a moderate threat in most games, are probably the easiest fights in the game if only because they're solo and weak to everything. The graphics kinda suck. Yeah the models and environments are nice, but those are, relatively, easy these days and frankly the game is really repetative with them. The animations, dynamic lighting, physics, clipping... are all pretty terrible. It was hard to take Ciri seriously when every scene she failed miserably to actually draw her sword, it just teleported to her hand after the cutscene, and something on her belt was constantly vibrating or slapping her on the ass. The music is alright, if repetative, but sounds in general are obnoxious. Voice acting is all over the place. There's endless screeching from non-hostile NPCs every time a fight is near them, even just a fist fight, which is espcially fun during the tourney brawl. And someone decided taking the three most annoying NPCs in Whiterun, the kid that constantly tries to threaten you, the jackass that talks down to you, and the idiot that's constantly yelling, and mixing them was a good idea for 90% of the background NPCs. The story is trash. I know it gets praised for it's "innovative" quests but they're all just walk over there and follow a red line to the target. It's the standard RPG "kill 10 bears" quests with a little extra legwork and generally less monsters. Even when you do detective work the game makes 0 effort to remember past quests, from a game "known" for remembering your every decision, another thing it doesn't actually do at all. And most of the writing is just generic dark fantasy. Shit is terrible, because everyone is terrible, because everything is terrible. No reasons, nothing you can do, even when you could clearly do something. On top of that it's frustraing playing a character that's such a complete and total pussy. Old man doesn't want to pay full price for a job because he was wrong on the monster? No big deal. Jarl strong arms you with trumped up charges? Roll over and take it. Obnoxious bitch throws you into a lake because she doesn't want to listen to your explanation on how you got mind fucked and effectively raped? Better make sure all those dialog options are apologies or laughing it off. I wanted to play the game to completion to see if it in any way deserved its reputation, but it does not. Overall the only reason I can think this game gets a pass for being such a steaming pile of crap is that it's "indie" but considering how much money was spent on it it's time to stop using that term for it. It's AA at least, if not AAA, and it checks off a significant number of the major failures of AAA games for the last decade except microtransactions.

Satisfactory is a great game, but I have plenty of issues with it. Let me start off by saying some positive aspects: 1. The Progression system in this game is incredibly satisfying, and you feel proud when you figure something out. 2. It's a very nice looking game that has plenty of different environments to explore. 3. There's a very small amount of hand holding. Once you have a base, that's it. You're free to explore. 4. Most games like these don't tend to have a combat system. And while it's not the greatest, it works well enough. 5. There's plenty of world to explore and find new things. 6. There isn't a specific way the game forces you to make things, put what you want wherever you want it. Pretty cool right? Now here's some negatives I have. 1. The AI in this game can be a little unfair. There were times when it would take an hour just to get my inventory back from monsters very close to my base, even at the beginning of the game. 2. There are plenty of bad fps drops, my pc that can run many bigger games struggles to run this one, even with graphics turned down as much as possible. 3. Very buggy. Getting stuck in objects and slowly dying isn't fun. 4. After a while, around tier 6 I started to get very bored of unlocking things. It starts to feel very similar. 5. Plenty of time in this game is spent just sitting around, doing nothing. Some more creativity in base building would be nice. Overall, I would give this game a positive rating. But if it were put on a scoreboard, it would probably be around a 6.5 to a 7. It's worth the price, but could use plenty of improvements.

I don't usually write reviews for game, in fact it's my first one, and the reason behind it is simple: It really deserves it! I played the first Shadow of Mordor, really liked it, because it's a well made game, there were no major flaws, except it was a little short on maps, I wanted to see more of the Mordor. And now I have exactly what I wanted! Graphics are a better, although not mind-blowing for a 2017 game, but what's good is that it's well-optimized! No lags or stuttering, or infamous bugs like you can often see in some open world games (I'm looking at you, Assassin's Creed.) Only glitchy stuff I had was that one time my mantle tried to strangle me for like, 3 sec, we've seen far worse. I really like the music as well, it's really immersive, and goes well with the universe. The universe, then again, is really great! Not surprising since it's LOTR's you could say, but although I did like the movies, I'm not really a fanboy nonetheless. Anyway, gotta admit, it's immersive, I played about 40h in 4 days, so... Yeah. (Haven't finished the game yet btw.) Now for the final part: The gameplay! If you like this kind of game and especially if you liked Shadow of Mordor, you'll defo like this one, it has everything SoM had and so much more! A lil' bit of RPG to spice things up: You have 6 pieces of gear (bow/dagger/blade/mantle/armor/ring) divided in 4 tiers (normal/rare/epic/legendary), and you can add gems to them, a bit like in Diablo 3. Items have your level, you can level them up a bit doing some challenges, legendaries can be leveled up to 60 (max level) if you want to keep them throughout your progression. The nemesis system has been improved, you can now assault fortresses with your armies, fights are epic! Your armies can have special "assets" like archers, graugs, banners... Drakes that you can ride... If you want to know how Daenerys feels, now you can, and it's awesome! The skills, you have about everything you had in the first opus, and more! Now each skill has upgrades (up to 3), the only thing bugging me is that you can only have one upgrade for a skill at a time, so the domination upgrade, or the elf-shot upgrade for the drain, not both :( but well it forces you to adapt a bit your build to your gameplay and to the situation, it's a good thing. Multiplayers: There's next to nothing, but the small things present are nice. You can avenge another player by killing the orc that killed him, or defend/assault a fortress online. Both of these things get you nice rewards too! To finish, I'd like to say a word about the microtransactions: If you don't like them, you can just ignore them, and you can still farm all the legendaries and have them all, you can even have gold coins doing daily challenges to buy chests without putting in money, so for those that don't like that, ignore. I haven't bought any coins, and have about 25 legendaries on the 60/70 available, and most of them are not really useful anyway so no big deal. However, for those who like to speed up their progress, they can, and the game can be even more profitable in the meantime, meaning more reasons to have a Shadow of Mordor 3, while doing absolutely no harm to those who won't use them, it's a win-win! Serisously though, microtransactions can be bad in multiplayers game because they can dig a gap between paying-users and free-users, but in a solo game, where you won't even feel it if you don't want to, what's the harm ?

Few games have had me so engrossed and challenged as XCOM 2. I enjoyed the first one but I had some hangups involving how to manage income and where to focus outside of combat. In addition to that, the permadeath system made me downright terrified to take any chances with strategy. XCOM 2 fixed every single problem by saving your game at every turn in combat which while it may make the game too easy for more adept players, for newbies like me, it let me feel a lot more free to play around and breathe and redo any mistakes I made quickly. Because of that, I felt a lot more free to customize soldiers and even had a little fun writing bios for several soldiers based off friends I knew. They always took well to hearing how well or how proficient their character did, and joked when my actions got them killed or captured. The game felt a lot more balanced with subtle changes like limiting ammo clip size and balancing the classes (sharpshooters are still extremely powerful but the other classes can balance a team out). The game never lets up on the challenge and there is a constant tension in the air but you never feel overwhelmed and burned out. What really set XCOM 2 apart from most strategy games is how great the cinematics are. When you attack an enemy, the camera focuses on the soldier firing and each kill leaves you with an incredible sense of satisfaction. Waiting on baited breath to see if your attack hit makes the payoff all the better. All in all, XCOM 2 is by far the best turn based strategy game I have ever played. I wish other strategy games were as cinematic as this one.

Vampyr is a flawed game, that's certain. But it's also one of the most engaging I've played in some time. It's part action rpg, part mystery adventure game, the action aspects being the weaker of those parts. To start with the good news, the story and atmosphere are top notch. The voice acting is fantastic and London feels truly like a place that God has abandoned. Your choices as a vampire/physician are interesting and conflicting. The characters all weave together like a web, and you'll discover that feeding generally has consequences. The game features a system whereby you can keep certain characters alive and healthy so that if you feed on them later, they'll grant you greater XP. I find this trade off very satisfying and interesting. I only killed a few named characters in the game and I did so after making sure they were healthy like I was a farmer raising pigs for the slaughter. It made me feel the impact of my actions and sympathize with the duality of the main characters struggle of needing to feed on blood, but also being a healer. It made me choose my targets selectively after I had passed my own judgement on them. The story isn't anything "new" necessarily, but once you've read enough stories and played enough games few things are. That being said, I liked unraveling the mystery at the center of the game as well as learning the stories behind many of the characters, who each have their own relationships, fears and desires. Walking around and and talking to characters periodically after you've learned more about them from somebody else reveals hidden depths that makes them feel real. In these areas Vampyr shines and it's where most of the enjoyment is held. For the negatives, there are several. The combat is fairly weak, and I learned simply to tolerate it. While it is somewhat clunky throughout, it's passable once you learn the tempo. You don't feel like a badass vampire to start, yet I found once I had upgraded a few select skills and weapons that I was nearly unstoppable. It's not a smooth difficulty curve at all. One boss battle about a third through the game is much, much harder than anything before it and very frustrating. But after it I leveled my sword and my vampiric melee attack and demolished every other enemy in the game. This also tempered any desire to explore the skill tree because it was unneccessary and I just focused on increasing my health and stamina. My biggest gripe is probably with the map. A minimap would be immensely helpful. I found myself lost constantly in dead ends very close to my objective. The world is stuffed with doors and gates that you gain the ability to unlock as you progress, but it's not explicit whenever this happens. You find yourself having to check every door hoping you can open it this time and it will open a shortcut. The game world is not huge but as most alleys look nearly identical you never really learn it the way you do with a game like say, Dark Souls. That's a game without a map at all but it connects so beautifully that when you manage to open a shortcut later on, you instantly know where it lets you out. You also cannot see npcs on the map which can be brutal. There are multiple characters I never even encountered because I didn't know where they were. You have a sort of "detective vision" that allows you to see blood, and this is generally how you find where an npc is (you can see the blood in their body), but it only shows them when you are fairly close. When I wanted to do my rounds checking that everybody was healthy, I always missed several of them. It's reminiscent of one of the frustrations of older video games and one that I haven't dealt with in quit a while and didn't realize I had forgotten about. It's a nuisence I don't miss. Overall, this was a very enjoyable experience and one I will probably play through again, but I would love if some modders got their hands on it and made some quality of life improvements. It's didn't blow me away like Vampire The Masquerade Bloodlines did, a game this one will obviously be compared to. But it didn't dissapoint me either. It wasn't what I expected, and what I got was not something I would normally seek out, but ultimately I'm quite pleased with the time I spent with the game.

I can't recommend this game enough. Like many I wasn't sure about this game before buying it. It seems so different than what we are used to, but after picking it up it's become my favourite multiplayer shooter. Graphics: Great looking graphics and it runs well even on my 2 year old mid level gaming comp. The maps are just covered in detail. The graphics really draw you into the world in a great way and there are some truly beautiful moments. Sound: Sound is HUGE in this game and the way they've implemented it is simply great. Not only is sound and sound traps extremely important to the player but it's layered, positioned and sounds amazing. Combined with the graphics you will very much feel like you are actually in the bayou hunting down zombers. Gameplay: Overall it's fun and addictive. With any PVP games you'll have some balancing issues and times that aren't fun for you but that's not so bad here. I'm not sure there is one way to "win" a match but there are ways to lose one. You'll buy hunters who you can gear out with late 1800's guns and gear. Then team up and head on out. You'll likely want to find the bosses around the map. Bosses are strong bots that you have to take down. Once you do that you'll wait around for your bounty to appear, at which point you'll head for a boat/horse to take you home. The fun isn't really in doing that, although that can be fun. The fun really comes in because at any point during doing this you can run into other players who will try to kill you so they can get out with the bounty. This creates a bunch of varying scenarios based on where you are, what you're trying to do and the gear you've brought. Gunplay: Guns are fun to use. There is a wide selection and you can reliably kill people with almost all of them. Most guns are bolt-action/single shot guns with slower reloads which really slows down player fights in a fun way. Every fight feels like a big event and huge emphasis gets put on tactics and positioning. Progression: Progression is fun at first but it does hit a ceiling pretty fast. You either grind out all the guns and find your own ways to progress (trying to get 10 level 50 hunters) or prestige, which puts you back to level 1 and you have to regrind everything. Prestiging can give you some exclusive skins. The gun grind is pretty fun since the starter guns are good in their own way so it's not the worst. Skill needed: Headshots are 1 hit kills with any gun (depending on distance). FPS skills are very important here since guns don't fire fast and 1 or 2 hits will kill you. Positioning and tactics are also very important since you do get downtime in fights to flank and change position. I wouldn't pick this as your first fps game but if you're well versed in fps get on in. Bugs: We have to talk about the bugs since they do exist and can effect your game. Sometimes assets don't load in quickly, you can get stuck sometimes, texture and lighting bugs seem common. Devs are active and release updates regularly but some of the updates are causing new bugs to come out. Hopefully that is fixed soon. Overall: Do you like fps games? Get this one.

review: Maybe i'm pedantic but i can't recommend this game for the full price for the pc platform. If you're not a fanboy, a weeaboo or more of a console player than a pc gamer, then read on, otherwise succumb to your base instincts... Pros: - mostly nice graphics 8/10 or so - wasn't too greedy on my ssd (25something gigs, really low for the quality of the graphics) - very fast - haven't experienced any glitches etc on my setup (gtx 1060 with both an old bulldozer 8350 and a ryzen 1800x) - challenging enemies: if you don't spend a bit of time dodging attacks and 'reading' their patterns you're missing on a big part of the game (the biggest i'd say, not much to this game apart from tons of combat), battles can be very strategic. Enemies follow patterns on their attacks, it's fun trying to guess what their stamina is and how to exhaust them/bait their attacks once you understand their programming and defeat them taking minimal damage. There's a couple of enemies that seem to be broken - Boreal Outrider Knight comes to mind, who seem to have endless stamina, with which you need to either use brute force, play very patiently against their patterns or try to use glitches to your advantage (there's tons of glitches you can exploit, narrow passages/corners, half open doors the enemies can't get through etc). - 'lightweight' rpg, simple mechanics yet not overly simplistic (e.g. witcher3 is an order of magnitude more 'complicated' than ds3, both in fighting/gaming mechanics and everything else really), manages to be fun enough - has a fun-ish manga tune to it, even though the setting is european (methinks, based on the architecture of buildings etc), you can walk around holding a sword twice your size, smacking things on the head - that's worth something Cons: - if you play this game without a controller you'll be frustrated.. alot.. - it's a straight port from console to pc, zero effort has been put into making this game pc friendly, it's not worth the full price if you're buying for your pc and plan to use pc controls occasionally: the first time i used an item from my inventory using my mouse i happened to be standing in front of a npc, using the mouse instead of my controller resulted in the character attacking after using the item, npc almost died and i lost favour with them... It's really frustrating trying to play this game with a keyboard as well, again, zero effort has been put into something that would take minimal coding and would have made the game playable on a pc (while at the same time this game sells for 40£, like a proper pc game). I'm dead serious, steam should have a warning on this game's store page, the rage this game can cause when played with a keyboard/mouse setup is unreal.. - idiotic mechanics at times: if you 'fall' from a step (like a foot high step) on an npc it might damage them/cause aggression - the control is lacking, if you're used to fast paced games where 100ms of latency is a thing, this game will frustrate you beyond belief, for example: [list] [*] swinging a sword can take about a second, if you change your mind while you're swinging said sword you have to wait for the animation to finish. If you're one of these gamers who survive on red bull and blink one eye at a time when playing, because 25ms is a lifetime and blinking both eyes will give your opponent a competitive advantage, then this is probably not the game for you [*] if you press the roll button while you're swinging your sword, that roll will be cached - this game has a ridiculously long input buffer and actions get cached but you can't 'override' them by hitting something else.. If you get staggered while a roll is cached there's no way you can change your cached action, your character will stagger for a second and then the cached actions will be played. For the life of me i can't understand who came up with this system or the reason behind it, it can be incredibly annoying during boss fights, where for example you might press attack, roll, attack, then your roll fails because the boss hit you and you stagger and then after a second or two of your character being staggered/acting like drunk, instead of rolling away while you're furiously hitting the roll button, the character stabs into the air because of the cached action from 5 seconds ago, while the boss proceeds to ravage you from behind.. The only way around this is to play this game in "slow motion", one keystroke/button push at a time and expect that once you start an action there's no turning back (even if it is a 3 second animation of your character trying to lift his/her sword, during which you could have rolled a ciggy and finish your latte) [/list] - 10? npcs, with a combined total of 20 kind of meaningful conversations, maybe about 5 of them present you with a choice, maybe a couple of choices actually have consequences.. - i got the feeling that there's a lot of lore in this game (to be fair, i haven't played the previous souls games), however my main source of understanding what's going on was google.. There's absolutely nothing in the game content wise, compared to witcher the content is 1/100, compared to planescape torment 1/1000, how is this game branded an rpg when trine has a (literally) richer story is beyond me.. - multiplayer is extremely laggy about 30% of the time (typically during invasions...) I live in London, my broadband is 'fibre' bt infinity2, ping times are single digits with anything hosted in the UK, low double digits with anything in europe, no online problems outside ds3

review: I fucking adore Doom 2016. Everything in that game clicked so well for me, the combat was satisfying, the music was amazing, the world design felt tailor made for the slayer's momentum, it's so good. So, naturally, I was hyped for Doom Eternal. There's a couple things that I felt could be refined and tweaked from the original, mainly the combat could be expanded a little so it doesn't become stale, but other than that I just wanted more. Doom Eternal is a very different game to its predecessor. It feels like a soft reboot in a lot of ways, a reboot of a reboot. A 'hell' of a lot of stuff has been changed, arguably too much. The combat has been deepened, with enemy weak points and new abilities, which is really cool, but way too much has been introduced. There's a wider array of settings, but they feel way less deliberate than the original. There's now a far more complex parkour system, which is fun and breaks up the battles, but arguably too much. There's now like 5 different skill trees. There are way more collectables. There's now a hub world for no reason whatsoever seriously why is this here. The story (which was admitedly kind of boring in Doom but at least it was something) has done a complete 180, swapping from the kinda serious, kinda sarcastic style to the most boring plot in a video game ever made. There's no drive to do anything because I don't even know what I'm doing half the time. It's nice to see a AAA studio give the developers a lot of creative freedom with how they approach a sequel, but I think there was a missed opportunity here. Doom left so much room to expand and develop what had been created, and while this sequel does do that in some aspects, it feels like an entirely different game in others. I'm not saying it's not good, because there's a lot here that a lot of people I'm sure will love. For me though, it just doesn't work. The soundtrack's fucking great though holy shit

Quick Review Pros: - Graphics are better than previous outings - Campaign UI is more functional - Line tactics are easier to implement - Still has that addictive Total War Formula - Addition of levels and attributes for armies is a nice touch that helps to alleviate your sadness when your favorite general dies Cons: - The battle AI is better, but still seems to bug out and do illogical things a lot (ignore take and hold points, etc) -It takes forever for the AI turns to process, and you don't even get to see most of the action taking place - Politics is nowhere near as robust as advertised - The overall game is quite buggy, I even crashed out of the tutorial - Stripped out multiplayer when compared to Shogun II - Sometimes all you have to do to win a battle is hold a point for a short amount of time, this is completely illogical when considered in the context of the larger game - The hardest part of the campaign is keeping your empire’s happiness level in the positive - The number of scouts, champions, dignitaries, and even armies has an annoying hardcap that I can only assume is meant to make the game more “accessible” Verdict: Total War games always ship with bugs. Sure, Creative Assembly quickly polishes the games up with a few patches, in fact they've already started for Rome II, but it generally takes them several months time to get the game smoothed out. So why then do people keep playing games in the Total War series? Well that's simple: even though the games release with more bugs than you would usually expect in an AAA title, they are so grand in scope and addicting to play that these attributes eclipses any problems. Unfortunately, this outing is a departure from the Total War formula in that it is both buggy and limited by design choices. With hardcaps on armies, navies, and agents and fewer decisions to be made in the day to day governing of your nation, the game becomes a lot less epic in scale. When this reduction of features is combined with a campaign AI that takes forever to process a turn, and often ends up making a lot of stupid decisions, the player can't help but wonder what went wrong here. I paint a dreary picture above, but the truth is that even with this watered down Total War experience the draw of the series is still there. There is still that joy in winning a massive battle or taking over another faction's territory for your own, and this thrill is enhanced in some battle types now that the real time Battle AI can actually pose a threat. Where Shogun II's battle AI could be depended upon to lose battles even if the player controlled a lesser force, Rome 2's artificial generals will take you to task and quickly route your men. This more able AI isn't yet perfect, and will often ignore the seemingly tacked on control points of some encounters - but it still poses a far stiffer challenge than prior Total War offerings. I love the Total War series, but even though this latest addition brings some welcome additions and tweaks, I would ultimately say Rome II takes a step back from the formula that has made the games so appealing. Despite this, the same Total War allure from the earlier incarnations is present and the diamond in the rough that is Rome II shines through - Rome II will still draw you in and keep you entertained turn after turn, it just might be fewer turns this time around. This review is for coop mode only, for thoughts on PVP try another review. This review was compiled right before the launch patch was deployed. I've fully read the patch notes and made specific notes about fixes listed in this launch patch at the bottom of the review. This review is going to be HUGE, only read it if you are serious about the game. This game is not ready for final release, it is quite rough around the edges. First up, the PC used during play sessions had an intel 7700 and nvidia 1070 on 16GB ram with a pci-express NVME storage device. The audio is amazing! Totally reminds me of BC2 on "wartapes" mode if anyone remembers that game. For audio lovers, this is a great experience. A GREAT EXPERIENCE! That is all I can say, awesome job audio crew, awesome job. The graphics are cartoony and the performance is bad. The mipmapping is terrible and textures constantly pop in and pop out. For example when looking at the ground and then climbing a few stairs, the ground lost most of its detail when viewing from one meter higher up. This is a constant effect throughout the game and textures pop in and out and in and out again. It is like there is little to no detail farther than 10 meters from the player, just muddy blurry stuff. The aliasing is absolutely crazy and the antialiasing settings make everything a blurry mess. I finally gave up trying to find out which settings combination worked for me at 1080 res with supersampling and switched to 4k resolution with everything turned to low or off. At least aliasing is no longer a problem. Stuttering happens all over the place. When running around it appears that everything is constantly loaded and unloaded so this is probably causing the stutter. It is visible when running around corners and stuff, black holes and areas that quickly get rendered in. Maybe I lost some weight? All that shilly shallying. For some reason after each optimization pass in beta we lost detail. Maps lost detail, characters lost detail. I guess in this case optimization meant keep removing stuff and compressing all the textures until they were ready for mobile devices. The game folder size went from 47GB in beta without all the maps to fully launched at 34GB with maps that didn't previously exist. Destroy objectives are anti-team oriented. What I mean by this is that players will trip over eachother to race to destroy these objectives before anyone else. Higher points means faster cosmetics unlock. Other players that may have spent time actually clearing out the enemies get zero points for the demo man that strolls up and shoots a rocket into his own team mates to blow up that objective. Team mates will blow eachother up planting, blow eachother up with nades, etc. The developer needs to fix this by allowing everyone in the nearby area to be awarded the same points or remove these objectives entirely. This is supposed to be a coop mode where people work as a team, if the developer doesn't redesign this it will remain cutthroat as per any other anti-team mechanic out there. Hey walaa pick me up! When the player dies and gets separated from the team it can be hard to catch back up. If the choo choo train is humming right along it can be impossible to feel useful to the team. Respawn points are quite a distance back from the cap point so while your best players are heading to cap point C you are spawned at A running toward B to then get to C. If C was a destroy point and it goes down in five seconds, they are moving to D and you still haven't got to B yet or end up pinned down with enemies that were skipped by and frankly should be despawned. The observer commander mechanic is clunky. Trying to be precise with the binocs is a challenge (should be able to use the map instead even if that means only being able to select areas in LOS, put a line of sight cone on the map I don't care) and air support calls take forever which disrupts the pace of the game. Offensive air support is dangerous to call in because team mates are all over the map, veteran players are rushing ojectives and noobies are wandering in enemy territory instead of taking/defending a capture point. (which means dying to friendly air support and getting frustrated) Class system is poorly designed. Don't see why there has to be certain guns limited to three classes, breacher get shotguns, marksman get some bolt and semi rifles, advisor get one or two special small machine guns, etc. These weapons should just sit in the rifleman class, most players choose the rifleman class even when they have other options available. There are too many classes for the sake of having classes. Let's not let PVP kit restrictions hamper COOP play, please. I'd rather not get into detail for the classes specifically other than to note that during beta the players were slowed down while the enemies were made faster. This causes the gunner and the marksman to fall behind in effectiveness. (especially considering the map and positioning constraints discussed below) The breacher with shotguns is all around better than the marksman at 100m range, and any rifleman weapon with a drum and bipod is a more mobile version of the gunner and when trying to stay on the choo choo train that is very important. Which way did he go? Which way did he go? The outdoor maps look huge. The problem is the usable space is not huge. There is a giant invisible bubble around the player that keeps them on track. When finding oneself out of bounds, the gun is no longer usable and the truck slows down to a crawl. This makes classes like the marksman and gunner unable to climb that pile of rocks and take an overwatch position on the team to cover them during an attack run. Click click click. With the sheer amount of enemies the game throws at its players, selecting a weapon that doesn't use a drum / extended mag leads to some hilarious deaths when the player click click click an empty gun. This is why most vets use a drum. Enemy count doesn't scale very well. By this I mean that each player seems to spawn a large number of world enemies and defend wave enemies, so servers that start half full can seem impossible, especially if one player leaves or dies. There can be defense wave upon wave and then add an air support call on to the one team member still standing. Balance is all over the place and sometimes it is impossible for a good team to even clear the first objective. It's like the dice were rolled at the start and it was decided that we have no possible chance to win. It is often done with style too, I mean wiped, then murdered again, then headshotted, then blown up with a nade, blown up with a rpg, then air striked, blasted by the technical, bombed by the suicide vest enemy, shot full of holes, and then naded again. It is hilarious sometimes and the chatbox lights right up with omg and wow. Enemy run speed is bugged or something. In many cases the enemy zooms around the map at mach speeds and swarms a capture point. Is this supposed to be their run speed when nobody is looking at them? Often times they retain this inhuman run speed after being engaged and shoot the player dead, there is nothing to do about it. Honestly I'd rather the enemy spawned out of thin air right next to me than to spawn across the map and swarm a location at hyper speeds. Rockets are bugged. There is a notable delay after firing and when they exit the launcher. This makes for a number of deaths where the trigger was pulled, launcher sounds played, but no rocket comes out. It also causes deaths when shooting out a window then moving because the rocket fires into a wall killing the owner and any team members nearby. To add to that, after recent patches a rocket often glitches out and doesn't even do any damage but vanishes into whatever object/ground fired at. Seems to vanish on direct hits to enemies as well, they shrug it right off and then shoot the owner during reload. Continued in comments.

[b]So I feel like I've played enough of this game now to write a review...[/b] [h1]The good.[/h1] [list] [*]The gameplay: While simple, is very fun. It's soccer, with cars, but the cars have boosters, and can fly :). It's great and engaging, it challenges you to learn new techniques to stay ahead of your opponents. The feeling when you hit that first aerial goal is amazing..trust me ;). [*]Graphics and performance: The graphics aren't anything to write home about, but this is a good thing in this case. This game runs beautifully on most systems, low or high end alike. I have seen a system with 2gb of ram and a dual core cpu with a gtx 440 gpu run this game on medium settings at 40fps. On my medium spec system it runs at 80-100fps on max settings. [*]Longevity: As mentioned before, this game challenges you to learn new things and experiment to grow in skill. I always feel like I am getting better, and not just stagnating in skill. [*]DLC: Best cars in the game are free! DLC just for cosmetic purposes! [*]There are of course, other good elements to this game, those however are the main points in my opinion. I'd rather alert you to the potential difficulties in the remainder of this review. [/list] [h1]The bad.[/h1] [list] [*]Matchmaking: The matchmaking does a decent job of pairing you with good opponents. BUT! If two players of unequal skill levels are playing together in a party, it will find a match to the skill level of the better player. This makes it unpleasent for the lower tier player. Ping is NOT at all accounted into the matchmaking. I live in an area far from the server locations, I am used to getting 200+ ping. Anything under 250 ping is playable. Sometimes however I can enter a ranked match with ping in excess of 600, this is not playable, and is basically a garunteed derank. This won't be a problem for most people, but for those of us living in the dark parts of the world, beware! Not the smoothest experience. [*]Community: While not nearly as bad as the CSGO community, it has it's fair share of trollers and salty kids. This should be a given with a large multiplayer game, but it's liable to get worse as the game grows, so take note! [/list] [h1]Verdict[/h1] Is Rocket League a good game? ... Yes. Is it fun? ... Yes, especially with friends. Is it worth the price? ... Yes, definitely, but if you struggle financially, wait for a sale, as is the case with all games. Should YOU buy it? ... If you like the idea and want to try it out, yes. If you don't like racing or soccer, you may still love it (as is the case with myself), if you want a serious racing or soccer game though, look elsewhere. HIGHLY RECCOMENDED

Firing firearms in this is satisfying, taking down enemy has some interesting details dependent on what you use. Other use of gear is also very nice, surreal effects and nice detail. Game sound is very well done if using audio gear with good imaging capabilities, can track direction of various sounds very well. Update to this game could be said to be quicker or more frequent based on what I read from people, but the game does have odd balance issues with the AI in co-op difficulty scaling and AI design choices. Mainly the choice of the AI shooting and tracking targets accurately easily through walls when they can't see you and take you down. That was previous patch but it should be addressed now in this recent patch. If there is a more frequent polling released from the developers, I would heavily welcome that if it is easily accessible so they can further understand their frequent player base would like to see for the Sandstorms future. Also so they don't a hostile or aggressive words from someone on Live chat on the games stream for game suggestions or Q&A. PVP and normal checkpoint is very popular which is good to see people playing the first game modes from Early access till this current game version / or patch. Hardcore game play mode, please try to match the speed the players in the lobby are playing at in Normal match making or custom server games. Would be nice to work overall as a team, even if you have no microphone input. The return of Insurgency game mode Out-Post is long overdue, but the right time for many co-op player base of the game to return to enjoy some more hours of game play. Game performance is still something to talk about this game depending on what you are aiming to produce for your visual fidelity. 1060 6GB and a 8600k is solid overall for this game with SSD. Lower than this hardware will require you to run at medium or lower, I run my Visual settings at mixed Medium to high. Shadow is always to be set at Medium, no higher. Good to play the game for 150 plus hours for new comers of this kind of First Person experience. Playing Insurgency Sandstorm for more than 800 hours might get you feeling that this game is boring, look into mods being developed for different game-play experience for Co-op focused community players. Find some new things to do in the game can be quite fun to adding more hours to playing this overall good game. Would recommend this game for something different to play for a few hours if you find this game interesting.
