This game has changed in the last 2 years. When I first bought this game it didn't have nearly as much content and was filled with a lot of bugs, at best it was very rough and highly unpolished. Even with all the bugs and issues that came with the new content and updates I continued to play hoping this game would improve and become the game I knew it could be. Back in 2015 I recommended this game to others simply because I knew while it was rough and unpolished, it had a lot of potential that most games lack. Then things kept getting worse, saves disappeared during updates, crashes, and then came the price change. I know a lot of people were angered at this price spike, due to the issues it had, and the fact it didn't seem worth the new cost. I had changed my own review to reflect this concern, even went as far as saying I couldn't recommend the game at full price. Today I can say the game runs a lot better then it did in 2015, has far more content, still has quite a few bugs that have been in the game since I bought it, can't say before then. Even with the bugs, and new bugs arriving, they are starting to finally fix some of them, not as many as I'd like to see fixed at once but that's just me, maybe a few others. So in light of everything, including the current update/bug fix sperts that's been going on, I can say I'd recommend this game again, however I will say to anyone who is interested to try to get this game during a sale as I still don't think it's polished enough to be worth a full $60, maybe $45 tops at this time given the cost of the DLC and all the bugs still within the game, not to mention the need for a bit more optimization. Even still the game can be rough for new players, so if you are new try single player or on your own server with your friends for a while to get the hang of things before playing on a random server with other people.

OK this is a game where you control a medieval noble family trying to make the most of your realm. You make decisions about religion, culture, military, economic development, going on pilgrimages, arranging marriages, hiring spies and assassins, etc. It's part role playing game, where you make decisions from specific characters' points of view, and part strategy. The idea of playing through the middle ages not just from a Civilization point of view but really from the point of view of one royal family with high stakes battles, a variety of quirks and a whole story ... is great. I really liked the characters within the family in Total War: Rome and this has built on that and made it more involved. The family development system is flawed but still cool. I like the "lifestyles" concept with the learning trees. Finally, the art is cool. The game looks good (the music is ok not great). Paradox tries to make the technology and military dynamic realistic. I think there are improvement opportunities on the military side but the more I play the more I like it.

Well, where do we begin? This game is good. Like, very very good. Let's start with the goods; [b] The Goods [/b] [list] [*] Visuals - The game is just gorgeous with extensive attention to detail. [*] Music - Nothing stellar or out of ordinary but fits with harmony. [*] Lore - Same with above, complimenting the experience. [*] Combat - Combat is one of my favourite aspects of the game; I would often have to restrain myself from attacking Neutral NPC's just for more of it. [*] Skills - Many skill to choose from, with many combinations. You can combine skills to achieve interesting results. [*] Environment - You can pretty much interact with everything you see. [*] Exploration - Do this, you will be rewarded. [*] Side Stories and Character Arcs - Please, please and please, complete all side quests. It's worth it. [*] RPG Elements - I have to say, this game makes my top 10 RPG's list. No questions. Some quests can't be completed as they conflict with other quests, which further emphasises the next point. [*] Decisions - The game has so many "game changing" decisions. So much so that I couldn't keep track of the causality and finally gave up the habit of "quicksave & quickload" before critical points. It really is worth playing without this, because each choice you make shapes your journey in multiple ways. [u] Every choice matters [/u] [/list] [b] The Bads [/b] [list] [*] The Main Story - I will not spoil the main plot, but with all the goods above, I found the the main story disappointing. It wasn't too bad, but heck, it could have been done better. (We can debate on this) It felt like it was prolonged just to add a few extra hours of story but I would have been okay with less with more intensity. It could have all been more concise. [*] Crafting UI - This was sadly poorly executed. I wasn't very fond this. [*] Quests UI and tracking - The game's biggest challenge. Some quests just slip by because the UI is quite un-encouraging and you just forget about them. [/list] tl;dr: A fine game to play, but it will require you to think.

Doom is back guys. More action, more demons, more music, more blood, more awesomeness. Doom Eternal is Doom 2016 to the thousand power. Faster, more fluid, better looking, more visceral. Now, Doom Slayer has more weapons, skills and movement capability so demons are also faster, more inteligent, more aggressive, absolutely relentless. Doom Eternal is hard, but it gives you more tools to deal with it. Level design is way better than it's predecessor's, with different hi-tech, alien facilities, and planets to visit. The OST is awesome, not only for the tracks themselves, but also for the way the music and sound effects are mixed with the action. I've played every Doom since 1993 (excluding the console versions), and Doom Eternal is the perfect new-gen evolution of the original game and its sequel. I've also played most of the 1st person shooters (singleplayer campaigns, forget about crappy multiplayer shooters) and Doom Eternal is absolutely the best of them IMO. Ok, the plot is not so deep, dialogs and cutscenes are scarce, lore is mostly told via collectibles (it shouldn't be bad, should it Darksoulers?), and it has probably other narrative flaws, but it's pure fun and enjoyment in every aspect since the first minute of gameplay. I haven't played it's multiplayer yet but, as far as I know, it's an asynchronous 2vs1 mode. 2 players play as one of the 6 or 7 different kinds of pickable demons with their own skills, the other plays as the Slayer. To summarize, the best 1st person shooter ever IMO, don't waste your time and give these demons a pound of led and chainsaw.

The graphics style is a classic 2D pixel design, but feels detailed enough that even if you aren't a fan of 'retro' looking games it should not deter you. Plus, I love the music in this game - its either super relaxing or a downright bop. I haven't played the co-op mode yet, but I feel that this would be a fun game to have a friend join in on and have heard good things about the experience. My rating: 8 of 10 My review: Mutant Year Zero: Road to Eden provides a different approach to the XCom style of game, The mechanics for XCom veterans will be easy to step into especially given the impression that the tactical combat engine "steals" a fundamental amount of mechanics from XCOM. That's not bad tho! The good parts: What I really LOVE: Outside of combat you can walk around realtime with yout group (or split up) so it's more like an RPG in that regard. It's not turn based movement outside combat, so thiy is like a hybrid with the best of both worlds. The stealth mechanics are nice and let you set up for ambush situations. The possibility to spread you team allows you to get an overwiew of the situation and isolate what is obviously the biggest threat and/or the weakest enemey without cover, so you can deal with your selected target as a priority. The weapons, while simple in concept (Pistols, crossbow, rifle, shotgun, etc) have a distinct Post-apocalyptic style that I really enjoy. The characters and their dialogues are nice. I really enjoy the atmosphere of the game (set in post-apocalyptic Scandinavia) as well, the sound design is fantastic. The game is polished, the performance is great (but capped at 62 fps). The bad parts: Very linear game, but at least within that corset you can explore a little. Replay value is not given so far imho, we need some DLC. The game essentially gives you attackes the chances as "not possible/no sight" etc, 25%,50%,75%,100%. The enemy visions and spot areas/fields are sometimes very random and might exploit you despite beeing careful. It is a really nice game with great atmosphere and you should consider buying it if you like XCom and are open to a different theme and approach.

Dusk is a retro-styled fps game about a prospector who is abducted by a weird cult, put on hooks, frees himself, and then goes on a beer and diamond-fueled killing spree in revenge. You shoot them, stab them, blow them up, reflect their fireballs and bullets back at them, make them go insane with glowy rocks, eat their cooked gibs, blow up their walls in search of secrets, break their stuff looking for more ammo, invade their twisted hell dimension, kick their leaders low-poly butt with bullets, and then beat up their god after holding a sun-focusing magnifying glass to his horrifying tenticle-mouth-face. All of this goes down with a atmosphere and music that will creep you out and fuel your unending need for violence and destruction. The imagery here is insane, and it should be, considering its Lovecraftian inspiration. Everything from the level design and art-direction to the enemies and their lack of sanity is absolutely perfect for the tone, which is a mix of horror and comedy. Horror, because this game actually unnerved me a few times with its low-texture monsters with blank-eyed stares and pitch black hallways filled to the ceiling with gore, and comedy, because there are genuinely funny jokes, easter-eggs and secret references. I finished this game in 11 hours on normal because I suck at this kind of game, and even then there were a few areas that killed me here and there. This game is hard, but not at all impossible, and it was a thrilling ride and well worth the effort. I didn't find all of the secrets, because I'm not a psychic. For the Worthy: BUY IT. ITS FUN. Let me start off by saying that Ive been sitting on how to make this review for a while... I am still playing through the game and I havent finished just yet but I will... Having said that, it pains me to give a thumbs down but I feel I have to. For various reasons... I have skimmed some of the comments below some of the good and some of the bad... I agree with alot that is being said but here is my take on it... I "like" the game, I really do... But there are things that I hate about it too. I feel like this game still needs work... Yes imo its just a reskin of XCom.. However, XCom did it better. 1). Playability, This game is very linear and you have very little freedom as to where you are going. Even if you clear an area? You cannot go back to kill more stuff so you can level up once you clear that area of the map, its done with... That brings me to my second concern 2). The map. The global map is just fine, its actually pretty cool looking and I love the way it is visually. However.. I feel like each zone should have its own map as well. With the areas being fairly large, maybe it could have a map that has the fog of war option. Meaning you descover that smaller map as you explore the zone. Thus helping us to be sure we cleared out all the goodies on the map ( this has been diving me nuts tbh heh ) For completionists like myself that strive to get all the achievements in the game picking up all the notes and whatnot =) 3). Functionality - Keybinds -.- I had to go as far as to reassign the walking keybind to a different key on the other side of the keyboard. Muscle memory to playing XCom for over 500+ hours I would press 1 and be walking all over lol. The thing that bugged me most about the keybinds? Was the map turning, it should be Q and E ( for almost 99% of games out there that have that sorta feature. Xcom, Tycoon games, Farming games... Almost everything I have ever played ) But this game... Makes you press Q and hold it while you grip and turn the map? Clunky in my honest opinion. 4). Prices- they are so so high.. I played on the difficulty that you get healed after every match.. But I know had I not? It probably would have been a nightmare. Because even with that level of play, I still on occasion used healthpacks that I had bought. The weapon modification prices are a bit high as well as you hardly EVER find weapon parts. 5). Kinda bugged me that we couldnt ever use all 5 characters at once. I think it might have been fun to have a bit stronger enemies or bigger parties after clearing out some of the stragglers and have a big ole war =) Now for the good stuff I liked the gameplay, I am a turn based nut lol... I liked that you did better if you killed stealthily over brute forcing it... Scared the hell out of me a few times when I got caught but I then thought through and changed strats. 1). Characters are unique and the mutations are super fun. I love the look of the heroes and enemies alike. The artworks great =) 2). Ive enjoyed the storyline so far and I even take the time to read all the notes, books drops etc.. I find them very interesting. 3). The game isnt easy, as where you can just do it in one sitting, and you do have to be wary of how you tackle some hurdles 4). I also like how you can split the party, how you can make some of them "hide" and inactive, while you roam around on the others or set up an ambush then you can choose to engage them or leave them hidden. Cool idea. big thumbs up from me. I would definitely say if you like turn based games pick this one up, but on sale. The pricetag is a bit steep for the replayability. But its worth a look see to have at some point, I dont for a moment regret buying it. I feel like at the time of me posting this review I am about halfway through the game, if at some point things do change to address some of the concerns, I may then adjust my review =) Till then GL all and happy gaming!

[h1]This is a masterpiece[/h1] [b]TLDR[/b]: I think we'll look back in 20 years and be like "remember Doom Eternal? I hope a FPS as good as that will come out someday soon". It's an Instant Classic. Building upon Doom 2016 with more mobility, more diversity, resource management, rewarding challenge, which all result in a perfect fast arena FPS gameplay. Also, there is a freaking lore bible because.. why not? So, Doom 2016 was cool, nobody argued on that. But Eternal is a big improvement. So much that I don't think I can really have fun on Doom 2016 anymore. [b]Doom 2016 made you feel like a badass, Doom Eternal makes you one.[/b] Eternal builds upon 2016's ideas, the chest pieces arenas with micro decisions each second, pushing for contact. They were good ideas, and now it works so well! First, [b]You can move much faster[/b], making you able to evade encounters, dodge attacks, seek melee and resources. Dashing, jumping, grappling, climbing... You are moving in the environment like a lightning bolt. [b]Resources are key[/b]. They evaporate in a heart beat, especially ammunition. It's a resource management game where if you don't have health, ammo or armor, you are f*cked and need to go after those immediately. You have all the tools to do so, at any time (chainsaw's first charge recharges after a while, zombies piñatas spawn regularly...). [b]Diversity[/b]. More enemies and weapons means that the game is much more diverse but also more complicated, it could have been impossible to remember all those. But the game made it easy thanks to clear and logical strategies. When you see a new enemy, a tutorial pops up with its weakness. They give us a solution, but in an arena there is tons of different enemies with their own weakness, ideal weapon to kill them with. So it is in the execution of those strategies that the challenge reside. Also, with stronger weapons unlocked, you find better, quicker strategies. [b]Hard to master[/b]. This is the one that divides players. To put it simply: it's really hard. I beat it in hard mode the first playthrough and even though I sometime struggled, I learned, got better. The maurauder is a pain, but by getting your *ss kicked you start to understand how to manage him. The same for doom hunters, archviles... The game made me really master it compared to Doom 2016, I feel like I know almost every gameplay details and techniques now. [b]Pacing[/b]. The game is very fast paced. Still, you can slow down with plateforming, puzzles, secret hunting, lore reading. It's all there to rest a little between fights if you desire. (secrets are much more fun than in 2016, you can fast travel at the end to pick them up, it's smarter that those levers you hated). [b]Huge campaign[/b]. 30 hours for 100% in hard. More than twice the length of the last Doom and it doesn't become boring at any point. Every environment is a new, beautiful surprise. The story never stalls, it's rich but optional. So if you don't care about the lore and all, don't worry the game doesn't force it. And if you care... there is an entire huge Bible covering each world, characters, enemies. And it's a well written sci-fi take on biblical themes with bits inspired from Berserk. They even contain some legit tension and plot twist, which is the first time a codex gave me that. The only negative critics I have: [spoiler]That one hidden toy in the well at level 9... seriously?[/spoiler], the music's dynamic range (the original composer didn't deliver in time so the devs improvised with the unmastered bits) a shame but it's still beautiful. [b]To finish this long *ss review[/b]: if your heart can take fast paced gameplay, if you like FPS in general, [b]PLAY IT[/b].

Current hours played: 63. I come writing this review having beat the game completely and having done every side mission. First off, this game is brilliant. The controls are quick and simple, the landscapes are beautiful, and there is a nice craft system. The story is very linear, and plays out much like you would expect a movie to play. The side quest rewards are good enough to warrant doing them even. Moving around the map is simple enough, and while there isn't a fast travel, the world doesn't feel big enough to need it. If you want to skip around a big group of zombies for instance, you can climb the buildings. If you want to go through them instead of climbing, you can use a skill to hop off their heads. If you want to physically go through them, you can mow them down with a weapon as well. In this regard I feel they give players a bit of freedom to decide how to handle situations rather than leaving 1 ideal situation that players have to figure out. Crafting in the game doesn't leave as lasting an impression as I would have liked. First off, they put a timer on physically crafting an item, even though the game is paused. This gets tedious when you have to craft 10+ items in a row. The other thing is they don't let you craft more than 1 item at once. So if you have a stack of items to make into something else you have to go 1 by 1. The single redeeming factor here is that the game's engine has a LOT of craftable items, so while it is tedious to make things, you get a lot to choose from at least. The final part I want to talk about is optimization. I have a Radeon R9 270x with 4gb of ram, and I have to turn my display setting to 1280x800 instead of my usual 1920x1080. I realize this game is meant for Nvidia, but for everyone out there running AMD you'll need a high end GPU to run this effectively. I also had to reduce draw distance by more than 70%. In conclusion, this game is really fun and worth playing. They are adding a hard mode and other neat little extras next patch so I anticipate more replay value coming soon!

DUSK may be another one of the old-school FPS imitations that frankly we may have seen a bit too much of in the past few years, but it is by far the best of the bunch. To start off with, the aesthetic of this game is incredible. It is gritty, it is dark, and it is downright disorienting sometimes. The developers nailed the art and atmosphere of this game and it all comes together in one cohesive package. Enemies and guns both have designs that help you immediately tell them apart from one another, which is incredibly important in a fast paced game such as this DUSK. You also have many options for toying with the graphics of this game so you can make it look just like games did back in the 90s. Gameplay wise, DUSK shines just as bright as the legendary games that inspired it. While it does have some faults, such as inconsistent difficulty with boss fights (end bosses are incredibly easy), a noticeably weak second episode (not too bad, but lost interest during it), and one enemy that could have used a bit more tweaking. DUSK delivers when it comes to the fast paced combat, complex level design, satisfying weapons, and just plain old fun. To comment on the included multiplayer mode, it is fairly dead. Duskworld is incredibly fun to play, but you will need to find friends or join a DUSK mp group to get the full experience. I have not delved into the DUSK SDK yet, but it looks fairly promising. DUSK modding could certainly benefit from a steam workshop page. Overall, I recommend picking up DUSK to any fan of classic first person shooter games. The value for money is good and the game will rarely disappoint. If I had a few suggestions on if they decided to make a sequel to this game I would say to slow down on the progression of weapons and save a few for late on in the game. Not only that, but maybe at least one weapon that stands out from the rest, like how Quake had the lightning gun, half life the hivehand, just something unconventional and suprising. Overall great job New Blood Interactive & I look forward to your future works!

In this game, you stamp passports. EXCITING! But don't let the mundane description fool you: the game is a masterpiece in it's own right. Papers, Please is a testament to how dated graphics and a simplistic core element can be used as a vehicle for a rich experience by implementing the power of choice. Each person, every randomly generated life you come across, awaits your stamp of Approval or Denial. Their minor reactions feed the player's psyche to continue the grind, checking papers and comparing photos, cross-referencing lists for potential criminals or fraudulent seals, churning out dozens of people to feed his or her faceless, nameless "Family". Abusing your power or neglecting your duties don't result in an immediate game over, instead you receive citations in increasing severity based on how problematic the offense was. Decorated the applicant side of your immigration booth with nonsense? If your boss sees it, you get fined, but you can always hide the drawings of "Son" underneath official papers during inspections, then put them back up later. The game rapidly escalates in difficulty, but decreases in reward and intrigue, allowing the player to merge seamlessly from a "game" with a clear carrot-and-stick bait, to an experience where I actually questioned whether or not this was designed as gameification of the career to attract, immerse and train border agents in the process, and exemplify the tribulations and consequences of those choices.

The people that say "nothing ever happens in this game" are full of crap. It's very true that a majority of the game is walking and just delivering packages for people. However it's what happens between delivers is what makes Death Stranding so interesting. The amount of crazy stuff that happens in this game both in-game and story wise is so insane, it's 100% every penny. Firstly, if you hate stealth/slow paced games you'll hate this game. Straight up there is no going around this, you won't have fun. If you do however BTs (Beached Things) are the scariest thing to sneak past in games. They are extremely dangerous, super sensitive to hearing even your breathing, and one touch sets off an entire hornets nest. Sneaking past BTs though makes you feel like a stealth GOD though. The other biggest "enemy" can be the word itself. Rain has now become Time Fall and will destroy package's condition, so you need to use repair spray, find cover from the rain, or be able to find a path around the rain itself. You need to keep your balance if your weight is too high and you can actually trip on a rock, totally knocking over your supplies (which is equal parts annoying and hilarious). However all of this can be over come with the "multiplayer" aspect of the game. Players can leave behind stuff like climbing rope, ladders, etc. for other players to use/find and use. You even get to a point where players start to help rebuild roads to make some delivers a joke. It's an amazing feeling to get thousands and thousands of likes for something you left behind that's helping EVERYONE. Death Stranding is roller coaster of being super relaxing and chilling while listening to some calming music, exploring the destroyed yet beautiful world. Then into a heart pounding experience sneaking past the scary as hell BTs and just trying to make that last delivery with an inch of life in you. Then total confusion with how crazy and out there the story gets, though that comes with the territory when it comes to Kojima games. This games is 100% worth every penny.

On my Xbox I have countless hours in Skyrim (I've completed every single quest, and side quest including DLC's). If you're a fan of the Elder Scrolls series and you wonder how it stacks up, here is my $0.02. Side note: Although these games are both fantasy based, they really should not be compared while playing. They're seperate games, not games from the same series. This review is just for people that have played Skyrim and are curious if this is the modern day version. [h1]Character Dev.[/h1] Right off the bat you'll notice that character development, or more accuratly character [i]freedom[/i] isn't as strong as Skyrim, since you can't change how Geralt (the main character) looks, how he fights (Bow and arrow, Mage, etc.). With this said, character development is still perfect for this game. Geralt has a story to him, which defines why he fights how he fights and why you can't change the looks, outside of haircuts of course. One thing this game is missing that I miss about Skyrim is a stealth aspect. Granted, Geralt is quite the beast but I still think it would be sweet to be able to sneak up on human enemies at the very least. There are a couple of stealth missions and not having to worry about actually getting detected by the enemies is kind of dissapointing. [h1]Open World Roaming[/h1] This is something that I didn't really notice until later in the game, but compared to Skyrim roaming the map just isn't quite as good. Sure you still meet bandits and distressed travelers that need help and such, but that's about it. In Skyrim you can meet some pretty interesting characters roaming the roads (M'aiq the Liar, for instance). Outside of this, both games have some gorgous terrain, and if they were made in the same year with the same game engines I would be very hard pressed to choose a favorite. [h1]NPC's and Story[/h1] This catagory is where the Witcher absolutly blows Skyrim away for me. The emotional connections that this game builds with the other characters are outstanding. Skyrim is [b]very[/b] dull when it comes to this aspect. The story in this game is like no other. It's much like taking your favorite movie and making it into a video game, except you have control over what happens next. Choices [b]do[/b] matter in this game, as there are multiple endings to even most of the quests. [h1]In Conclusion...[/h1] If you like RPG's and you like story rich games then this is for you, no question about it. Do yourself a favor though and don't look anything up about the game. Just play it as if you have no internet access. Trust me, not knowing what is going to happen next and what your decisions will lead to is what this game is built on. The Witcher 3 officially replaces Skyrim as my favorite RPG to date, which is somthing I thought I would never say. [spoiler]#teamtriss ;)[/spoiler]

If you enjoyed DOOM (2016) and were hoping to see a game that would keep the same tone, or something built around that formula, this game might not be for you. If it wasn't a sequel, and was judged entirely outside of the perspective that the prior game inescapably brings into the conversation, it would be easier to justify all the questionable decisions that were made in DOOM Eternal. It would've been an okay game, maybe not the best one to represent the franchise, let alone the genre it once shaped, but it would've been somewhat appealing to a certain type of gamer, as is. That said, IT IS a sequel, and for a game, that one would think builds upon something that wasn't entirely broken, it sure tries to fix right about everything, except the things, that actually needed fixing. DOOM Eternal doesn't really address the biggest criticisms of the previous game. It isn't any less repetitive, and, in fact, puts even more effort and production into the sequences that are focused only on delivering plot (yes, there is a story going on somewhere there, apparently). Why they couldn't have been written into the gameplay more naturally without breaking its natural flow, is beyond me. This is not the biggest thing, that breaks the flow, however. Between constantly searching for ammo or armor, by trying to pull off one of way too many special attacks, and platforming back and forth from one hazardous area to another, only to realize you're not using the optimal weapon for a certain enemy type, there is sometimes a momentary window of good ol' monster slaying, while jumping around them oldschool style. And frankly, when there is so little flow going on, it may seem that it's the fun parts, that occasionally break the grind. Another incredibly frustrating thing is that I always kept relying on ALL of the special weapons - and there are way too many of those - while barely using (or needing) three of the eight main weapons. Also, there are only two types of grenades in the game, and two buttons to use them - but instead of binding each button to each grenade, one is used to switch between them. This is just sheer stupidity. Your arsenal is outright unbalanced in this game, even outside of the comparison with the previous title. Certain types of particularly bullet-spongy enemies don't exactly rectify that. Platforming on its own, as far as game mechanics go, is not half as bad as some of the hysteria on the internet would let you believe. But it is inexplicable, that the player movement was redesigned specifically for this game, and yet the levels look like they were designed for something completely different. Is there a single aspect of this game, that wasn't corrupted by its identity crisis? Unless you're very inexperienced with the genre, I suggest to turn off the tutorials, because the number of game pausing textual hints is INFURIATING. They show up all the time, sometimes one right after another, and don't stop until the very final boss battle. Do they not know what the point or definition of a tutorial is? Multiplayer tutorials are also utterly annoying, and are on by default. Speaking of the final boss battle, I am truly amazed that in the year 2020, in one of the biggest Bethesda titles we are still getting the most generic, dull and unoriginal, worst possible kind of a mainstream final boss in a game with "DOOM" in its title. And that is really the ultimate problem with this game - remove the name, swap the characters and the monsters, and you got yourself a salvable title. But this whole thing with "DOOM" in the name? Nope. There are just too many things you have to keep in mind in order to do well, and there are games that benefit from having somewhat convoluted mechanics, but when you're given a bunch of giant kickass weapons with a bunch of demons to kill, all you should wanna do is to have some fun killing them. Yet all these things end up getting in the way of having fun.

I picked up Subnautica last year when it was still in early access and it showed a lot of promise, especially given the pedigree of the developer's previous projects. After playing it for a while and enjoying what it had to offer, I put it down and let it sit until the recent 1.0 release where I eagerly picked it back up again. For the most part i've enjoyed myself and the new additions to the game that I had not experienced in the later stages of early access and I do believe this is inherently a good game. However, at this point in time I cannot in good conscience recommend this game as it is right now. For a full release, Subnautica has quite a number of bugs that still plague it. Most I encountered were benign, yet detracted from the immersion the world tried so hard to create. Namely, the game's assets have extremely noticable pop-in issues, sometimes not even loading in until the player is directly next to them. Creatures and resources occasionally become stuck within the game's geometry because of this issue causing unintended (and often humourous) side effects. Unfortunately, as my playthrough continued other, more detrimental bugs reared their ugly heads. At one point while traversing some underground caverns, part of the cave system failed to load completely causing a bit of a navigation headache. Yet the worst bug I happened to stumble upon was a complete softlock that occured by accidentally redocking my PRAWN Suit with the Cyclops as its docking bay doors were closing. I had no choice but to quit the game, losing several hours of progress and souring the experience for me as a whole. I'd like to complete the game at one point if only because I've gotten so close to the end, but for those who are interested in Subnautica as a fresh purchase, I would advise you wait until Unknown Worlds releases bugfix patches to address the more serious problems that may arise from regular gameplay.

If you are an old RCT player, and you liked the "tycoon" part, you will be probably a bit disappointed by this game. Sure, the building part is huge, you can really manipulate your coasters and your park's scenery in every possible way you want, but there is no scenarios/missions/objectives editor at all. Also, the 3D controls to manipulate objects are hard to learn, and harder to master. So, after you have done the few (either very easy or infuriatingly hard because of the broken economy dynamics) missions in the career campaign, you are stuck with the sandbox part only. You can't download user created scenarios with missions from the workshop, because there aren't. There are sandbox parks, but they aren't playable as challenge, I really wonder why, So I advise the ones that are interested in the tycoon/economic part of the game to not buy it, at least until a proper scenarios/missions editor is released. _____________________________ Update 22/04/2018 The editor has finally arrived, but overall there are still a lot of missing things comparing it with RCT 3, and not only attractions (like elevators, chairlifts, coasters, and various track rides), but also broken economy dynamics and infuriating lack of control of some of the park aspects (for example if guests get stuck somewhere, you will have to find them manually), and a lot of bugs are still present. The DLCs released until now are largely money grabbers, good cosmetics but few improvements, and too expensive. Conclusions: The only people that will really appreciate this game are park builders, and even them will not like the lacking things in the base game (and, as for now, in the DLCs too). Management/Tycoon game enthusiasts better stay clear of this very incomplete game.

What is Stellaris? Its a real time strategy game. Yet its also so much more. Stellaris is at its fundamental level a dream. A dream of space. Like most Paradox games, I have held out on writing a review until they actually worked out the kinks of the game. Nearly 800 hours in now and with much of the critical DLC I can now say that Stellaris is hands down the greatest 4x space simulator ever designed. The story and event chains are engaging, the AI is competent, and with the recent Le Guin update the economy is deep and opens up a world of different play styles. I think what really sets Stellaris apart from other strategy games is the feeling of actual investment you have in the fate of your stellar empire. You design it from the ground up, and then get to roleplay its interactions through massive variation. My most memorable playthrough was ironically with a fanatically egalitarian and pacific crew of cute molluscoids I dubbed the Seban Republic. They just wanted to peacefully secure their borders and live their best life. Yet they were in a rough neighborhood of hostile xenophobic and authoritarian races who constantly invaded them. Yet the Seban perserveared through the tribulation and at the end were instrumental in winning the War in Heaven against the awakened ancients, and saving the galaxy from an apocalyptic enemy. I really became attached to those cute yet determined little guys. My most memorable moment was when the united fleets of the Seban Republic defeated a horrific blitz of genocidal robots in the home system of a vassal state that at one point had been a determined enemy. The story arc of the Seban from a bunch of happy go lucky dudes who just wanted to explore in peace to the last best hope of the Galaxy was simply amazing. And the game did not make it easy either. At the Admiral difficulty level with ironman engaged, you have to earn that win. And that is the true magic of Stellaris. You actually care about what is happening in the game, and the game is competent enough to make situations you encounter potentially game ending. If you love strategy games, and you love roleplay, you will love this game.

Got the game about a month ago and I am really enjoying it (220 hours clocked and still not finished the main campaign ). It is like a breath of fresh air and I haven't had this much fun playing a game, in particular an rpg, in a long while. I like the fact that you play an ordinary dude in a historical context and you are not there to save the world from utter destruction or an obscure force. The learning curve can be steep at the beginning and the game does not hold your hand. At first, I was a bit discouraged by combat (Henry is the son of a blacksmith and has never used a sword so he's got to learn) but persevered, learned skills and it is now fun and faster. The same goes with archery and everything else. Until you've upped some skills, you will bite the dust a few times (and even after if you are not careful those bandits can kill you, often fleeing may be the best alternative). It's not the game world adapting to you as you level up but you who must adapt to the world depending on your capacities and skills. You've got to observe the world, practice skills, and there may be more alternatives and more people to talk to than what the journal says to complete some quests. I like how quests are not a pure good/evil thing as we now see too often. Music is great, not pompous, and fits the medieval world perfectly. Haven't run into any quest breaking bugs yet but then I don't go killing everyone but observe and explore first and then make decisions.

Played for free to see if I wanted to buy the game at half off, which I was very much leaning towards. After all, downloading nearly 50 gigs of the game takes some time. As I started to play, I found the game interesting, but not at all what you would want from an "Open World Game". The game immediately forces you into a story plot in which you are forced to take sword fighting lessons, and do a tutorial like quest. When I am playing a game, I do not want it to feel like I am watching a T.V show, this game accomplishes exactly that, it feels like watching a T.V drama. The cutscenes are so long, i found myself watching a five minute long cutscene only to be baffled that I am still playing a game when I am throws into the action. The NPCs are very unnatural looking and will seemingly walk around like a mindless drone, will not make eye contact with you, and will not budge when you walk into them. They just kind of walk around with a blank stare on their face. The Character Customization lacks. They have made this game so "T.V showlike" that, of course, you cannot customize your character. If you unequip your gear at the beginning of the game, or sell it to a trader, YOUR CHARACTER WILL STILL BE WEARING THE SAME CLOTHES IN THE CUTSCENES. Not being able to customize the character in any way pretty much makes the main character seem unrelateable. Fighting is clunky. The fighting is clunky and I mean really clunky. You target an opponent, you can click or right click. Depending on which you do, you will either perform a swing or a quicker stab move. At least in the intro, you can end up in a few fistfights and do basic sword training. I very much wanted to begin to react to the open world, but it seems I have lost interest after taking a break from the game after the first time playing it, which ended in getting shot off my horse in what seemed to be some kind of beginning cutscene sequence. The bottom line is that if I am playing a Medeival Open World game, I want it to feel sandboxy, like the decisions I make will have a drastic and longterm effect on the world. If I want to watch a T.V drama about Knights, I could just watch a show like "Knightfall". This was a big disappointment.

game: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition

review: 5/10 Immersive and beautiful marred by extremely red flag problems and a distinct lack of self defense. 1.) NO AUTOSAVE. Its 2018 and somehow the devs haven't managed to figure out how to program something so simple, yet mandatory in all games since like 1995. In fact I think the last time in my life I worried about this was playing Diablo 1 on Windows 1995. ESPECIALLY for a simple game where all there is to do is catalog and build, to suddenly lose an entire day's worth of effort...failing grade automatically right here. Which leads me to the next point-- 2.) Crashes. It works well for the most part but I've had it crash a few times and the lack of autosave means losing chunks of time here and there depending on the intensity of your OCD with saving. The first time I lost about half a days exploring/scanning/building, which is sufficient to completely kill the mood of what should be an otherwise relaxing game. Now I have to anxiously worry constantly about the next crash and how much work I'll lose the next time it happens. 3.) No map/waypoint system. Navigation is extremely irritating, between day/night cycles, flashlights constantly running out of batteries that have to be recharged/replaced, murky water, and no map or waypoint system (at least as far into the game as I am) navigation just sucks. In a futuristic setting with nano technology, space travel, and turning fish into pure drinking water, can I please get at least a piece of paper and a No.2 pencil? Its a huge wasted opportunity to disclude charting in an exploration game. Your job? Explore and discover. Your biggest handicap? Future humanity has map amnesia (even though they can navigate the stars). Maybe much farther into the game you get some sophisticated system but if its not available in the beginning as a fledgling survivor it may as well not exist. 4.) Inventory/Items are extremely annoying. Everything takes up TONS of room and storage is very limited. When you need more storage, you have to fill up your inventory with metal, craft a floating chest, go back underwater, place the chest, fill it up. No naming system, to autofill, no moving them once placed (even though they float), no color coding, no lining them up neatly. When you eventually unlock more storage schematics, none of them can be placed in the escape pod. In fact NOTHING can be placed in the escape pod, for no reason. Being completely confused by this irrational situation, I scoured the web to discover the escape mod is in fact, unmutable. You have to go build an entire underwater base, just to have access to some sane storage space. Which is a huge resource investment. You starting to see the paradox? You much have lots of stuff, to have room for stuff. Which means until you build the base, you're constantly shuffling around a tiny handful of ingredients, back and forth back and forth, sometimes building new chests. Never mind constantly starving and dehydrating to death, which fills your inventory up even more and decreasing the room for resources. WHY can't we build any storage in the escape pod??? Inventory should be much larger as well, or allow us to stack similar items. Or get an underwater pet with saddlebags or SOMETHING. The tedium of early game resource management is eyegougingly bad. 5.) Non existant combat. I eventually could build a knife. "Yay! I can kill things finally." Nope. Apparently the knife is a rubber ducky masquerading as a violent instrument. It can't kill anything, at all. At best I've been able to hurt and scare away one fish. Nothing dies from stabbing no matter how repeated. I got a carnivorous predator stuck on terrain once, and proceeded to shank him for 5 minutes during which time no death nor harvesting of meat occurred. Why is it even called a knife? The only use so far has been to harvest 2 types of coral which are pointless. I now have a cool undersea submersible, a knife that does nothing, and NO SPEARGUN!? How do I have ships and and underwater base, but still not a single viable weapon??? Oh and that submersible got chomped by a giant leviathan type monster, so now thats gone, because I couldn't kill or even hurt it. WHY IS THERE NO SPEARGUN ITS AN UNDERWATER SURVIVAL GAME!!! 6.) Giant merch store advertisement in center of the start menu, about 4x as big as the 'play' button hiding in the corner. SUPER tacky. Next are you gonna hustle us about your new mix cd? I'm really torn with this game. Its one of the most beautiful immersive games I've seen in a long time, and fills a void I haven't felt since Myst. I almost went and bought a second copy today and started researching VR headsets for my scuba diver friend as a gift, but after having some really infuriating problems and realizing how unfriendly the game is for nongamers, I decided against it. Theres no way I could subject my nongamer friend to a game that is unstable with no autosave, almost no explanation for anything, hard to navigate and keep track of everything. If I as a hardcore gamer can't deal with the problems, then I can't imagine your casual gamer putting up with it. I love the potential this game has, but its starting to feel like another No Man's Sky. Hire some competent programmers, put all the mandatory QoL features in the game, fix the save memory leak which is apparently the official excuse for no autosave, ADD ACTUAL COMBAT and maybe I'll give it another shot. Until then I'm going back to more polished games.

Y'know I'm mixed on this. I like DS 1,3, really don't like DS2 and hate Bloodborne. Sekiro seems like a bad fit, but the combat feels really good. It's smooth, responsive, with a fast pace and rewarding quick reactions without turning into a slap the guard button fest. The platforming is great too, the thought that the company that put together the downright atrocious crystal area from DS1 and this game are the same one is shocking. But Sekiro doesn't seem to understand its own strengths. It makes an amazing system for dueling challenging enemies, and in fact emphasizes that idea in its intro cinematic, but fills every map with scads of random enemies that alone are trivial to beat and together seem like they're intended for a very different sort of game (perhaps one where you have a bigger sword). It had some of the best grapple climbing vertical movement anywhere, but slaps invisible walls all over the place so that the player is forced into one or two solutions for each problem. I think these flaws would be forgivable, reducing Sekiro from a great game to perhaps just an uninspired/ill-directed one, but Sekiro's incredibly small health pool leaves no room for design oversights. One stunlock due to an unspotted archer can lead to punishment that feels ill-deserved. At first I thought Sekiro had done a good job of making this sort of thing less punishing, since you can revive and run back to the last idol to restore the resurrection token, but in reality this just doubles the run back time compared to a souls game. It's really much faster to just run back and get your souls then keep going, than it is to lose, revive, run back, rest, run back, keep going. It's not as if money and the skill bar are a huge loss, some of Sekiro's skills are anemic at best, but it's still very frustrating. Another issue is the lack of progression. Yes, not all games need to have clear RPG mechanics, and you get more skills through the skill bar, but that's about it. Bosses drop beads that you can eventually use to become slightly less like wet toilet paper, but bosses already felt rewarding to beat in souls games. The random enemies, however, feel like a complete waste of time in a way that no other soulsborne game can match. Killing them nets you a small amount of money that you can use for...spirit charges? Maybe some vendors eventually? At that rate, why not simplify things and get rid of money, using only drops to give items and having spirit charges drop off enemies? It feels like From just needed something to take away when you die, and money got the short stick. The broad lack of use for what the enemies drop makes traipsing through the world of Sekiro feel fluid, fast paced, and deeply unrewarding. One of those experiences where you, mid-game, realize that playing video games is a waste of time which is a pretty good signal that the pointlessness meter is set a bit too high. But, maybe you become very good at running and overrule every JRPG instinct telling you not to run from random encounters. That would certainly be a way to go about the game, but the bosses are below standard on the From scale. Probably somewhere above DS2 pre-dlc but beneath OG Dark Souls. My mind is specifically drawn to an ogre you meet in the early game's first area, where the enemies are meant to introduce you to the game's mechanics so that you've seen them all and become accustomed. His grab attack has pretty inconsistent windup, sometimes very long, other times near instantaneous, and one time when he used it, he threw me off the cliff to instant death. Now, this is something that happens in DS all the time, but it's never good design, and it's worse in Sekiro because, in this case, Shadows Die Once. That's right, no getting your souls back, no getting your echoes from some dude, your money and exp are gone because From remembered the invisible walls that stopped you from sneak attacking but forgot the ones that stopped a throw. As far as game design goes, this is just lazy, which is a moniker that could befit a bunch of the design choices here. But, finally, we come to the big From question: Does the game punish you permanently for deaths? This is something that From does occasionally, most notably in DS2 with a diminishing health bar restored by finite items, and in Bloodborne by forcing the player to farm blood vials. It's never good and encourages cheesy behavior like quitting the game mid bossfight to avoid losing money/exp, or avoiding fighting bosses until you're incredibly overpowered to avoid losing a finite resource. In this case, Sekiro performs a new cardinal sin that has never been seen in a soulsborne game before: It punishes others for your mistakes. Trying to learn a boss? Bad move, your friends all now have corona and you're a dick. I get that's meant to give the player a sense of mortality and fallibility, but punishing for dying in a "you're a bad person for this" sense is the worst way to do it. You can restore it with a, you guessed it, finite resource, but it's finite so if you're bad at the game (or the game feels like being bad) prepare to feel bad too. Actually, yknow what, tl;dr, game should have been called Sekiro: Shadows Die Once, Prepare to Feel Bad edition.

I have been trying to enjoy this game, but fact of the matter is - I can't. The game is based on a Swedish RPG - yet there's not a single RPG moment in it (a bunch of stats doesn't equate to a RPG). The optmisation or should I say lack there of is abyssmal, I can't even push a solid 60 fps - now thankfully it's a game where it doesn't really matter if you cap it at 50 or play at 144 for instance. The only somewhat fun thing in this game is the combat, but it's not brilliant nor is it overwhelmingly fun it's just... fun, for a while, it does get stale quickly though. The upside to the combat is that it is quite lethal, the downside is that it easily leads to scum-saving - but that is a choice you either do or don't do, so I can't really blame the game for that. More often than not do I find myself taking out enemies that are out of sight from their friends with the use of CC and silenced weapons, which after a while becomes incredibly boring but there's generally no other choice because some enemies do way too much damage, while you do too little. In a sense it reminds me of games like Baldur's Gate or the more contemporary Pillars of Eternity, in the way that the map and each area is set-up, the game would really benefit with a 'zone'-specific map as well though. But each area feels smaller than in the other mentioned games, and has pretty much the same set-up without any real deviations all through out: You traverse an area, collect some scrap and items, you encounter 1-3 groups of enemies with 2-5+ enemies in each group. I've so far not encountered any real deviations to this, with the exception of places where you don't kill the groups of enemies because they're of a too high level (yet). Another downside is the lack of confirming what you want to do, which has lead to numerous mistakes where a character has just ran away instead of switching weapon when I was pressing the 'X' icon, something which has never happened to this extent and I've been playing these types of games since X-Com: Terror from the Deep. My overall feeling about the game is that it is flat and lacks depth. Don't get me wrong, the world is great - but that has nothing to do with the producers as much as it has to do with the Mutant franchise that saw the light of day back in 1984 and dare I say that most of the humour doens't come from Mutant: Year Zero PnP RPG but rather Mutant: Heirs of Doom (anyway, where it comes from is hardly relevant here). And it is fun to once again see a duck in a computer game, haven't seen that since Drakar och Demoner: Själarnas Brunn. A few things that would make me recommend the game would be things like: better optimization, proper RPG elements, more to do in the world other than rinse repeating (Yes I know, the whole concept with the Arks is that outside of the Arks there's no real society) small-ish areas. A larger and more expansive Ark. Creating your own characters. At the end of the day, I'm not saying it's terrible, but it's not really good either and because of that, I can't really recommend it. That said, I'm glad that it got traction, because that means that they (TBL) can (if they want) expand upon it and make a sequal that is actually worth spending time on. And yeah, I've only played 8 hours, I honestly can't bring myself to play more because it's not a game that I feel like finishing.

It's a fun game, the first bit of building your raft and surviving the elements is a great survival experience for sure. But remember, this is early access, so unless you are ready to deal with the "idk when the next update is" stuff I wouldn't recommend buying in now. The game is horribly optimized, single player, seems to be okay until your raft gets too big. Once you try to play survival multiplayer the game becomes unplayable for the host. Everyone else connected to the game will get great performance, but the host will dip down to 5 fps, so the only people enjoying themselves is everyone except the host. There is no end game content. They can say the oil rig/large island is end game, but all you do is land, search some shit, spam your spear at things, and go from there. Beyond surviving and expanding your raft, there's no goal, there's no point. Sure yes, I find it quite relaxing to just hang out on my raft sometimes, but if I'm hungry for "something to do", I'm left with nothing to do other than find the next oil rig, which will be identical to the first, second, and tenth one you have seen. All in all, it has a lot of potential, but I feel the word "potential" is overused with these early access games. A lot of these games sell you on an idea and hope people buy in "early" to show their commitment to the game. Most of these ideas "have potential", Raft's developers do a good job at keeping contact with the community, and they seem like they have good intentions, I don't want to shit on them and prance around saying "ADD THIS ADD THAT DEVELOPERS ARENT DOING ANYTHING AHH ABANDONWARE" but I feel they need to start adding items, new islands, new landmarks, and new things to find, soon, because otherwise, it's starting to feel like a dead game and a "take it as it is" and like there won't be any improvements.

Mkay then. I'm not even going to F around with any kind of flowery language. This game is hard. You're going to lose. A lot. Even on the "Easy" settings. You'll die. You'll start picking up momentum, then the zombies will bum rush your colony, get into your houses, start snatching up your people. Game over save file deleted GFYS try again. Get used to this chain of events. No manual saves here. You can "save and quit" and the game will autosave occasionally but that's it. One slot. You either run with the map, or you restart like a filthy coward. That being said, this game is pretty damned good. Very playable for an early release title. The minimal resource management and unit controls are a bit controversial depends on how micro you like your RTS. I personally like the fact that this game doesn't get bogged down with elements such as resource depletion, supply lines, multiple unique abilities for each unit etc... You're not constantly pecking away with repetitive button combinations in order to eek out every last special attack from every unit. You're not basing your decisions on a some stupid resource tile running dry. You can take the time to make good moves, and you'll need to take the time if you don't fancy a zombie gangbang. TAB is what I would call "a pure strategy game" It's more about conscientous base building, perimeter defense, and overall "big picture" positioning than anything else. You can pause the game any time you want, build some stuff, change your mind, delete everything, build it again... You aren't penalized for doing this in pause mode. You can do a mockup of your next expansion, figure out where your new perimeter is going to be without wasting time and resources in getting everything placed just right. It's great. *PRO TIP* Space bar = Pause. Use it whenever possible. In fact, get used to living with your hand on the space bar. TLDR; A challenging RTS with minimal resource management. Play it if you want to find out how much you suck at games. Caveats: - The map rolls are awful some times. You'll get a few that are just unplayable. No building room, no resources. No fun. - There are quite a few unit glitches to work out. The pathfinding is unreliable. Units will some times get stuck on buildings, terain. They can also fail to detect/refuse to enage targets on certain parts of the map. Not persistent, but all potentially game changing.

18 Hours: Quite fun, but it's really just memorization and rolling to evade. Being light with a dagger or heavy with a shield are easy strategies. Had to break momentum and farm souls in the second location to proceed. 50 Hours: I love it. It's fun once you've learned how the majority of systems and the designs work. Getting there is not an easy task. I take long breaks between long sessions, roughly one area fully explored at a time. There's lots of room for character exploration but I won't be switching away from pyro/balanced or replaying the game. And, it's still just spamming some buttons. That's not to detract from the first sentence; I love this game. The environments and creatures are beautiful. The humor and unique levels keep me going. One complaint is the toxic mix of multiplayer. There should be a separation between "I'm here for hardcore online and end game min/maxing" and "I'm just trying to play the fu***** game and stay immersed". There's lots of players who will sit in one area for hours farming online, with perfected ambush and spam, with host advantage. It's so off-putting. When I run into another person who connected while playing their single player story it feels great, win or lose. I remain immersed but with a breath of fresh air. Another is the difficulty design. I chose DS3 as my first From Software game because I suspected the rest were overhyped. To an extent I was correct. It's rolling and R1 spam as mentioned earlier; epic combat system. And, a lot of enemies are made deliberately frustrating for the sake of "difficulty" instead of testing a player's skills. For example, delaying the last move in an enemy combo to an unnatural 4 breaths when the pacing was already 1-2-1-2. Or another example: adding 5 more rapid attacks to a familiar enemy combo. It ruins the pace of the battle and comes off extremely cheap. I suspect the rest of the games are worse.

(Apoligies if the review's a bit all over the place, I typed this in a pretty well-justified burst of rage) I wish I could recommend Doom Eternal, I really do, but I just can't. Especially with the new anti-cheat system (more on that later). To start off, let me just say that I've been anticipating this game's release since its announcement at E3 2018, although I didn't purchase it until about one month after release. I played this game right after coming hot off of the heels of Doom 2016 which I had beaten shortly before playing Eternal, but there's something about Eternal that just feels... off. Doom 2016 is more linear than Eternal, but it gives you the choice of which gun you use to kill your enemy since there are no specific weaknesses that the demons have against your arsenal. Doom Eternal may have more open-ended level design, but it forces you to switch between weapons constantly to even stand a chance against demons in battle. Eternal also places too much emphasis on its story (which isn't even that good if you ask me), whereas Doom 2016 had a story which, while interesting, isn't the focus of the game. 2016 places a lot of emphasis on getting you into the action and keeping the flow going, and explaining the story later. And even when you're following the story in 2016, it doesn't feel out of place. 2016's approach to storytelling was generally more immersive than Eternal as well, keeping you in first-person at all times, even during cutscenes, making you feel like YOU are the unstoppable force that strikes fear into the demons, but in Eternal most cutscenes are in third-person which didn't make me feel like I was the slayer, but merely guiding him on his quest to save humankind. And whereas Doom 2016 felt like a consistent experience, with balanced demon battles and focused level design, Doom Eternal feels like a clusterfuck of ideas, with locations that sound cool in concept, but vary a bit too much from each other and don't feel consistent when played back-to-back if you ask me. But all that? That's not even the worst part. Bethesda decided to implement an anti-cheat system into the game which not only causes performance problems in both multiplayer AND single-player, but it also has the highest priorities on your operating system and could thus lead to your system getting compromised by hackers if a security flaw is ever discovered in the anti-cheat. All-in-all, it's a good game, but Bethesda just HAD to fuck it up one way or another.

Pair this with an increasing number of audaciously placed shooting traps which are guaranteed to shoot in a way that makes you tumble all over the place, and you get what must be the most fiddly and annoying platforming I have seen in quite a while. Walljumping helps sometimes, but can leave you cascading down a way too long elevator gauntlet as you try to catch yourself and just shoot away from all the clusters of tiny moving platforms you are trying to connect with. Especially the 9th level, as far as I got so far, is about as fun for me as trying to balance a needle on top of a matchstick. The huge stretches of constantly bullet-overloaded tiny patches of ground you have to cross really just become boring, tedious and so unfun that I simply quit even with one life remaining on easy, just cause there are also no stage checkpoints. So yeah, if you loved megaman, but hated the magic appearing platform segments and the moving track bits... don't get this game. Cause it went overboard with all that cluttered mess, which really drags the whole experience down.

I like this game a lot. I love that there's two gameplay perspectives which really helps keep the game fresh. When I'm ready for a challenge I like to play killer, but if I'm in a more lackadaisical mood I'll play survivor, and in either case I get to play more DBD, which has been a great way to pass the time. I'll leave a warning that the learning curve is steep. And you reach a certain ceiling where it gets really hard to get much better without a vast library of perks, namely for killers. The game comes with 5 or so, I think - and by now there's something like 17 killers, all of them with 3 unique perks. So you have to unlock those perks, and then level up a certain killer enough times to get that perk on just that one killer, but then do that for any killers you want that perk for. It doesn't have to be a complete barrier for entry, you can still do quite well with most of the killers with their base perks. Similarly, survivor gameplay is so similar between matches that the perks help, but it isn't like you aren't able to play the game if you don't have "the meta" unlocked on a certain character. But that is a barrier to entry, when a lot of your peers have been playing this game for three years now, and meanwhile you're new to the game, wishing you could be like them. So just go into it knowing that there's a decent grind if you want to get "up there". But outside of that, in general gameplay and such - it's a blast. Killing is a challenge but rewarding, surviving can also be a challenge, and is rewarding. If you have friends to play with the game gets considerably more fun. There's loads of guides and streamers to help get a hang of the game if you're having a hard time of getting started. And once you do get generally started, and get the grasp of the game and start lasting a little longer per chase, it really does get just a lot of fun.

If you haven't picked up a copy of Rome 2, then your missing out! Put the rough launch aside, the game has come a long way, Creative Assembly have done a great job with releasing patches and the game is in a fully playable state. I would reccomend you check if your computer can run it though, as it's quite power hungry, especially to play on full settings. With a good rig, you won't be seeing these problems that other users report, I myself have never had any issue running the game. Technicals aside. Building and managing has undergone a huge transformation from previous total war games, making it both more efficient but at the same time more tactical, as you now simply don't click on a city and "build build build" everything you possibly could, making far more thought go into the whole process. At the same time they've introduced provinces, so building and getting a clear overview of your empire has never been easier. There are some great additional features to this game aswell, such as a cinematic camera, which places you right into the action, which never looked better as now armies are far more diverse rather than clone like, looks even better with the blood and gore pack!. Army stances on the campaign is also another big game changer. I could go on, but it would ruin the fun! Grab a copy if you enjoyed previous total war games, plenty of mods on the workshop to tailor the games' finepoints also if you are into customising more to suit your preferred playstyle. If your new to total war, then this game will deffinatly ease you into it, with the tutorial campaing. Good luck and happy conquering!

I played this game both before its enhanced edition update came out and after. Most of its horrid encounter design has been washed away. No more instant murder swarms of regular spiders, no more 36 STR wererat rogues. The combat in this game has been so revamped and redesigned it is virtually indistinguishable from a heavily combat heavy tabletop session (excepting the CRPG standard of many, many more enemies to fill out areas that would otherwise be empty). But now with a half decent party you can progress through the game without abusive and boring levels of SaveScum. The story was not bad, not super deep or incredibly compelling, but companion quests can be fun, and the voice acting is solid. Some moments are a lot more compelling than others. Secret ending is probably the best, but there are a large variety of endings for different storylines. The kingdom Manegment is actually OK to good now. The only times it get overloaded is right before the end of the game, with 20+ event cards. But your supposed to just go deal with the main plot at that point, so it mirrors the P&P Adventure Module. Wide assortment of items, lots of different companion combinations, can make your own custom companions (best done early rather than latter for gold cost). All in all I would strongly suggest you buy this game.
